text: The heart is the {{c1::first}} functional organ to develop in the embryo.
extraInfo: Beats spontaneously by week 4.

text: The heart begins to beat spontaneously at week {{c1::4}} of development.
extraInfo: Visible on ultrasound at about 6 weeks.

text: Cardiac looping begins at week {{c1::4}} and establishes {{c2::left-right}} asymmetry.
extraInfo: Requires cilia and dynein.

text: A defect in {{c1::dynein}} can lead to dextrocardia, often seen in {{c2::Kartagener}} syndrome.
extraInfo: Also known as primary ciliary dyskinesia.

text: The {{c1::truncus arteriosus}} gives rise to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The smooth parts (outflow tract) of the left and right ventricles are derived from the {{c1::bulbus cordis}}.
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The trabeculated parts of the left and right ventricles are derived from the {{c1::primitive ventricle}}.
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The trabeculated parts of the left and right atria are derived from the {{c1::primitive atrium}}.
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The left horn of the sinus venosus gives rise to the {{c1::coronary sinus}}.
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The right horn of the sinus venosus gives rise to the {{c1::smooth part of the right atrium}} (sinus venarum).
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The {{c1::endocardial cushions}} contribute to the atrial septum, membranous interventricular septum, and AV/semilunar valves.
extraInfo: Vital for septation.

text: The {{c1::right common cardinal vein}} and right anterior cardinal vein give rise to the superior vena cava.
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The {{c1::septum primum}} grows toward the endocardial cushions, initially narrowing the foramen primum.
extraInfo: Part of atrial septation.

text: The {{c1::foramen secundum}} forms in the septum primum before the foramen primum closes.
extraInfo: Prevents interruption of right-to-left shunt.

text: The {{c1::foramen ovale}} is an opening in the septum secundum.
extraInfo: Functions as a one-way valve in utero.

text: Increased {{c1::left atrial pressure}} after birth causes the foramen ovale to close.
extraInfo: Lungs expand, decreasing pulmonary resistance.

text: A {{c1::Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO)}} is caused by the failure of the septum primum and septum secundum to {{c2::fuse}} after birth.
extraInfo: Can lead to paradoxical emboli.

text: The muscular interventricular septum is formed by the {{c1::upward}} growth of the floor of the ventricle.
extraInfo: Forms most of the septum.

text: The {{c1::membranous}} interventricular septum is the most common site for a VSD.
extraInfo: Formed by fusion of aorticopulmonary septum and endocardial cushions.

text: The aorticopulmonary septum is formed by {{c1::neural crest}} cells.
extraInfo: These cells migrate to the truncal and bulbar ridges.

text: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to {{c1::spiral}} results in Transposition of the Great Vessels.
extraInfo: Associated with maternal diabetes.

text: Skewed development of the aorticopulmonary septum leads to {{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}}.
extraInfo: Characterized by VSD, overriding aorta, RVH, and pulmonary stenosis.

text: Partial development of the aorticopulmonary septum results in {{c1::Persistent truncus arteriosus}}.
extraInfo: One large vessel leaving the heart.

text: The valve of the foramen ovale is formed by the {{c1::septum primum}}.
extraInfo: The septum secundum provides the structural rim.

text: The smooth part of the left atrium is formed by the incorporation of the {{c1::primitive pulmonary vein}}.
extraInfo: Embryonic derivative.

text: The heart tube begins forming from {{c1::mesoderm}} during the 3rd week of gestation.
extraInfo: Embryonic origin.

text: {{c1::Dextrocardia}} occurs when the heart tube loops to the {{c2::left}} instead of the right.
extraInfo: Seen in Kartagener syndrome.

text: The {{c1::aorticopulmonary septum}} divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
extraInfo: Requires neural crest migration.

text: Conotruncal abnormalities like Tetralogy of Fallot are often associated with {{c1::DiGeorge}} syndrome.
extraInfo: Failure of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.

text: {{c1::Neural crest}} cells migrate to the truncus arteriosus and bulbus cordis to contribute to outflow tract formation.
extraInfo: Failure of this migration leads to conotruncal abnormalities like Tetralogy of Fallot or Transposition of the Great Vessels.

text: The {{c1::aorticopulmonary septum}} divides the truncus arteriosus into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
extraInfo: This septum must spiral 180 degrees during development.

text: The aorticopulmonary septum is formed by the spiraling and fusion of the {{c1::truncal}} and {{c2::bulbar}} ridges.
extraInfo: Neural crest cells are the primary cell type driving this process.

text: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to {{c1::spiral}} results in Transposition of the Great Vessels.
extraInfo: This results in two independent, parallel circuits.

text: {{c1::Persistent truncus arteriosus}} is caused by a partial or total failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form.
extraInfo: This condition is always accompanied by a VSD.

text: Tetralogy of Fallot is caused by the {{c1::anterosuperior}} displacement of the {{c2::infundibular (conotruncal)}} septum.
extraInfo: The displacement leads to pulmonary stenosis and an overriding aorta.

text: Neural crest cells migrate through the {{c1::pharyngeal (branchial) arches}} to reach the outflow tract.
extraInfo: Disruption of this pathway often affects both the heart and craniofacial structures.

text: {{c1::DiGeorge}} syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) is strongly associated with neural crest cell migration failure and conotruncal defects.
extraInfo: Classic heart defects include truncus arteriosus and interrupted aortic arch.

text: The truncus arteriosus gives rise to the {{c1::ascending aorta}} and the {{c2::pulmonary trunk}}.
extraInfo: The division is mediated by the AP septum.

text: The smooth part of the right ventricle (conus arteriosus) is derived from the {{c1::bulbus cordis}}.
extraInfo: The bulbus cordis also forms the smooth part of the left ventricle.

text: The smooth part of the left ventricle (aortic vestibule) is derived from the {{c1::bulbus cordis}}.
extraInfo: The proximal 1/3 of the bulbus cordis forms the ventricles; the midportion (conus cordis) forms the outflow tracts.

text: The {{c1::spiral}} nature of the aorticopulmonary septum ensures the aorta connects to the left ventricle.
extraInfo: If it fails to spiral, the aorta connects to the right ventricle (TGA).

text: The membranous portion of the interventricular septum requires fusion of the muscular septum, endocardial cushions, and the {{c1::aorticopulmonary}} septum.
extraInfo: This is the most common site for ventricular septal defects (VSDs).

text: The mnemonic {{c1::CATCH-22}} describes the features of DiGeorge syndrome, where C stands for Cardiac defects (conotruncal).
extraInfo: CATCH: Cardiac, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia.

text: Transposition of the Great Vessels is a common cardiac finding in infants of {{c1::diabetic}} mothers.
extraInfo: It requires a shunt (PDA, VSD, or PFO) for survival after birth.

text: {{c1::Endocardial cushions}} in the conotruncal region receive neural crest cells to assist in dividing the outflow tract.
extraInfo: These are distinct from the AV endocardial cushions.

text: A defect in the {{c1::neural crest}} cells can result in both a Persistent Truncus Arteriosus and a {{c2::Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)}}.
extraInfo: The AP septum normally contributes to the closure of the IV foramen.

text: The {{c1::conus cordis}} is the portion of the bulbus cordis that specifically forms the outflow tracts of both ventricles.
extraInfo: It is the middle segment of the bulbus cordis.

text: In Tetralogy of Fallot, the overriding aorta is a result of the {{c1::malalignment}} of the aorticopulmonary septum.
extraInfo: The aorta sits above the VSD.

text: The aorticopulmonary septum begins to form at the {{c1::distal}} end of the truncus arteriosus and grows {{c2::proximally}} toward the ventricles.
extraInfo: The growth follows a spiral path.

text: In {{c1::Tricuspid atresia}}, the absence of a tricuspid valve is often associated with an atrial septal defect and a {{c2::VSD}}.
extraInfo: While not strictly a conotruncal defect, it often involves associated outflow abnormalities.

text: The 'boot-shaped' heart on X-ray in Tetralogy of Fallot is due to {{c1::Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH)}}.
extraInfo: The RVH is a response to the pulmonary stenosis.

text: {{c1::Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)}} is a critical process for neural crest cells before they begin migration to the heart.
extraInfo: This allows them to detach from the neural tube.

text: The {{c1::fourth}} pharyngeal arch artery contributes to the aortic arch on the left and the subclavian artery on the right.
extraInfo: Neural crest cells also populate these arch arteries.

text: The {{c1::sixth}} pharyngeal arch artery gives rise to the pulmonary arteries and the ductus arteriosus.
extraInfo: The AP septum divides the outflow into these 6th arch derivatives.

text: A 'string of pearls' or 'egg on a string' appearance on X-ray is characteristic of {{c1::Transposition of the Great Vessels}}.
extraInfo: Due to a narrowed mediastinum from the parallel arrangement of the vessels.

text: The most important prognostic factor in Tetralogy of Fallot is the severity of {{c1::pulmonary infundibular stenosis}}.
extraInfo: This determines the degree of right-to-left shunting and cyanosis.

text: The {{c1::Hox}} gene family and {{c2::TBX1}} are critical for regulated neural crest migration to the outflow tract.
extraInfo: TBX1 mutations are specifically linked to the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

text: Complete closure of the interventricular septum occurs at approximately {{c1::8}} weeks of gestation.
extraInfo: This coincides with the completion of the AP septum fusion.

text: Atrial septation begins with the growth of the {{c1::septum primum}} toward the {{c2::endocardial cushions}}.
extraInfo: The septum primum initially forms the roof of the common atrium.

text: The opening between the free edge of the septum primum and the endocardial cushions is the {{c1::foramen primum}}.
extraInfo: This foramen is eventually obliterated as the septum primum fuses with the cushions.

text: Before the foramen primum closes, programmed cell death in the upper septum primum creates the {{c1::foramen secundum}}.
extraInfo: This ensures continuous right-to-left shunting during fetal development.

text: The {{c1::septum secundum}} grows to the right of the septum primum and covers the foramen secundum.
extraInfo: It is a thicker, more muscular structure than the septum primum.

text: The permanent opening in the septum secundum is called the {{c1::foramen ovale}}.
extraInfo: The remaining part of the septum primum acts as a one-way valve for this opening.

text: The {{c1::septum primum}} forms the valve of the foramen ovale.
extraInfo: It allows blood to flow from the right atrium to the left atrium but prevents backflow.

text: Closure of the foramen ovale after birth is triggered by {{c1::increased}} left atrial pressure and {{c2::decreased}} right atrial pressure.
extraInfo: This occurs when the lungs expand and pulmonary vascular resistance drops.

text: Failure of the septum primum and septum secundum to fuse after birth results in a {{c1::patent foramen ovale (PFO)}}.
extraInfo: PFOs are found in approximately 25% of the adult population.

text: The ventricular septum is composed of a thick {{c1::muscular}} part and a thin {{c2::membranous}} part.
extraInfo: Septation usually completes by the end of the 7th week.

text: The {{c1::muscular}} interventricular septum grows upward from the floor of the common ventricle.
extraInfo: It does not completely reach the endocardial cushions on its own.

text: The {{c1::interventricular foramen}} is the temporary opening between the muscular septum and the endocardial cushions.
extraInfo: It is later closed by the membranous septum.

text: The membranous interventricular septum is formed by the fusion of the {{c1::endocardial cushions}} and the aorticopulmonary septum.
extraInfo: The AP septum must spiral to align correctly with the ventricular septum.

text: The most common site of a ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the {{c1::membranous}} septum.
extraInfo: Membranous VSDs are more common than muscular VSDs.

text: The {{c1::aorticopulmonary septum}} divides the truncus arteriosus and bulbus cordis into the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
extraInfo: This septum undergoes a 180-degree spiral during development.

text: Formation of the aorticopulmonary septum requires the migration of {{c1::neural crest}} cells.
extraInfo: Neural crest cell defects can lead to Conotruncal heart defects like Tetralogy of Fallot.

text: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral results in {{c1::transposition of the great vessels}}.
extraInfo: This results in the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle.

text: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to develop results in {{c1::persistent truncus arteriosus}}.
extraInfo: This is characterized by a single large vessel receiving blood from both ventricles.

text: {{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}} is caused by the anterior and superior displacement of the infundibular septum.
extraInfo: This leads to pulmonary stenosis, RV hypertrophy, overriding aorta, and VSD.

text: The {{c1::endocardial cushions}} are essential for the formation of the atrial septum, ventricular septum, and AV valves.
extraInfo: Defects here are common in Trisomy 21.

text: {{c1::Atrioventricular (AV) canal}} defects are the most common cardiac anomaly in patients with Down syndrome.
extraInfo: This involves a combination of ASD, VSD, and common AV valves.

text: A patent foramen ovale can allow a venous thrombus to enter systemic circulation, known as a {{c1::paradoxical embolus}}.
extraInfo: This can manifest as a stroke in a patient with deep vein thrombosis.

text: The septum secundum is located to the {{c1::right}} of the septum primum.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: Secundum is Second (to the right).

text: In fetal life, the high pressure in the {{c1::right atrium}} keeps the foramen ovale open.
extraInfo: Right atrial pressure is high due to high pulmonary vascular resistance.

text: {{c1::Muscular}} VSDs are often multiple and are colloquially referred to as 'Swiss cheese' defects.
extraInfo: These are caused by excessive cavitation of the myocardial wall.

text: Small membranous VSDs often {{c1::close spontaneously}} during the first year of life.
extraInfo: Management is usually conservative if the patient is asymptomatic.

text: A large VSD can lead to a left-to-right shunt which may eventually reverse, a condition called {{c1::Eisenmenger syndrome}}.
extraInfo: Reversal occurs when pulmonary hypertension causes right-sided pressure to exceed left-sided pressure.

text: The smooth parts of the left and right ventricles (outflow tracts) originate from the {{c1::bulbus cordis}}.
extraInfo: Specifically, the conus arteriosus and the aortic vestibule.

text: The {{c1::foramen primum}} is located between the septum primum and the endocardial cushions.
extraInfo: Its failure to close results in an ostium primum ASD.

text: The septum secundum grows {{c1::inferiorly}} from the roof of the atrium.
extraInfo: It stops short of the cushions, leaving the foramen ovale.

text: Aortic and pulmonary valves are derived from the {{c1::endocardial cushions}} of the outflow tract.
extraInfo: These valves are also known as semilunar valves.

text: Mitral and tricuspid valves are derived from the {{c1::endocardial cushions}} of the AV canal.
extraInfo: These valves are also known as atrioventricular valves.

text: The aortic valve is derived from the embryological structure known as the {{c1::truncus arteriosus}}.
extraInfo: The truncus arteriosus is partitioned by the conotruncal septum.

text: The pulmonary valve is derived from the embryological structure known as the {{c1::truncus arteriosus}}.
extraInfo: The truncus arteriosus gives rise to both great arteries and their respective semilunar valves.

text: {{c1::Neural crest}} cells contribute to the formation of the aortic and pulmonary valves.
extraInfo: Migration of these cells is essential for conotruncal septation.

text: The mitral and tricuspid valves are formed from the fusion of the {{c1::superior}} and {{c1::inferior}} endocardial cushions.
extraInfo: Failure of this process results in AV canal defects, common in Down syndrome.

text: Abnormalities in {{c1::neural crest}} cell migration often result in outflow tract valve defects and conotruncal abnormalities.
extraInfo: Examples include Tetralogy of Fallot and Persistent Truncus Arteriosus.

text: The aortic valve normally possesses {{c1::three}} cusps.
extraInfo: These are the left, right, and posterior (non-coronary) cusps.

text: The most common congenital cardiac valve abnormality is a {{c1::bicuspid aortic valve}}.
extraInfo: Affects approximately 1-2% of the population.

text: Bicuspid aortic valve is associated with an increased risk of early-onset {{c1::aortic stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Calcification typically occurs earlier than in a normal tri-leaflet valve.

text: Bicuspid aortic valve is frequently associated with {{c1::Turner}} syndrome (45,XO).
extraInfo: Turner syndrome patients should be screened with echocardiography.

text: Bicuspid aortic valve is commonly associated with {{c1::coarctation}} of the aorta.
extraInfo: This is a narrowing of the aorta typically distal to the left subclavian artery.

text: The tricuspid valve separates the {{c1::right atrium}} and the {{c1::right ventricle}}.
extraInfo: It is an AV valve derived from endocardial cushions.

text: The mitral valve separates the {{c1::left atrium}} and the {{c1::left ventricle}}.
extraInfo: It is the only heart valve with only two leaflets normally.

text: Ebstein anomaly is characterized by the {{c1::atrialization}} of the right ventricle.
extraInfo: The right ventricle becomes small and the right atrium becomes massive.

text: Ebstein anomaly is often associated with maternal {{c1::lithium}} use during pregnancy.
extraInfo: This is considered a classic teratogenic effect.

text: Ebstein anomaly involves the apical displacement of the {{c1::tricuspid}} valve leaflets.
extraInfo: The valve is moved downward into the right ventricle.

text: Endocardial cushions are formed via {{c1::epithelial-mesenchymal transition}} (EMT).
extraInfo: This process is vital for the formation of the septa and valves.

text: Development of the outflow tract requires the migration of {{c1::neural crest}} cells through the pharyngeal arches.
extraInfo: This link explains why some craniofacial defects occur with heart defects (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome).

text: Valvular {{c1::stenosis}} refers to the narrowing of the valve orifice, obstructing forward flow.
extraInfo: Can be congenital or acquired (e.g., rheumatic heart disease).

text: Valvular {{c1::regurgitation}} refers to the backflow of blood through a valve that does not close properly.
extraInfo: Also known as valvular insufficiency.

text: The {{c1::conotruncal}} septum divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
extraInfo: It must spiral 180 degrees during development.

text: Failure of the conotruncal septum to spiral results in {{c1::transposition of the great vessels}}.
extraInfo: The aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary trunk from the LV.

text: The mitral valve is also known as the {{c1::bicuspid}} valve because it has two leaflets.
extraInfo: Not to be confused with a 'bicuspid aortic valve' which is a pathology.

text: During heart development, the AV canal is partitioned by the growth of {{c1::endocardial cushions}}.
extraInfo: These cushions eventually thin out to form the chordae tendineae and valve leaflets.

text: The semilunar valves are the {{c1::aortic}} and {{c1::pulmonary}} valves.
extraInfo: They lack chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.

text: The atrioventricular valves are the {{c1::mitral}} and {{c1::tricuspid}} valves.
extraInfo: They are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles.

text: Defects in neural crest cell migration are a primary cause of {{c1::conotruncal}} heart defects.
extraInfo: This includes conditions like Transposition of Great Vessels and Tetralogy of Fallot.

text: Mature valve leaflets are primarily composed of {{c1::connective tissue}} covered by a layer of endothelium.
extraInfo: The three layers are the fibrosa, spongiosa, and ventricularis/atrialis.

text: The {{c1::adenohypophysis}} (anterior pituitary) is derived from surface ectoderm via Rathke pouch.
extraInfo: Surface ectoderm also gives rise to the lens of the eye and the epidermis.

text: The {{c1::neurohypophysis}} (posterior pituitary) is derived from neuroectoderm.
extraInfo: The neurohypophysis is an extension of the hypothalamus.

text: The {{c1::adrenal medulla}} is derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: Neural crest cells are often referred to as the 'fourth germ layer'.

text: The {{c1::adrenal cortex}} is derived from mesoderm.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: Mesoderm = Muscle, Meat, Middler (Cortex).

text: The {{c1::nucleus pulposus}} of the intervertebral disc is the postnatal remnant of the notochord.
extraInfo: The notochord also induces the overlying ectoderm to differentiate into neuroectoderm.

text: The {{c1::lens}} of the eye and the olfactory epithelium are derived from surface ectoderm.
extraInfo: Surface ectoderm derivatives often involve external-facing structures or glands secreting 'outward'.

text: The {{c1::retina}} and the optic nerve are derived from neuroectoderm.
extraInfo: The CNS, including the brain and spinal cord, is derived from neuroectoderm.

text: {{c1::Melanocytes}} are derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: Defects in neural crest migration can lead to conditions like Waardenburg syndrome.

text: The epithelial lining of the GI tract, liver, and pancreas are derived from {{c1::endoderm}}.
extraInfo: Endoderm forms the 'internal' linings of the respiratory and digestive tracts.

text: Thyroid {{c1::follicular cells}} are derived from endoderm.
extraInfo: The thyroid gland starts at the base of the tongue and descends to the neck.

text: Thyroid {{c1::parafollicular (C) cells}} are derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: These cells secrete calcitonin and are associated with Medullary Thyroid Cancer.

text: The {{c1::spleen}} is derived from mesoderm (specifically dorsal mesogastrium).
extraInfo: Unique because it is an intraperitoneal organ supplied by the foregut artery (celiac) but is NOT endodermally derived.

text: The {{c1::kidneys}} and ureters are derived from mesoderm.
extraInfo: Specifically the intermediate mesoderm.

text: The {{c1::parotid}} gland is derived from surface ectoderm.
extraInfo: Conversely, the submandibular and sublingual glands are derived from endoderm.

text: {{c1::Odontoblasts}} (which produce dentin) are derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: Enamel, however, is derived from surface ectoderm.

text: The epithelial lining of the {{c1::bladder}} and urethra is derived from endoderm.
extraInfo: Most of the urogenital system is mesodermal, but the lining of the bladder is endodermal.

text: The heart, blood vessels, and {{c1::lymphatics}} are derived from mesoderm.
extraInfo: Mesoderm = Middle/Muscle/Marrow/Myocardium.

text: {{c1::Schwann cells}} are derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: They provide myelination for the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS).

text: Oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and ependymal cells are derived from {{c1::neuroectoderm}}.
extraInfo: These are the glial cells of the Central Nervous System (CNS).

text: {{c1::Microglia}} are the only CNS glial cells derived from mesoderm.
extraInfo: They are part of the monocyte/macrophage lineage.

text: The {{c1::pia and arachnoid}} mater (leptomeninges) are derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: Contrast this with the Dura mater.

text: The {{c1::dura mater}} is derived from mesoderm.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: 'D'ura is for 'D'erived from mesoderm.

text: Mammary glands and {{c1::sweat}} glands are derived from surface ectoderm.
extraInfo: Includes sebaceous glands and the epidermis.

text: The {{c1::aorticopulmonary septum}} is derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: Failure of neural crest migration leads to Transposition of Great Vessels or Tetralogy of Fallot.

text: The {{c1::dermis}} of the skin is derived from mesoderm.
extraInfo: The epidermis (outer layer) is surface ectoderm, while the dermis (inner layer) is mesoderm.

text: The epithelial lining of the {{c1::auditory tube}} and middle ear cavity is derived from endoderm.
extraInfo: These arise specifically from the 1st pharyngeal pouch.

text: The bones of the {{c1::face}} and the skull vault are primarily derived from neural crest cells.
extraInfo: This is why craniofacial abnormalities are common in 'neurocristopathies'.

text: All {{c1::muscle}} types (skeletal, smooth, cardiac) are derived from mesoderm.
extraInfo: Skeletal muscle comes from the myotome of the somites.

text: The anal canal {{c1::below}} the pectinate line is derived from surface ectoderm.
extraInfo: Above the pectinate line, the anal canal is derived from endoderm.

text: Blood in the umbilical vein has a PO2 of approximately {{c1::30}} mmHg and is {{c2::80}}% saturated with O2.
extraInfo: This is the highest oxygenated blood in the fetal circulation.

text: The {{c1::ductus venosus}} shunts blood from the umbilical vein to the IVC, bypassing the {{c2::hepatic (liver)}} circulation.
Most of the oxygenated blood reaching the heart via the IVC is diverted through the {{c1::foramen ovale}} and pumped out the aorta to the head and body.
extraInfo: This preferential flow ensures the brain receives the most oxygenated blood.

text: Deoxygenated blood from the SVC is expelled from the RV into the pulmonary artery and then through the {{c1::ductus arteriosus}} to the descending aorta.
extraInfo: The high resistance of fetal lungs prevents blood from entering pulmonary circulation.

text: At birth, the infant's first breath {{c1::decreases}} pulmonary vascular resistance, which {{c2::increases}} left atrial pressure relative to right atrial pressure.
extraInfo: This pressure change leads to the physiological closure of the foramen ovale.

text: The {{c1::foramen ovale}} closes due to increased {{c2::left}} atrial pressure and decreased right atrial pressure after birth.
extraInfo: It becomes the fossa ovalis.

text: {{c1::Indomethacin}} is a drug often used to help close a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).
extraInfo: Indomethacin is a NSAID that inhibits prostaglandins, which are required to keep the DA open.

text: {{c1::Prostaglandins (PGE1 and PGE2)}} function to keep the ductus arteriosus {{c2::open (patent)}}.
extraInfo: KEEPS it open (PGE = kEEp).

text: The umbilical vein becomes the {{c1::ligamentum teres hepatis}} after birth.
extraInfo: It is contained within the falciform ligament.

text: The umbilical arteries become the {{c1::medial}} umbilical ligaments.
extraInfo: Note the spelling: medial (from arteries) vs median (from urachus).

text: The ductus arteriosus becomes the {{c1::ligamentum arteriosum}}.
extraInfo: Closure is triggered by increased O2 and decreased PGE.

text: The ductus venosus becomes the {{c1::ligamentum venosum}}.
The foramen ovale becomes the {{c1::fossa ovalis}}.
The urachus becomes the {{c1::median}} umbilical ligament.
extraInfo: The urachus is a remnant of the allantois.

text: The notochord becomes the {{c1::nucleus pulposus}} of the intervertebral disc.
In the fetus, the shunt through the ductus arteriosus is {{c1::right-to-left}} due to high pulmonary vascular resistance.
The {{c1::allantois}} is the embryologic structure that becomes the urachus.
Closure of the ductus arteriosus is primarily mediated by an increase in {{c1::oxygen (from respiration)}} and a decrease in {{c2::prostaglandins (from placenta removal)}}.
The ductus arteriosus connects the {{c1::pulmonary artery}} to the {{c2::aorta}}.
The highest oxygen saturation in fetal circulation is found in the {{c1::umbilical vein}}.
extraInfo: Saturation is approximately 80%.

text: The umbilical arteries carry {{c1::deoxygenated}} blood from the fetus to the placenta.
The {{c1::foramen ovale}} allows blood to bypass the lungs by shunting from the right atrium to the left atrium.
Indomethacin closes a PDA by inhibiting the enzyme {{c1::cyclooxygenase (COX)}}.
Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) consists of two {{c1::alpha}} and two {{c2::gamma}} chains.
extraInfo: Adult hemoglobin (HbA) consists of two alpha and two beta chains.

text: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) has a higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin (HbA) because it binds {{c1::2,3-BPG}} less avidly.
The remnant of the umbilical vein, the {{c1::ligamentum teres hepatis}}, is found in the {{c2::falciform}} ligament.
{{c1::Alprostadil (PGE1)}} is used clinically to maintain a patent ductus arteriosus in neonates with cyanotic heart disease.
extraInfo: This is necessary for survival in conditions like transposition of the great vessels or tetralogy of Fallot.

text: After birth, systemic vascular resistance {{c1::increases}} due to the loss of the low-resistance {{c2::placenta}}.
The {{c1::medial}} umbilical ligaments are remnants of the umbilical arteries, while the {{c2::median}} umbilical ligament is a remnant of the urachus.
extraInfo: Medial = Arteries (two of them); Median = urachus (one in the midline).

text: The fetal {{c1::umbilical vein}} becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis in the adult.
extraInfo: It is contained within the falciform ligament.

text: The ligamentum teres hepatis is contained within the {{c1::falciform ligament}}.
extraInfo: It is the remnant of the umbilical vein.

text: The fetal {{c1::umbilical arteries}} become the medial umbilical ligaments.
extraInfo: Note the distinction between medial and median.

text: The fetal {{c1::ductus venosus}} becomes the ligamentum venosum.
extraInfo: The ductus venosus shunted blood from the umbilical vein to the IVC, bypassing the liver.

text: The fetal {{c1::ductus arteriosus}} becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
extraInfo: The ductus arteriosus shunted blood from the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta.

text: The fetal {{c1::foramen ovale}} becomes the fossa ovalis.
extraInfo: It shunted blood from the right atrium to the left atrium.

text: The fetal {{c1::allantois/urachus}} becomes the median umbilical ligament.
extraInfo: A patent urachus can cause urine to leak from the umbilicus.

text: The fetal {{c1::notochord}} becomes the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc.
extraInfo: This is the core of the IV disc.

text: The ligamentum arteriosum is a remnant of the {{c1::ductus arteriosus}}.
extraInfo: Found between the left pulmonary artery and the aortic arch.

text: The {{c1::medial}} umbilical ligaments are remnants of the umbilical arteries.
extraInfo: Contrast with the median umbilical ligament (urachus).

text: The {{c1::median}} umbilical ligament is the remnant of the urachus.
extraInfo: Contrast with the medial umbilical ligaments (umbilical arteries).

text: The {{c1::truncus arteriosus}} gives rise to the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk.
extraInfo: Derived from neural crest cell migration.

text: The smooth parts (outflow tracts) of the left and right ventricles are derived from the {{c1::bulbus cordis}}.
extraInfo: Includes the conus arteriosus and aortic vestibule.

text: The trabeculated parts of the left and right atria are derived from the {{c1::primitive atrium}}.
extraInfo: The smooth parts have different origins.

text: The trabeculated parts of the left and right ventricles are derived from the {{c1::primitive ventricle}}.
extraInfo: The smooth parts (outflow) come from the bulbus cordis.

text: The smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) is derived from the {{c1::right horn of sinus venosus}}.
extraInfo: The left horn becomes the coronary sinus.

text: The coronary sinus is derived from the {{c1::left horn of sinus venosus}}.
extraInfo: It receives blood from most of the cardiac veins.

text: The smooth part of the left atrium is derived from the {{c1::primitive pulmonary vein}}.
extraInfo: This is formed by the incorporation of the pulmonary vein.

text: The superior vena cava is derived from the {{c1::right common cardinal}} vein and right anterior cardinal vein.
extraInfo: The cardinal veins are part of the early embryonic venous system.

text: Closure of the ductus arteriosus is stimulated by an increase in {{c1::oxygen}} and a decrease in PGE2.
extraInfo: Occurs shortly after birth when breathing begins.

text: To close a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), you can administer {{c1::indomethacin}}.
extraInfo: An NSAID that inhibits prostaglandin synthesis.

text: To keep a ductus arteriosus open, you can administer {{c1::prostaglandins (PGE1)}}.
extraInfo: Often used in ductal-dependent congenital heart diseases.

text: The {{c1::left recurrent laryngeal}} nerve loops around the ligamentum arteriosum.
extraInfo: Damage to this nerve results in hoarseness.

text: The umbilical vein carries {{c1::oxygenated}} blood from the placenta to the fetus.
extraInfo: Postnatally becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis.

text: The umbilical arteries carry {{c1::deoxygenated}} blood from the fetus to the placenta.
extraInfo: Postnatally become the medial umbilical ligaments.

text: The {{c1::allantois}} connects the fetal bladder to the yolk sac.
extraInfo: The lumen of the allantois becomes the urachus.

text: The {{c1::nucleus pulposus}} is the only remnant of the notochord in adults.
extraInfo: Found in the center of the intervertebral discs.

text: The ligamentum venosum is found on the {{c1::inferior}} surface of the liver.
extraInfo: Remnant of the ductus venosus.

text: The right horn of the sinus venosus becomes the {{c1::sinus venarum}}.
extraInfo: This is the smooth-walled part of the right atrium.

text: The outermost, tough connective tissue layer of the heart is the {{c1::fibrous pericardium}}.
The {{c1::serous pericardium}} is composed of two layers: the parietal and visceral layers.
The {{c1::parietal layer}} of the serous pericardium lines the internal surface of the fibrous pericardium.
The visceral layer of the serous pericardium is also known as the {{c1::epicardium}}.
The {{c1::pericardial cavity}} is the potential space between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium.
Sensory innervation of the fibrous and parietal pericardium is provided by the {{c1::phrenic nerves (C3-C5)}}.
Pericardial pain is often referred to the {{c1::shoulder (C3-C5 dermatomes)}} due to the phrenic nerve's origin.
The {{c1::fibrous pericardium}} prevents acute chambers over-distention and anchors the heart within the mediastinum.
The main arterial supply to the pericardium is the {{c1::pericardiacophrenic artery}}.
The pericardiacophrenic artery is a branch of the {{c1::internal thoracic artery}}.
The {{c1::transverse pericardial sinus}} is a passage located posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
The {{c1::oblique pericardial sinus}} is a blind-ended pocket located posterior to the left atrium.
The visceral layer of the serous pericardium (epicardium) receives autonomic innervation from the {{c1::cardiac plexus}}.
In {{c1::cardiac tamponade}}, fluid accumulation in the pericardial cavity leads to restricted ventricular filling.
The fibrous pericardium is attached inferiorly to the {{c1::central tendon of the diaphragm}}.
Unlike the parietal layer, the {{c1::visceral layer (epicardium)}} is insensitive to pain.
The {{c1::phrenic nerve}} descends between the fibrous pericardium and the mediastinal pleura.
Venous drainage of the pericardium primarily enters the {{c1::pericardiacophrenic veins}} and the azygos system.
The fibrous pericardium is continuous with the {{c1::tunica adventitia}} of the great vessels.
A {{c1::pericardial friction rub}} is a classic physical exam finding heard in patients with acute pericarditis.
The space used by surgeons to ligate the aorta and pulmonary trunk during bypass is the {{c1::transverse pericardial sinus}}.
The visceral layer (epicardium) consists of a single layer of {{c1::mesothelial cells}}.
The base of the pericardial sac is fused to the {{c1::diaphragm}}.
The phrenic nerve contains somatic afferent fibers that transmit {{c1::pain}} signals from the parietal pericardium.
The {{c1::sternopericardial ligaments}} anchor the fibrous pericardium to the posterior surface of the sternum.
{{c1::Pericarditis}} is inflammation of the pericardium that can cause sharp substernal chest pain.
The {{c1::pericardial fluid}} within the cavity acts as a lubricant to reduce friction during heart contractions.
The oblique sinus is bounded superiorly by the {{c1::pulmonary veins}}.
Pain from the pericardium is typically worsened by {{c1::inspiration}} or lying supine (in pericarditis).
The {{c1::left atrium}} is the most posterior part of the heart.
extraInfo: Enlargement of this chamber can compress the esophagus or the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

text: Enlargement of the left atrium can compress the {{c1::esophagus}}, causing {{c2::dysphagia}}.
extraInfo: This is often seen in the context of mitral stenosis.

text: Enlargement of the left atrium can compress the {{c1::left recurrent laryngeal nerve}}, causing hoarseness, a condition known as {{c2::Ortner syndrome}}.
extraInfo: The nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X).

text: The {{c1::right ventricle}} makes up most of the anterior surface of the heart.
extraInfo: It is the chamber most likely to be injured in penetrating chest trauma.

text: The apex of the heart is primarily formed by the {{c1::left ventricle}}.
extraInfo: The apex is typically located in the left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

text: The pericardial cavity lies between the {{c1::parietal}} and {{c2::visceral}} layers of the serous pericardium.
extraInfo: The visceral layer is also known as the epicardium.

text: The {{c1::phrenic nerve}} provides sensory innervation to the fibrous and parietal pericardium.
extraInfo: It originates from spinal levels C3, C4, and C5 ('keep the diaphragm alive').

text: Pericarditis can cause referred pain to the {{c1::shoulder}} due to the innervation of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5).
extraInfo: The dermatomes of the shoulder (supraclavicular nerves) also involve C3 and C4.

text: The {{c1::transverse}} pericardial sinus is located posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, and anterior to the superior vena cava.
extraInfo: It is a useful landmark for surgeons to clamp great vessels during bypass.

text: The {{c1::oblique}} pericardial sinus is a blind-ended pocket posterior to the heart, bounded by the pulmonary veins.
extraInfo: It is formed by the reflection of the serous pericardium onto the heart.

text: The coronary sinus, which receives most of the venous drainage from the heart, empties into the {{c1::right atrium}}.
extraInfo: It is located in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus.

text: The SA node is located at the junction of the {{c1::superior vena cava}} and the {{c2::right atrium}}.
extraInfo: It is the primary pacemaker of the heart.

text: The AV node is located in the {{c1::posteroinferior}} part of the interatrial septum, near the opening of the coronary sinus.
extraInfo: This area is known as the Triangle of Koch.

text: The {{c1::crista terminalis}} is a smooth ridge in the right atrium that separates the smooth-walled sinus venarum from the pectinate muscles.
extraInfo: The SA node is located at the superior end of this ridge.

text: The {{c1::fossa ovalis}} is a remnant of the fetal foramen ovale and is located in the interatrial septum.
extraInfo: A patent foramen ovale (PFO) can lead to paradoxical emboli.

text: Right heart dominance (85% of people) means the {{c1::posterior descending artery (PDA)}} arises from the {{c2::right coronary artery (RCA)}}.
extraInfo: The PDA supplies the posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum.

text: Left heart dominance (8% of people) means the {{c1::posterior descending artery (PDA)}} arises from the {{c2::left circumflex artery (LCX)}}.
extraInfo: In these individuals, the LCX supplies the entire posterior wall of the LV.

text: Co-dominance (7% of people) means the PDA arises from both the {{c1::RCA}} and the {{c2::LCX}}.
extraInfo: Dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the PDA.

text: The {{c1::left anterior descending (LAD)}} artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum and the anterior wall of the left ventricle.
extraInfo: It is the most common site of coronary artery occlusion ('widow-maker').

text: The {{c1::left circumflex (LCX)}} artery supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle.
extraInfo: It travels in the coronary sulcus.

text: The {{c1::right coronary artery (RCA)}} typically supplies the SA node and the AV node.
extraInfo: Occlusion of the RCA can result in bradycardia or heart block.

text: The {{c1::moderator band}} (septomarginal trabecula) is found in the right ventricle and carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.
extraInfo: It helps coordinate the contraction of the papillary muscles to prevent valve regurgitation.

text: The {{c1::mitral}} valve is the only bicuspid valve in the heart.
extraInfo: It is also known as the left atrioventricular valve.

text: The {{c1::ligamentum arteriosum}} is the fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus, connecting the pulmonary trunk to the arch of the aorta.
extraInfo: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the arch of the aorta lateral to this ligament.

text: Coronary blood flow is greatest during {{c1::diastole}}.
extraInfo: During systole, the contracting myocardium compresses the coronary arteries, especially in the left ventricle.

text: The {{c1::phrenic}} nerves pass anterior to the lung roots (hila), while the {{c2::vagus}} nerves pass posterior.
extraInfo: This is a key anatomical relationship in the mediastinum.

text: The {{c1::tricuspid}} valve is located between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
extraInfo: It has three leaflets: anterior, posterior, and septal.

text: The {{c1::descending (thoracic) aorta}} lies posterior to the left atrium.
extraInfo: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) uses this proximity to visualize the heart clearly.

text: The base of the heart is primarily formed by the {{c1::left atrium}}.
extraInfo: It faces posteriorly toward the bodies of vertebrae T6-T9.

text: The most commonly occluded coronary artery is the {{c1::LAD (left anterior descending)}}.
extraInfo: It supplies the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum and the anterior wall of the left ventricle.

text: The LAD supplies the anterior {{c1::2/3}} of the interventricular septum.
extraInfo: The posterior 1/3 is supplied by the PDA.

text: Coronary dominance is determined by the artery that gives rise to the {{c1::PDA (posterior descending artery)}}.
extraInfo: Most people (85%) are right-dominant (PDA arises from RCA).

text: In right-dominant individuals (85%), the PDA arises from the {{c1::RCA}}.
extraInfo: In left-dominant (8%), it arises from the LCX; in codominant (7%), it arises from both.

text: The LCX supplies the {{c1::lateral}} wall of the left ventricle.
extraInfo: Leads I, aVL, V5, and V6 on ECG show changes in this territory.

text: The PDA supplies the {{c1::posteromedial}} papillary muscle.
extraInfo: This muscle is uniquely vulnerable to rupture because it has a single blood supply (usually from the PDA).

text: The anterolateral papillary muscle has a dual blood supply from the {{c1::LAD}} and the {{c2::LCX}}.
extraInfo: This makes it more resistant to ischemia compared to the posteromedial papillary muscle.

text: Coronary blood flow peaks during early {{c1::diastole}}.
extraInfo: During systole, the contracting myocardium compresses the coronary arteries, reducing flow.

text: The SA node is usually supplied by the {{c1::RCA}}.
extraInfo: Occurs in approximately 60% of individuals; RCA also supplies the AV node.

text: The AV node is supplied by the {{c1::PDA}} (branch of the dominant artery).
extraInfo: Occlusion of the RCA in a right-dominant person can result in heart block.

text: An infarct in the RCA/PDA territory would typically present with ST elevation in leads {{c1::II, III, and aVF}}.
extraInfo: This represents an inferior wall MI.

text: The PDA supplies the posterior {{c1::1/3}} of the interventricular septum.
extraInfo: The anterior 2/3 is supplied by the LAD.

text: Left dominance is defined as the PDA arising from the {{c1::LCX (left circumflex artery)}}.
extraInfo: Occurs in about 8% of the population.

text: The RCA arises from the {{c1::right}} aortic sinus.
extraInfo: The LCA arises from the left aortic sinus; the non-coronary sinus is the posterior sinus.

text: Anteroseptal MI (V1-V2) is caused by occlusion of the {{c1::LAD}}.
extraInfo: Often involves the proximal LAD.

text: The right marginal artery supplies the {{c1::right ventricle}}.
extraInfo: It is a branch of the RCA.

text: Posterior wall MI is often due to occlusion of the {{c1::RCA}} (in right-dominant patients).
extraInfo: Can be seen on ECG as ST depressions in V1-V3.

text: Codominance (7%) occurs when the PDA arises from both the {{c1::RCA}} and {{c2::LCX}}.
extraInfo: This is the least common type of coronary dominance.

text: The LAD supplies the {{c1::anterolateral}} papillary muscle alongside the LCX.
extraInfo: This dual supply provides protection against rupture during MI.

text: The RCA supplies the {{c1::right atrium}} and most of the right ventricle.
extraInfo: It also supplies the SA and AV nodes in most people.

text: Anterolateral MI (V5-V6, I, aVL) is typically caused by occlusion of the {{c1::LAD}} or {{c2::LCX}}.
extraInfo: These arteries provide the main supply to the lateral and anterior aspects of the LV.

text: The LCA divides into the {{c1::LAD}} and the {{c2::LCX}}.
extraInfo: The LCA arises from the left aortic sinus.

text: Inferior wall MI is most commonly associated with occlusion of the {{c1::RCA}}.
extraInfo: This is because the RCA usually gives rise to the PDA which supplies the inferior wall.

text: Rupture of the {{c1::posteromedial}} papillary muscle can cause acute mitral regurgitation.
extraInfo: This typically occurs 3-5 days after an inferior MI.

text: The most common location for coronary artery atherosclerosis is the {{c1::LAD}}.
extraInfo: Followed by the RCA and then the LCX.

text: The PDA supplies the {{c1::inferior}} wall of the ventricles.
extraInfo: This area is reflected in ECG leads II, III, and aVF.

text: In a right-dominant heart, the {{c1::AV nodal artery}} arises from the RCA.
extraInfo: Ischemia here can lead to bradycardia or heart block.

text: The coronary sinus receives blood from the coronary veins and empties into the {{c1::right atrium}}.
extraInfo: It sits in the posterior coronary sulcus.

text: The artery that supplies the apex of the heart is the {{c1::LAD}}.
extraInfo: The LAD wraps around the apex in many individuals.

text: Cardiac output (CO) is the product of {{c1::Stroke Volume (SV)}} and {{c2::Heart Rate (HR)}}.
extraInfo: CO = SV x HR. In early exercise, CO is maintained by HR and SV. In late exercise, CO is maintained by HR alone (SV plateaus).

text: The Fick principle states that CO = (Rate of O2 consumption) / ({{c1::Arterial O2 content}} – {{c2::Venous O2 content}}).
extraInfo: This measures the volume of blood required to transport a certain amount of oxygen to the tissues.

text: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) can be calculated as {{c1::1/3}} SBP + {{c2::2/3}} DBP.
extraInfo: At resting heart rates, diastole accounts for two-thirds of the cardiac cycle.

text: Stroke volume (SV) is defined by the formula: SV = {{c1::EDV}} – {{c2::ESV}}.
extraInfo: EDV = End-diastolic volume; ESV = End-systolic volume.

text: Stroke volume is increased by increased {{c1::preload}}, increased {{c2::contractility}}, and decreased {{c3::afterload}}.
extraInfo: SV CAP: Stroke Volume affected by Contractility, Afterload, Preload.

text: Contractility (and SV) increases with sympathetic stimulation via {{c1::β1}} receptors, which increases {{c2::cAMP}} and intracellular calcium.
extraInfo: This leads to increased Ca2+ pump activity in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

text: The drug {{c1::Digoxin}} increases contractility by inhibiting the {{c2::Na+/K+-ATPase}}.
extraInfo: Inhibition leads to increased intracellular Na+, which decreases Na+/Ca2+ exchange, increasing intracellular Ca2+.

text: Cardiac contractility is decreased by {{c1::acidosis}}, {{c2::hypoxia/hypercapnia}}, and {{c3::non-dihydropyridine}} calcium channel blockers.
extraInfo: Verapamil and diltiazem are non-dihydropyridine CCBs that act as negative inotropes.

text: Preload is approximated by the {{c1::ventricular end-diastolic volume}}.
extraInfo: It is the degree of stretch of the cardiac muscle fibers at the end of diastole.

text: Venodilators like nitroglycerin primarily {{c1::decrease}} preload.
extraInfo: By increasing venous capacitance, they reduce the volume of blood returning to the heart.

text: Afterload is approximated by {{c1::Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)}}.
extraInfo: It represents the 'load' the heart must pump against.

text: Vasodilators like hydralazine primarily {{c1::decrease}} afterload.
extraInfo: Arterial vasodilators reduce the resistance the left ventricle must overcome to eject blood.

text: According to Laplace’s law, Wall Tension = ({{c1::Pressure}} × {{c2::Radius}}) / (2 × {{c3::Wall Thickness}}).
extraInfo: The LV compensates for increased afterload by increasing wall thickness (hypertrophy) to reduce wall tension.

text: Ejection fraction (EF) is the ratio of {{c1::Stroke Volume (SV)}} to {{c2::End-Diastolic Volume (EDV)}}.
extraInfo: EF = SV / EDV. It is an index of ventricular contractility.

text: A normal ejection fraction is typically {{c1::≥ 55}}%.
extraInfo: EF is decreased in systolic heart failure but often preserved in diastolic heart failure.

text: Stroke work is the area within the {{c1::pressure-volume loop}}.
extraInfo: It represents the work done by the ventricle during one cardiac cycle.

text: Myocardial oxygen demand is increased by increased {{c1::afterload}}, {{c2::contractility}}, {{c3::heart rate}}, and {{c4::ventricular diameter}}.
extraInfo: Increased diameter increases wall tension via Laplace's law, requiring more O2.

text: Pulse pressure (PP) is defined as {{c1::SBP}} minus {{c2::DBP}}.
extraInfo: PP is proportional to Stroke Volume and inversely proportional to arterial compliance.

text: Pulse pressure is {{c1::decreased}} in states like aortic stenosis, cardiogenic shock, and cardiac tamponade.
extraInfo: Conditions that decrease stroke volume generally decrease pulse pressure.

text: Pulse pressure is {{c1::increased}} in states like aortic regurgitation, hyperthyroidism, and exercise.
extraInfo: Aortic regurgitation causes a high SV and low DBP, leading to a 'wide' pulse pressure.

text: Chronic hypertension causes {{c1::concentric}} left ventricular hypertrophy due to increased afterload.
extraInfo: Sarcomeres are added in parallel to handle the high pressure.

text: Volume overload (e.g., aortic/mitral regurgitation) causes {{c1::eccentric}} hypertrophy.
extraInfo: Sarcomeres are added in series, leading to chamber dilation.

text: During exercise, the increase in CO is initially due to an increase in both {{c1::HR}} and {{c2::SV}}.
extraInfo: As exercise continues to high intensity, HR becomes the primary driver for further CO increases.

text: The Frank-Starling law states that the force of ventricular contraction is proportional to the {{c1::end-diastolic length}} of cardiac muscle fibers.
extraInfo: Increased preload leads to increased stroke volume in a healthy heart.

text: ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce both {{c1::preload}} and {{c2::afterload}}.
extraInfo: They reduce blood volume (preload) and cause vasodilation (afterload).

text: The administration of a {{c1::β1-blocker}} (e.g., metoprolol) will decrease contractility and decrease myocardial oxygen demand.
extraInfo: This is beneficial in managing stable angina and heart failure.

text: {{c1::Sympathetic}} stimulation increases the rate of Ca2+ reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via phosphorylation of {{c2::phospholamban}}.
extraInfo: This results in faster relaxation (lusitropy) and shorter contraction duration.

text: Total peripheral resistance (TPR) is a major determinant of {{c1::afterload}}.
extraInfo: MAP = CO x TPR. High TPR increases the pressure the ventricle must generate.

text: A patient with a failing heart (systolic dysfunction) will have a {{c1::downward/rightward}} shift of the Frank-Starling curve.
extraInfo: For a given preload (EDV), the stroke volume is lower than in a healthy heart.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: The four major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2) are {{c1::contractility}}, {{c2::afterload}}, {{c3::heart rate}}, and {{c4::diameter of ventricle (wall tension)}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: Heart rate, Afterload, Contractility, Diameter (H-A-C-D).

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: According to Laplace's law, wall tension is equal to ({{c1::Pressure}} × {{c2::Radius}}) / (2 × {{c3::Wall thickness}}).
extraInfo: T = (P x r) / (2h)

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Wall tension is {{c1::directly}} proportional to intraventricular pressure.
extraInfo: Higher pressure (afterload) increases the work of the heart.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Wall tension is {{c1::directly}} proportional to the radius of the ventricle.
extraInfo: This is why dilated hearts (e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy) have higher oxygen demand.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Wall tension is {{c1::inversely}} proportional to wall thickness.
extraInfo: This explains why the heart hypertrophies in response to high pressure: to reduce wall tension per unit area.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: In Laplace's law, Pressure (P) is most closely related to {{c1::afterload (systolic BP)}}.
extraInfo: Pressure must overcome afterload to eject blood.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: In Laplace's law, Radius (r) is most closely related to {{c1::preload (EDV)}}.
extraInfo: Increased filling (EDV) increases the radius of the chamber.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: {{c1::Concentric}} hypertrophy involves adding sarcomeres in parallel, leading to increased wall thickness.
extraInfo: Usually occurs due to chronic pressure overload.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Concentric hypertrophy is a compensatory response to chronic {{c1::pressure}} overload (e.g., hypertension, aortic stenosis).
extraInfo: By increasing wall thickness (h), the heart reduces wall tension (T).

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: {{c1::Eccentric}} hypertrophy involves adding sarcomeres in series, leading to chamber dilation.
extraInfo: Usually occurs due to chronic volume overload.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Eccentric hypertrophy is a compensatory response to chronic {{c1::volume}} overload (e.g., mitral/aortic regurgitation, endurance training).
extraInfo: The chamber radius increases to accommodate more blood.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: An increase in heart rate {{c1::increases}} myocardial oxygen demand.
extraInfo: The heart spends more time in systole and less in diastole (when coronary perfusion occurs).

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Of the determinants of MVO2, {{c1::heart rate}} is often the most significant factor in clinical settings.
extraInfo: Tachycardia is highly detrimental to patients with coronary artery disease.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: When the left ventricle dilates, the radius increases, which {{c1::increases}} wall tension according to Laplace's law.
extraInfo: This creates a vicious cycle in heart failure where a failing heart requires more oxygen.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Nitrates reduce myocardial oxygen demand primarily by decreasing {{c1::preload (radius)}}.
extraInfo: They cause venodilation, decreasing the volume of blood returning to the heart.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Beta-blockers reduce myocardial oxygen demand by decreasing both {{c1::heart rate}} and {{c2::contractility}}.
extraInfo: This 'chills' the heart and improves coronary perfusion time.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Aortic stenosis results in {{c1::concentric}} hypertrophy because the heart must generate higher pressure to eject blood.
extraInfo: The increased thickness 'h' helps normalize the wall tension 'T'.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Dilated cardiomyopathy leads to {{c1::eccentric}} hypertrophy and a significant increase in ventricular {{c2::radius}}.
extraInfo: This results in massive wall tension and high MVO2.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Increasing wall thickness (h) is a mechanism the heart uses to {{c1::decrease}} wall tension (T).
extraInfo: As seen in the denominator of the Laplace equation.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Chronic hypertension causes an increase in {{c1::Afterload}}, leading to concentric hypertrophy.
extraInfo: The pressure 'P' in Laplace's Law is elevated.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Myocardial oxygen demand is {{c1::greater}} during the isovolumetric contraction phase compared to the ejection phase.
extraInfo: Wall tension reaches its peak during isovolumetric contraction.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: In Laplace's law (T = P x r / 2h), 'T' stands for {{c1::wall tension}}.
extraInfo: Wall tension is the force acting to pull the myocardial fibers apart.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: In Laplace's law, 'h' stands for {{c1::wall thickness}}.
extraInfo: Increasing wall thickness distributes the pressure over more tissue.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Wall stress is another term often used interchangeably with {{c1::wall tension}} per unit of wall thickness.
extraInfo: Wall Stress = (P x r) / (2 x h).

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Lowering systolic blood pressure reduces myocardial oxygen demand by decreasing the {{c1::Pressure (P)}} variable in Laplace's Law.
extraInfo: This relates specifically to Afterload.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Volume overload causes sarcomeres to be added in {{c1::series}}, resulting in {{c2::eccentric}} hypertrophy.
extraInfo: Leads to a dilated chamber.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Pressure overload causes sarcomeres to be added in {{c1::parallel}}, resulting in {{c2::concentric}} hypertrophy.
extraInfo: Leads to a thicker wall.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right ventricle because it must overcome a much higher {{c1::afterload (pressure)}}.
extraInfo: This is a structural application of Laplace's Law.

topic: Cardiac oxygen demand and Laplace's law
text: Myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2) increases when the heart must work against {{c1::increased}} afterload or when {{c2::preload}} is significantly elevated.
extraInfo: Both increase the numerator in the Laplace equation.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: The equation for cardiac output (CO) using heart rate and stroke volume is CO = {{c1::HR}} × {{c2::SV}}.
extraInfo: CO is measured in L/min; SV is measured in mL.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: The Fick principle equation for Cardiac Output (CO) is CO = {{c1::O2 consumption}} / ({{c2::Arterial O2 content}} – {{c3::Venous O2 content}}).
extraInfo: This measures the volume of blood required to transport the O2 consumed by the body.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Stroke volume (SV) is calculated as SV = {{c1::EDV}} – {{c2::ESV}}.
extraInfo: EDV = End-diastolic volume; ESV = End-systolic volume.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) can be calculated as MAP = {{c1::CO}} × {{c2::TPR}}.
extraInfo: TPR = Total Peripheral Resistance; this is analogous to Ohm's law (V = IR).

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is approximated by the equation MAP = {{c1::2/3}} Diastolic Pressure + {{c2::1/3}} Systolic Pressure.
extraInfo: At normal heart rates, the heart spends twice as long in diastole as in systole.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Pulse Pressure (PP) is defined as {{c1::Systolic BP}} – {{c2::Diastolic BP}}.
extraInfo: Pulse pressure is directly proportional to Stroke Volume.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Ejection fraction (EF) is the ratio of stroke volume to end-diastolic volume, expressed as EF = {{c1::SV / EDV}}.
extraInfo: EF is a clinical index of ventricular contractility.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: A normal ejection fraction is typically ≥ {{c1::55}}%.
extraInfo: EF is decreased in systolic heart failure.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: To calculate the oxygen content in the Fick principle, mixed venous O2 is measured from the {{c1::pulmonary artery}}.
extraInfo: The pulmonary artery contains the most 'mixed' venous blood from the entire body.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Stroke volume is affected by three factors: {{c1::Preload}}, {{c2::Afterload}}, and {{c3::Contractility}}.
extraInfo: SV = Stroke Volume.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: An increase in contractility will result in a(n) {{c1::increase}} in Stroke Volume and a(n) {{c2::decrease}} in End-systolic volume (ESV).
extraInfo: Contractility is often increased by catecholamines or digoxin.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: According to the Fick principle, if O2 consumption is 250 mL/min, arterial O2 content is 200 mL/L, and venous O2 content is 150 mL/L, the Cardiac Output is {{c1::5}} L/min.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Pulse pressure is {{c1::inversely}} proportional to arterial compliance.
extraInfo: Decreased compliance (e.g., arteriosclerosis) leads to increased pulse pressure.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: During the early stages of exercise, Cardiac Output is maintained by an increase in both {{c1::Heart Rate}} and {{c2::Stroke Volume}}.
extraInfo: SV eventually plateaus, but HR continues to increase.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: During late, strenuous exercise, further increases in Cardiac Output are maintained primarily by {{c1::Heart Rate}}.
extraInfo: Stroke volume plateaus because filling time is limited at high heart rates.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: In states of very high Heart Rate (tachyarrhythmias), Cardiac Output may actually {{c1::decrease}} due to {{c2::shortened diastolic filling time}}.
extraInfo: Ventricular filling occurs during diastole.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) can also be expressed as MAP = {{c1::Diastolic BP}} + 1/3 {{c2::Pulse Pressure}}.
extraInfo: This is mathematically equivalent to (2/3 DBP + 1/3 SBP).

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Stroke volume {{c1::increases}} with increased preload.
extraInfo: This is described by the Frank-Starling mechanism.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Stroke volume {{c1::decreases}} with increased afterload.
extraInfo: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: The variable representing afterload in the calculation of Total Peripheral Resistance is {{c1::Mean Arterial Pressure}}.
extraInfo: TPR = (MAP – RAP) / CO.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) = ({{c1::MAP}} – {{c2::RAP (or CVP)}}) / CO.
extraInfo: RAP = Right Atrial Pressure; CVP = Central Venous Pressure.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Stroke Work is the work performed by the heart during one contraction and is represented by the {{c1::area within the pressure-volume loop}}.
extraInfo: Stroke Work = SV x Ventricular Pressure.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Pulse pressure is {{c1::increased}} in patients with Hyperthyroidism and Aortic Regurgitation.
extraInfo: High stroke volume leads to high systolic pressure; low diastolic pressure occurs in AR.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Pulse pressure is {{c1::decreased}} in patients with Aortic Stenosis and Cardiogenic Shock.
extraInfo: These conditions involve reduced stroke volume.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Myocardial oxygen demand is increased by an increase in {{c1::afterload}}, {{c2::contractility}}, {{c3::heart rate}}, and {{c4::ventricular diameter}}.
extraInfo: Ventricular diameter increases wall tension (Law of Laplace).

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Wall stress on the ventricle is calculated by (Pressure × {{c1::Radius}}) / (2 × {{c2::Wall Thickness}}).
extraInfo: This is the Law of Laplace; hypertrophy helps reduce wall stress.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Increasing contractility shifts the Frank-Starling curve {{c1::upward}} and to the {{c2::left}}.
extraInfo: This results in a higher stroke volume for a given preload.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: Decreasing contractility (e.g., Heart Failure) shifts the Frank-Starling curve {{c1::downward}} and to the {{c2::right}}.
extraInfo: This results in a lower stroke volume for a given preload.

topic: Cardiac output equations and Fick principle
text: In the Fick Principle, the term for 'Arterial O2 content – Venous O2 content' is also known as the {{c1::A-V O2 difference}}.
extraInfo: A wider A-V difference implies a lower CO if O2 consumption is constant.

text: The Frank-Starling law states that the {{c1::force of contraction}} is proportional to the {{c2::end-diastolic length}} of cardiac muscle fiber.
extraInfo: This is also referred to as preload.

text: On a Starling curve, the y-axis represents {{c1::Stroke Volume (or CO)}} and the x-axis represents {{c2::Ventricular EDV (Preload)}}.
extraInfo: Higher preload leads to higher stroke volume in a healthy heart.

text: {{c1::Positive inotropes}} (e.g., digoxin, dobutamine) shift the Starling curve upward and to the left.
extraInfo: This allows for a higher stroke volume at any given end-diastolic volume.

text: Heart failure shifts the Starling curve {{c1::downward}} and to the {{c2::right}}.
extraInfo: The heart becomes less efficient, requiring higher filling pressures to maintain stroke volume.

text: Exercise shifts the Starling curve {{c1::upward}} and to the {{c2::left}} due to increased {{c3::contractility}}.
extraInfo: Sympathetic stimulation during exercise increases myocardial performance.

text: The intersection of the cardiac function and vascular function curves represents the {{c1::operating point}} of the heart.
extraInfo: This is where venous return and cardiac output are equal.

text: In the combined cardiac and vascular function graph, the x-axis represents {{c1::Right Atrial Pressure (RAP)}}.
extraInfo: RAP is used as a surrogate for preload in these models.

text: Increased {{c1::inotropy}} increases the slope/height of the cardiac function curve without changing the {{c2::vascular function}} curve initially.
extraInfo: Examples include catecholamines and digoxin.

text: Changes in circulating volume specifically shift the {{c1::vascular function}} curve.
extraInfo: Fluid infusion shifts it right; hemorrhage shifts it left.

text: The x-intercept of the vascular function curve where venous return is zero is called the {{c1::mean systemic pressure}}.
extraInfo: This occurs when there is no flow in the circulatory system.

text: Mean systemic pressure (MSP) is primarily determined by {{c1::blood volume}} and {{c2::venous tone}}.
extraInfo: MSP increases with fluid infusion or sympathetic-mediated venoconstriction.

text: An increase in {{c1::Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR)}} decreases the slope of both the cardiac and vascular function curves.
extraInfo: Increased afterload reduces CO, and increased resistance reduces VR.

text: A decrease in TPR (e.g., exercise, AV shunt) {{c1::increases}} the slope of both the cardiac and vascular function curves.
extraInfo: This facilitates higher cardiac output and venous return.

text: {{c1::Arterioles}} account for the majority of Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR).
extraInfo: They are the primary resistance vessels in the systemic circulation.

text: {{c1::Veins}} provide most of the blood storage capacity (compliance) in the body.
extraInfo: They contain about 65% of the total blood volume at rest.

text: Sympathetic activity increases venous return by {{c1::decreasing}} venous compliance.
extraInfo: This is achieved through venoconstriction, which increases mean systemic pressure.

text: Loss of functional myocardium, such as in {{c1::Myocardial Infarction}}, results in a {{c2::downward}} shift of the cardiac function curve.
extraInfo: This reflects decreased contractility.

text: Acutely, {{c1::beta-blockers}} and {{c2::non-dihydropyridine CCBs}} decrease contractility, shifting the Starling curve downward.
extraInfo: Verapamil and diltiazem are the non-DHP CCBs with significant negative inotropic effects.

text: In chronic heart failure, the body retains fluid to increase {{c1::preload}} to maintain cardiac output via the Frank-Starling mechanism.
extraInfo: This shifts the operating point to a higher RAP (Right Atrial Pressure).

text: In an {{c1::arteriovenous (AV) shunt}}, TPR is decreased, leading to an increased slope of the vascular function curve and an increased {{c2::Mean Systemic Pressure}}.
extraInfo: This results in a significant increase in cardiac output.

text: Vasopressors increase {{c1::Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR)}}, which results in a {{c2::decreased}} cardiac output at a given preload.
extraInfo: This is due to the increased afterload against which the heart must pump.

text: The volumetric flow rate (Q) is equal to {{c1::flow velocity (v)}} multiplied by {{c2::cross-sectional area (A)}}.
extraInfo: Q = v * A.

text: Resistance (R) is directly proportional to {{c1::viscosity (η)}} and inversely proportional to {{c2::radius to the 4th power (r^4)}}.
extraInfo: Poiseuille's law: R = 8ηL / πr^4.

text: {{c1::Capillaries}} have the highest total cross-sectional area and the {{c2::lowest}} flow velocity.
extraInfo: The low velocity allows for efficient gas and nutrient exchange.

text: Blood viscosity increases in {{c1::polycythemia}} or {{c2::hyperproteinemic states}} (e.g., multiple myeloma).
extraInfo: Increased viscosity increases resistance to flow and work of the heart.

text: Anemia causes a {{c1::decrease}} in blood viscosity, which results in a {{c2::high-output}} state.
extraInfo: Decreased viscosity reduces resistance, increasing venous return and CO.

text: On the vascular function curve, a fluid infusion causes a {{c1::parallel shift to the right}}.
extraInfo: This increases the mean systemic pressure and the operating point's RAP.

text: In terms of vessels in series, the total resistance (Rt) is the {{c1::sum}} of the individual resistances.
In terms of vessels in parallel, the total resistance (Rt) is {{c1::less than}} any individual resistance.
The equation for blood flow (Q) is Q = {{c1::ΔP / R}}, where ΔP is the pressure gradient and R is resistance.
extraInfo: Flow is directly proportional to the pressure gradient and inversely proportional to resistance.

text: The resistance (R) of a vessel is proportional to the {{c1::viscosity (Η)}} of blood and the length of the vessel, and inversely proportional to the {{c2::fourth power of the radius (r⁴)}}.
extraInfo: Poiseuille equation: R = 8ΗL / πr⁴.

text: If the radius of a vessel is reduced by half, the resistance increases by a factor of {{c1::16}}.
extraInfo: Because resistance is inversely proportional to the radius to the 4th power (2^4 = 16).

text: Total resistance for vessels arranged in {{c1::series}} is the sum of the individual resistances (R1 + R2 + R3...).
extraInfo: Total resistance in series is always greater than any individual resistance.

text: Total resistance for vessels arranged in {{c1::parallel}} is calculated as 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3...
extraInfo: Total resistance in parallel is always less than any individual resistance.

text: Most organ systems in the human body are arranged in {{c1::parallel}}, which allows for independent regulation of blood flow to each organ.
extraInfo: This arrangement also ensures that total peripheral resistance is lower than if they were in series.

text: Blood flow velocity (v) is equal to {{c1::Q / A}} (Flow / Cross-sectional Area).
extraInfo: Velocity is inversely proportional to the total cross-sectional area.

text: The blood flow velocity is lowest in the {{c1::capillaries}} because they have the highest total cross-sectional area.
extraInfo: Low velocity in capillaries allows time for nutrient and gas exchange.

text: The highest resistance to blood flow in the entire cardiovascular system occurs in the {{c1::arterioles}}.
extraInfo: Arterioles are known as the primary resistance vessels; they regulate MAP and local blood flow.

text: Compliance (or Capacitance) is defined as the change in {{c1::volume}} per change in {{c2::pressure}} (C = ΔV / ΔP).
extraInfo: Compliance describes the distensibility of a vessel.

text: Most of the blood volume (~60-70%) is contained within the {{c1::veins}}.
extraInfo: Veins are known as capacitance vessels due to their high compliance.

text: Sympathetic stimulation of the veins {{c1::decreases}} venous compliance, which shifts blood toward the heart to increase preload.
extraInfo: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors mediate this venoconstriction.

text: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) is estimated by the formula MAP = {{c1::2/3 DBP + 1/3 SBP}}.
extraInfo: MAP is closer to DBP because more time is spent in diastole during the cardiac cycle.

text: The relationship between Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP), Cardiac Output (CO), and Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) is {{c1::MAP = CO × TPR}}.
extraInfo: This is the hemodynamic version of Ohm's Law (V = IR).

text: Pulse pressure is defined as the difference between {{c1::systolic blood pressure (SBP)}} and {{c2::diastolic blood pressure (DBP)}}.
extraInfo: Pulse pressure = SBP - DBP.

text: Pulse pressure is directly proportional to {{c1::stroke volume}} and inversely proportional to {{c2::arterial compliance}}.
extraInfo: Conditions like aortic regurgitation increase stroke volume and thus pulse pressure.

text: In the elderly, pulse pressure often increases because {{c1::arterial compliance}} decreases due to arteriosclerosis.
extraInfo: Stiffer arteries lead to higher systolic pressures and lower diastolic pressures.

text: Reynolds number (Re) is used to predict whether blood flow is {{c1::laminar or turbulent}}.
extraInfo: Re > 2000-3000 suggests turbulent flow.

text: According to the Reynolds number formula, a decrease in blood {{c1::viscosity}} (e.g., anemia) increases the likelihood of turbulent flow.
extraInfo: Anemia can cause functional murmurs due to increased turbulence.

text: Law of Laplace states that Wall Tension (T) = {{c1::(P × r) / (2 × h)}}, where h is wall thickness.
extraInfo: Increased wall thickness (h) is a compensatory mechanism to reduce wall tension in states of high pressure (P).

text: Viscosity of blood is primarily determined by {{c1::hematocrit}}.
extraInfo: Viscosity increases significantly in polycythemia and decreases in anemia.

text: Vessel resistance is most sensitive to changes in vessel {{c1::radius}}.
extraInfo: Because resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴.

text: Cardiac output (CO) is equal to {{c1::Oxygen consumption / (Arterial O2 - Venous O2 content)}} according to the Fick Principle.
extraInfo: CO = VO2 / (Ca - Cv).

text: Peripheral resistance is primarily regulated by {{c1::arterioles}} via the action of smooth muscle contraction/relaxation.
extraInfo: Arterioles account for the largest drop in pressure across the systemic circulation.

text: Decreasing vessel diameter (vasoconstriction) leads to {{c1::increased}} resistance and {{c2::decreased}} flow (assuming pressure is constant).
extraInfo: Flow is inversely related to resistance.

text: Turbulent blood flow can be heard clinically as {{c1::bruits or murmurs}}.
extraInfo: Caused by high velocity, large diameters, or low viscosity.

text: As blood moves from the aorta to the capillaries, the velocity of flow {{c1::decreases}}.
extraInfo: Velocity is lowest where the total cross-sectional area is highest (capillaries).

text: Hyperviscosity syndrome, as seen in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, leads to {{c1::increased}} vascular resistance.
extraInfo: Increased protein or RBCs increases viscosity (Η), which increases R.

text: In concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, the wall thickness {{c1::increases}} to minimize wall tension in response to high afterload (pressure).
extraInfo: Based on the Law of Laplace: T = (P × r) / 2h.

text: The intersection of the cardiac and vascular function curves represents the {{c1::operating point}} of the heart.
extraInfo: At this point, venous return and cardiac output are equal.

text: Positive inotropic agents like {{c1::digoxin}} or catecholamines shift the cardiac function curve {{c2::upward}}.
extraInfo: This results in increased cardiac output and decreased right atrial pressure (RAP).

text: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction shifts the cardiac function curve {{c1::downward}}.
extraInfo: This results in decreased cardiac output and increased right atrial pressure (RAP).

text: The x-intercept of the vascular function curve represents the {{c1::mean systemic pressure (MSP)}}.
extraInfo: MSP is the pressure in the system when cardiac output is zero.

text: An increase in blood volume or venous tone shifts the vascular function curve to the {{c1::right}}.
extraInfo: This increases the mean systemic pressure (MSP).

text: Acute hemorrhage or spinal anesthesia shifts the vascular function curve to the {{c1::left}}.
extraInfo: This decreases the mean systemic pressure (MSP).

text: An increase in Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) {{c1::decreases}} the slope of both the cardiac and vascular function curves.
extraInfo: The cardiac curve shifts down due to afterload, and the vascular curve rotates clockwise.

text: Exercise causes a decrease in TPR and an increase in inotropy, which together {{c1::increase}} cardiac output.
extraInfo: The change in right atrial pressure (RAP) is often minimal as the two effects offset.

text: An arteriovenous (AV) shunt {{c1::increases}} venous return and {{c2::decreases}} TPR.
extraInfo: This shifts the vascular function curve right and increases its slope.
