text: Mean systemic pressure (MSP) depends on {{c1::blood volume}} and {{c2::venous tone}}.
extraInfo: It is independent of Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR).

text: In the vascular function curve, the slope is determined by the {{c1::Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR)}}.
extraInfo: Higher TPR means a shallower (more horizontal) slope.

text: During isovolumetric contraction, the period of highest {{c1::O2 consumption}} occurs.
extraInfo: Pressure increases rapidly while volume remains constant.

text: The S1 heart sound corresponds to the closure of the {{c1::mitral and tricuspid}} valves.
extraInfo: It occurs at the beginning of isovolumetric contraction.

text: The S2 heart sound corresponds to the closure of the {{c1::aortic and pulmonary}} valves.
extraInfo: It occurs at the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation.

text: An S3 heart sound is heard during the {{c1::rapid filling}} phase of diastole.
extraInfo: Associated with increased filling pressures (e.g., mitral regurgitation, heart failure).

text: The S4 heart sound (atrial kick) is heard in {{c1::late diastole}}.
extraInfo: It is caused by blood entering a stiffened, non-compliant left ventricle.

text: On a pressure-volume loop, an increase in preload increases {{c1::stroke volume}}.
extraInfo: The end-diastolic volume (EDV) increases while the end-systolic volume (ESV) remains the same.

text: On a pressure-volume loop, an increase in afterload results in a {{c1::decreased}} stroke volume and an {{c2::increased}} end-systolic volume (ESV).
extraInfo: The heart must work against higher pressure, leaving more blood in the ventricle.

text: On a pressure-volume loop, increased contractility {{c1::increases}} stroke volume and {{c2::decreases}} end-systolic volume (ESV).
extraInfo: The ejection fraction increases.

text: The dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure curve is caused by {{c1::aortic valve closure}}.
extraInfo: It marks the start of isovolumetric relaxation.

text: The y-descent of the JVP curve represents {{c1::RA emptying into the RV}}.
extraInfo: This occurs right after the tricuspid valve opens.

text: The v-wave of the JVP curve represents {{c1::RA filling}} against a closed tricuspid valve.
extraInfo: It occurs during ventricular systole.

text: Blood flow (Q) is equal to ΔP divided by {{c1::Resistance (R)}}.
extraInfo: Similar to Ohm's law (I = V/R).

text: Resistance is inversely proportional to the {{c1::fourth power}} of the vessel radius.
extraInfo: R ∝ 1/r^4. Small changes in radius lead to large changes in resistance.

text: The {{c1::capillaries}} have the highest total cross-sectional area and the lowest flow velocity.
extraInfo: Low velocity allows for optimal nutrient and gas exchange.

text: The majority of Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) is provided by the {{c1::arterioles}}.
extraInfo: They are the primary site of blood pressure regulation.

text: Blood viscosity is primarily determined by the {{c1::hematocrit}}.
extraInfo: Viscosity increases in polycythemia and hyperproteinemic states like multiple myeloma.

text: Viscosity is {{c1::decreased}} in anemia.
extraInfo: Decreased red cell mass leads to reduced internal friction of blood.

text: Veins provide the majority of the blood {{c1::storage capacity}} in the body.
extraInfo: They are highly compliant vessels.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: {{c1::Isovolumetric contraction}} (Phase 1) begins after the mitral valve closes and is characterized by a rapid increase in {{c2::pressure}} with no change in volume.
extraInfo: This phase marks the start of systole and the production of the S1 heart sound.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The S1 heart sound is caused by the closure of the {{c1::mitral and tricuspid}} valves at the beginning of {{c2::isovolumetric contraction}}.
extraInfo: S1 is best heard at the apex (mitral) and left lower sternal border (tricuspid).

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Ventricular ejection (Phase 2) begins when {{c1::ventricular}} pressure exceeds {{c2::aortic/pulmonary}} pressure, causing the semilunar valves to open.
extraInfo: The volume of blood ejected during this phase is the stroke volume (SV).

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: {{c1::Isovolumetric relaxation}} (Phase 3) begins after the {{c2::aortic and pulmonary}} valves close.
extraInfo: This phase marks the start of diastole and the production of the S2 heart sound.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The S2 heart sound is produced by the closure of the {{c1::aortic and pulmonary}} valves at the start of {{c2::isovolumetric relaxation}}.
extraInfo: S2 is best heard at the left and right upper sternal borders.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Ventricular filling (Phase 4) begins when {{c1::atrial}} pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, causing the {{c2::mitral and tricuspid}} valves to open.
extraInfo: The majority of ventricular filling occurs early in this phase before atrial contraction.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Stroke volume (SV) is mathematically defined as {{c1::EDV (End-diastolic volume)}} minus {{c2::ESV (End-systolic volume)}}.
extraInfo: On a PV loop, SV is represented by the width of the loop.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The highest volume in the left ventricle during the cardiac cycle occurs at the end of diastole and is called {{c1::End-diastolic volume (EDV)}}.
extraInfo: EDV is determined by venous return and ventricular compliance.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The lowest volume in the left ventricle during the cardiac cycle occurs at the end of ejection and is called {{c1::End-systolic volume (ESV)}}.
extraInfo: ESV is determined by afterload and contractility.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: An increase in preload {{c1::increases}} the end-diastolic volume (EDV) and {{c2::increases}} the stroke volume.
extraInfo: This shifts the right side of the PV loop to the right.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: An increase in afterload {{c1::increases}} the end-systolic volume (ESV) and {{c2::decreases}} the stroke volume.
extraInfo: This makes the PV loop taller and narrower, shifting the top-left corner to the right.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Increased contractility (e.g., sympathetic stimulation) {{c1::decreases}} the end-systolic volume (ESV) and {{c2::increases}} the stroke volume.
extraInfo: This shifts the top-left corner of the PV loop to the left and increases the slope of the ESPVR.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::aortic valve}} opens at the end of isovolumetric contraction and closes at the start of {{c2::isovolumetric relaxation}}.
extraInfo: These transitions define the beginning and end of the systolic ejection phase.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::mitral valve}} closes at the start of isovolumetric contraction and opens at the start of {{c2::ventricular filling}}.
extraInfo: The time between closure and opening encompasses systole and isovolumetric relaxation.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: In aortic stenosis, the left ventricular pressure must be much {{c1::higher}} than aortic pressure to overcome the stenotic valve, leading to {{c2::increased}} afterload.
extraInfo: The PV loop shows a much higher peak systolic pressure and a reduced stroke volume.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Aortic regurgitation is characterized by the absence of a true {{c1::isovolumetric}} phase because the valve leaks during both relaxation and contraction.
extraInfo: The PV loop shows increased EDV, increased SV (due to backflow), and a massive pulse pressure.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Mitral regurgitation causes an {{c1::increase}} in EDV and a {{c2::decrease}} in ESV because blood is ejected into the low-pressure left atrium.
extraInfo: There is no true isovolumetric phase in MR either, as blood leaks into the LA as soon as the LV starts contracting.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Mitral stenosis leads to {{c1::decreased}} end-diastolic volume (EDV) and {{c2::decreased}} stroke volume due to impaired filling.
extraInfo: The PV loop is shifted to the left and is significantly narrower.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Myocardial oxygen consumption is increased by four main factors: {{c1::afterload}}, {{c2::contractility}}, {{c3::heart rate}}, and {{c4::wall tension}}.
extraInfo: The heart consumes more O2 to generate pressure (afterload) than to move volume (preload).

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Wall tension (Laplace Law) is directly proportional to {{c1::pressure}} and {{c2::radius}}, and inversely proportional to {{c3::wall thickness}}.
extraInfo: Formula: T = (P x r) / (2h). Hypertrophy is a compensatory mechanism to reduce wall tension.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: Ejection fraction (EF) is calculated as {{c1::SV / EDV}}, and a normal value is typically greater than {{c2::55%}}.
extraInfo: EF is a clinical index of ventricular contractility.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::incisura}} (dicrotic notch) seen on the aortic pressure curve represents the closure of the {{c2::aortic valve}}.
extraInfo: It marks the transition from systole to diastole.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: On the atrial pressure curve, the {{c1::a}} wave represents atrial contraction and is absent in patients with {{c2::atrial fibrillation}}.
extraInfo: The 'a' wave occurs at the very end of diastole.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: On the atrial pressure curve, the {{c1::c}} wave represents the bulging of the {{c2::tricuspid/mitral}} valve into the atrium during isovolumetric contraction.
extraInfo: This occurs during early systole.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: On the atrial pressure curve, the {{c1::v}} wave represents {{c2::atrial filling}} against a closed AV valve.
extraInfo: Giant 'v' waves are a classic finding in tricuspid or mitral regurgitation.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::y}} descent on the atrial pressure curve represents the rapid emptying of the atrium into the ventricle after the {{c2::AV valves open}}.
extraInfo: A rapid y-descent is seen in constrictive pericarditis (Friedreich's sign).

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The {{c1::x}} descent on the atrial pressure curve represents atrial relaxation and the downward pulling of the atrial floor during {{c2::ventricular systole}}.
extraInfo: The x-descent is blunted or absent in tricuspid regurgitation.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: {{c1::Concentric}} hypertrophy occurs in response to chronic pressure overload (e.g., AS, HTN), while {{c2::eccentric}} hypertrophy occurs in response to chronic volume overload (e.g., AR, MR).
extraInfo: Concentric = sarcomeres in parallel; Eccentric = sarcomeres in series.

topic: Pressure-volume loops and cardiac cycle phases
text: The slope of the {{c1::End-Systolic Pressure-Volume Relationship (ESPVR)}} is a measure of ventricular {{c2::contractility (inotropy)}}.
extraInfo: An increase in contractility shifts this line to the left and makes it steeper.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The {{c1::a wave}} of the jugular venous pulse (JVP) represents right atrial contraction.
extraInfo: It occurs at the end of diastole, just before the first heart sound (S1).

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The a wave is {{c1::absent}} in patients with atrial fibrillation.
extraInfo: This is because there is no coordinated atrial contraction in AFib.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: {{c1::Cannon a waves}} occur when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.
extraInfo: This creates a very high pressure pulse visible in the neck.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: Cannon a waves are a sign of {{c1::AV dissociation}}, such as in third-degree heart block or ventricular tachycardia.
extraInfo: The atrium and ventricle contract independently, occasionally simultaneously.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: A giant (but not cannon) a wave can be seen in {{c1::tricuspid stenosis}} or pulmonary hypertension.
extraInfo: This is due to increased resistance to right atrial emptying.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The {{c1::c wave}} of the JVP represents right ventricular contraction and the resulting bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium.
extraInfo: It occurs early in ventricular systole.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The {{c1::x descent}} represents atrial relaxation and the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve during ventricular systole.
extraInfo: It is the first downward deflection after the c wave.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The x descent is {{c1::reduced or absent}} in patients with tricuspid regurgitation.
extraInfo: Regurgitant blood flow into the atrium during systole cancels out the pressure drop of atrial relaxation.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The x descent is notably {{c1::prominent}} in cardiac tamponade.
extraInfo: Tamponade limits overall heart volume, making the systolic relaxation of the atrium more noticeable relative to the pericardial pressure.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The {{c1::v wave}} represents increased right atrial pressure due to filling against a closed tricuspid valve.
extraInfo: It peaks just after S2 during ventricular systole.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: A giant v wave is highly characteristic of {{c1::tricuspid regurgitation}}.
extraInfo: In TR, the atrium fills from both the vena cava and the leaking tricuspid valve during systole.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The {{c1::y descent}} represents the opening of the tricuspid valve and the subsequent emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle.
extraInfo: It occurs during early ventricular diastole.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The y descent is {{c1::absent or blunted}} in cardiac tamponade.
extraInfo: Intrapericardial pressure is so high that it prevents rapid early diastolic filling of the right ventricle.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: A {{c1::rapid or steep}} y descent is a classic finding in constrictive pericarditis.
extraInfo: The rigid pericardium allows rapid early filling until the expansion limit is hit abruptly.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: In constrictive pericarditis, the combination of prominent x and y descents creates a JVP tracing with a {{c1::W}} shape.
extraInfo: This is sometimes referred to as the M or W pattern.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: {{c1::Kussmaul sign}} is defined as a paradoxical increase in jugular venous pressure during inspiration.
extraInfo: Normally, JVP should decrease during inspiration due to negative intrathoracic pressure.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: Kussmaul sign is most commonly associated with {{c1::constrictive pericarditis}}.
extraInfo: It can also be seen in restrictive cardiomyopathy or right-sided heart failure.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: In tricuspid regurgitation, the x descent is often replaced by a large, fused wave known as the {{c1::cv wave}}.
extraInfo: This combined wave represents the massive systolic pressure increase in the right atrium.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The a wave of the JVP occurs just {{c1::before}} the first heart sound (S1).
extraInfo: Atrial contraction (a wave) provides the 'atrial kick' just before the tricuspid valve closes (S1).

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The v wave of the JVP peaks just {{c1::after}} the second heart sound (S2).
extraInfo: The v wave ends when the tricuspid valve opens at the start of diastole.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: {{c1::Friedreich's sign}} refers to an exaggerated, steep y descent seen in constrictive pericarditis.
extraInfo: It is the physical exam correlate of the 'dip and plateau' seen on invasive pressure tracings.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: In atrial fibrillation, the JVP tracing is characterized by the absence of an a wave and the presence of a prominent {{c1::v wave}}.
extraInfo: The absence of the a wave is the most specific JVP finding for AFib.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: Conditions like pulmonary valve stenosis or right ventricular hypertrophy cause a {{c1::giant a wave}} due to decreased right ventricular compliance.
extraInfo: The atrium must contract harder to move blood into a stiff or high-pressure ventricle.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The x descent of the JVP occurs during ventricular {{c1::systole}}.
extraInfo: It corresponds to the period when the ventricle is contracting and the atrium is relaxing.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The y descent of the JVP occurs during ventricular {{c1::diastole}}.
extraInfo: It corresponds to the early passive filling phase of the right ventricle.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The {{c1::c wave}} occurs nearly simultaneously with the carotid artery pulse.
extraInfo: The bulging of the valve into the atrium happens at the same time as ventricular ejection into the aorta.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: In tricuspid stenosis, the y descent is {{c1::slowed or prolonged}}.
extraInfo: The stenotic valve provides resistance, preventing the rapid emptying of the right atrium.

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: An overall elevation of the mean jugular venous pressure is a sign of {{c1::right-sided heart failure}} or volume overload.
extraInfo: JVP is a direct reflection of central venous pressure (CVP).

topic: Jugular venous pulse waveforms and tracings
text: The descent that is preserved (and often deep) in cardiac tamponade is the {{c1::x descent}}.
extraInfo: Differentiating tamponade from constriction: Tamponade has a prominent x and blunted y; Constriction has prominent x AND prominent y.

text: In Aortic Stenosis, the LV pressure must rise {{c1::higher}} than aortic pressure to eject blood.
extraInfo: This results in a significant pressure gradient across the valve during systole.

text: Aortic Stenosis is characterized by a(n) {{c1::increase}} in afterload.
extraInfo: The increased resistance at the valve requires higher systolic pressures.

text: In Aortic Stenosis, the PV loop shows a(n) {{c1::increase}} in peak LV systolic pressure.
extraInfo: The loop becomes 'taller' vertically.

text: Chronic Aortic Stenosis results in {{c1::concentric}} LV hypertrophy.
extraInfo: This is a response to pressure overload (Laplace Law: wall stress = Pr/2h).

text: In Aortic Stenosis, the stroke volume is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: The width of the loop narrows due to increased afterload and decreased compliance.

text: Aortic Regurgitation is characterized by a(n) {{c1::increase}} in End-Diastolic Volume (EDV).
extraInfo: This is due to the combination of normal filling and regurgitant flow from the aorta.

text: In Aortic Regurgitation, the total stroke volume is {{c1::increased}}.
extraInfo: Increased preload leads to increased SV via the Frank-Starling mechanism (widened loop).

text: In Aortic Regurgitation, there is no true {{c1::isovolumetric}} relaxation or contraction.
extraInfo: The leaky valve allows volume changes even when other valves are closed.

text: Chronic Aortic Regurgitation leads to {{c1::eccentric}} LV hypertrophy.
extraInfo: This is a response to volume overload, causing the loop to shift to the right.

text: Aortic Regurgitation results in a(n) {{c1::widened}} pulse pressure.
extraInfo: Due to high systolic pressure (high SV) and low diastolic pressure (regurgitation into LV).

text: Mitral Stenosis is characterized by a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in End-Diastolic Volume (EDV).
extraInfo: Impaired filling from the LA to the LV results in a smaller 'starting' volume for the LV.

text: In Mitral Stenosis, the stroke volume is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: Decreased EDV (preload) directly results in a lower stroke volume (narrower loop).

text: In Mitral Stenosis, the {{c1::Left Atrial}} pressure is increased to maintain LV filling.
extraInfo: This pressure increase is what causes pulmonary congestion and pulmonary hypertension.

text: Mitral Regurgitation causes a(n) {{c1::increase}} in End-Diastolic Volume (EDV).
extraInfo: Due to increased volume returning from the LA (which received regurgitant blood in the previous cycle).

text: In Mitral Regurgitation, the End-Systolic Volume (ESV) is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: The LV can eject blood into the low-pressure LA, allowing it to empty more effectively.

text: In Mitral Regurgitation, the total stroke volume is {{c1::increased}}.
extraInfo: The loop is wider, but 'effective' forward stroke volume (to the aorta) may be decreased.

text: Mitral Regurgitation lacks true {{c1::isovolumetric}} phases.
extraInfo: Blood leaks into the LA immediately as LV pressure rises (contraction) and falls (relaxation).

text: On a PV loop, the horizontal width represents {{c1::Stroke Volume}}.
extraInfo: SV = EDV - ESV.

text: The area inside the PV loop represents {{c1::Stroke Work}}.
extraInfo: Stroke Work = Stroke Volume x Mean Arterial Pressure.

text: In Mitral Regurgitation, ejection into the LA begins {{c1::immediately}} after the start of systole.
extraInfo: This bypasses the isovolumetric contraction phase.

text: Chronic Mitral Regurgitation leads to {{c1::eccentric}} hypertrophy.
extraInfo: A volume-overload state leading to chamber dilation and a rightward shift of the loop.

text: In Aortic Stenosis, LV compliance is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: The thickened wall (concentric hypertrophy) makes the LV stiffer, increasing diastolic pressures.

text: In Aortic Regurgitation, the regurgitation occurs during {{c1::diastole}}.
extraInfo: Blood flows from high-pressure aorta to low-pressure LV while the ventricle is relaxing.

text: In Mitral Stenosis, the {{c1::filling}} limb (bottom of the loop) is shortened.
extraInfo: Because the LV cannot fill to its normal capacity.

text: In Aortic Stenosis, the peak LV pressure is significantly {{c1::higher}} than the peak aortic pressure.
extraInfo: This gradient is the hallmark of valvular stenosis.

text: Both Mitral Regurgitation and Aortic Regurgitation involve increased {{c1::preload}}.
extraInfo: Increased EDV is seen in both due to volume overload.

text: The only valvular disease of the primary four that typically results in a decreased EDV is {{c1::Mitral Stenosis}}.
extraInfo: The obstruction prevents the LV from reaching its normal end-diastolic volume.

text: In Mitral Regurgitation, the 'isovolumetric' contraction line slants to the {{c1::left}}.
extraInfo: Because volume is being lost to the LA as pressure rises.

text: In Aortic Regurgitation, the 'isovolumetric' relaxation line slants to the {{c1::right}}.
extraInfo: Because volume is being added from the aorta as pressure falls.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: The second heart sound (S2) is produced by the closure of the {{c1::aortic (A2)}} and {{c2::pulmonic (P2)}} valves.
extraInfo: A2 normally precedes P2 because the left side of the heart has higher pressure and closes sooner.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: During inspiration, the decrease in intrathoracic pressure {{c1::increases}} venous return to the right ventricle.
extraInfo: This increased volume leads to a delay in the closure of the pulmonic valve.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Normal physiological splitting of S2 is heard only during {{c1::inspiration}}.
extraInfo: On expiration, A2 and P2 are heard as a single sound.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: In wide splitting, the S2 split is present during expiration and {{c1::widens/exaggerated}} during inspiration.
extraInfo: It occurs when there is a delay in RV emptying.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Common causes of wide splitting include {{c1::pulmonic stenosis}} and {{c2::right bundle branch block (RBBB)}}.
extraInfo: Anything that delays RV contraction or pulmonic valve closure.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Fixed splitting of S2 is the characteristic finding for a(n) {{c1::atrial septal defect (ASD)}}.
extraInfo: The split does not change with respiration.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: In an ASD, fixed splitting occurs because the Left-to-Right shunt increases {{c1::RV stroke volume}} through the pulmonic valve.
extraInfo: Inspiration increases venous return but decreases the L-to-R shunt, keeping the total RV volume constant across the cycle.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Paradoxical splitting occurs when the {{c1::P2}} sound occurs before the {{c2::A2}} sound.
extraInfo: This is the reverse of the normal physiological order.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: In paradoxical splitting, the S2 split is heard during {{c1::expiration}} and disappears during {{c2::inspiration}}.
extraInfo: On inspiration, P2 is delayed and moves closer to the already delayed A2.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Common causes of paradoxical splitting include {{c1::aortic stenosis}} and {{c2::left bundle branch block (LBBB)}}.
extraInfo: These conditions delay LV emptying or the closure of the aortic valve.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: In wide splitting, the delay in pulmonic valve closure is primarily due to increased resistance to flow in {{c1::pulmonic stenosis}}.
extraInfo: The RV takes longer to push blood through the stenotic valve.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Right bundle branch block (RBBB) causes wide splitting because it delays the {{c1::electrical activation}} of the right ventricle.
extraInfo: This delays the mechanical contraction and subsequent valve closure.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) causes {{c1::paradoxical}} splitting by delaying the closure of the {{c2::aortic}} valve.
extraInfo: A2 is delayed so much that it follows P2.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: A(n) {{c1::atrial septal defect (ASD)}} causes a fixed split because of the continuous volume overload of the {{c2::right}} ventricle.
extraInfo: The extra volume delays P2 regardless of the phase of respiration.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: In normal physiology, inspiration causes the pulmonic valve to close {{c1::later}} due to increased stroke volume.
extraInfo: Increased venous return (preload) to the RV is the primary driver.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Severe hypertension can cause {{c1::paradoxical}} splitting of S2 due to prolonged LV ejection time.
extraInfo: The high systemic resistance delays the closure of the aortic valve.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome can cause wide splitting if there is early activation of the {{c1::left}} ventricle.
extraInfo: Pre-excitation of the LV makes A2 occur earlier, widening the gap before P2.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Splitting of S2 is best heard at the {{c1::left upper sternal border}}.
extraInfo: This is known as the Pulmonic area.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: In normal physiology, expiration causes A2 and P2 to merge because {{c1::decreased}} venous return to the RV allows the pulmonic valve to close earlier.
extraInfo: The decreased RV volume results in earlier P2 closure, coinciding with A2.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Aortic stenosis leads to {{c1::paradoxical}} splitting because the LV must exert more pressure, which {{c2::prolongs}} the time until the aortic valve closes.
extraInfo: The delayed A2 ends up following P2.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: A key physical exam finding for ASD is a {{c1::midsystolic pulmonary flow murmur}} and a fixed split S2.
extraInfo: The murmur is due to increased volume crossing the pulmonic valve, not the ASD itself.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Pulmonic stenosis: Split {{c1::widens}} with inspiration; Aortic stenosis: Split {{c2::narrows}} (or disappears) with inspiration.
extraInfo: Useful for differentiating right-sided vs left-sided outflow obstructions.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: During inspiration, the A2-P2 interval {{c1::increases}} in physiological splitting.
extraInfo: P2 moves later, A2 might move slightly earlier due to pulmonary capacity increase.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) can lead to {{c1::paradoxical}} splitting of S2.
extraInfo: The outflow obstruction delays LV emptying and A2 closure.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: In wide splitting, {{c1::P2}} occurs significantly after A2, even during expiration.
extraInfo: Commonly seen in RBBB or Mitral Regurgitation (due to early A2).

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Mitral regurgitation causes wide splitting because the low-resistance path to the left atrium allows the LV to finish emptying {{c1::earlier}}, resulting in an early {{c2::A2}}.
extraInfo: This is a 'wide split' because A2 occurs early, rather than P2 being late.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) with a Left-to-Right shunt typically causes {{c1::wide}} splitting of S2.
extraInfo: Increased volume in the RV delays P2 closure.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: When A2 is delayed (e.g. LBBB), the split heard on expiration is {{c1::eliminated}} by the delay of P2 during inspiration.
extraInfo: This describes the mechanism of paradoxical splitting.

topic: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
text: Cardiac tamponade or severe asthma (Pulsus paradoxus) affects S2 splitting by {{c1::exaggerating}} the changes in venous return and ventricular volumes.
extraInfo: While not the primary diagnostic sign for these, it reflects the extreme heart-lung interactions.

text: Aortic stenosis is best heard at the {{c1::right 2nd intercostal space}} at the sternal border.
extraInfo: It is a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur that radiates to the carotids.

text: The {{c1::left 2nd intercostal space}} is the primary site for auscultating the pulmonic valve.
extraInfo: Commonly associated with pulmonic stenosis and flow murmurs.

text: The {{c1::left 4th and 5th intercostal spaces}} at the sternal border are the best locations to hear tricuspid and right-sided murmurs.
extraInfo: Includes Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis.

text: Mitral murmurs and the apex of the heart are best auscultated at the {{c1::5th intercostal space}} at the midclavicular line.
extraInfo: The mitral area is also where the S1 sound is usually loudest.

text: The S3 heart sound is associated with {{c1::rapid ventricular filling}} during early diastole.
extraInfo: Normal in children and pregnant women, but indicative of volume overload (e.g., HF) in older adults.

text: The S4 heart sound is associated with an {{c1::atrial kick}} into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle.
extraInfo: Always pathologic; seen in ventricular hypertrophy or acute MI.

text: Inspiration {{c1::increases}} the intensity of right-sided heart murmurs.
extraInfo: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart.

text: The {{c1::handgrip}} maneuver increases afterload by increasing peripheral vascular resistance.
extraInfo: Increases intensity of MR, AR, and VSD murmurs.

text: Handgrip {{c1::decreases}} the intensity of Aortic Stenosis (AS) and HOCM murmurs.
extraInfo: Increased afterload decreases the pressure gradient across the outflow tract.

text: Valsalva (strain phase) and standing {{c1::decrease}} preload by reducing venous return.
extraInfo: This increases the intensity of HOCM and MVP murmurs.

text: Squatting and passive leg raise increase {{c1::preload}} by increasing venous return.
extraInfo: This decreases the intensity of HOCM and MVP murmurs.

text: Aortic Stenosis presents as a {{c1::crescendo-decrescendo}} systolic ejection murmur.
extraInfo: Classic triad: Syncope, Angina, and Dyspnea (SAD).

text: Mitral Regurgitation is a {{c1::holosystolic}} murmur that often radiates to the {{c2::axilla}}.
extraInfo: Common causes include post-MI chordae rupture, MVP, or LV dilatation.

text: Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) is characterized by a {{c1::mid-systolic click}} followed by a late systolic murmur.
extraInfo: The click is due to sudden tensing of the chordae tendineae.

text: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) presents as a {{c1::harsh holosystolic}} murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border.
extraInfo: Smaller VSDs typically produce louder, higher-pitched murmurs.

text: Aortic Regurgitation presents as a {{c1::high-pitched decrescendo}} diastolic murmur.
extraInfo: Best heard at the left sternal border at end-expiration while leaning forward.

text: Mitral Stenosis is characterized by an {{c1::opening snap}} followed by a mid-diastolic rumble.
extraInfo: The interval between S2 and the opening snap (S2-OS) correlates with severity.

text: S1 is produced by the closure of the {{c1::mitral and tricuspid}} valves.
extraInfo: Marks the beginning of systole.

text: S2 is produced by the closure of the {{c1::aortic and pulmonic}} valves.
extraInfo: Marks the beginning of diastole.

text: Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during {{c1::inspiration}} because increased venous return delays pulmonic valve closure.
extraInfo: A2 and P2 separate during inspiration and merge during expiration.

text: {{c1::Fixed}} splitting of S2 is the classic finding for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD).
extraInfo: Occurs because the shunt maintains high flow through the pulmonic valve regardless of respiration.

text: Paradoxical splitting of S2 occurs when the {{c1::P2}} sound occurs before the {{c2::A2}} sound.
extraInfo: Seen in Aortic Stenosis and Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB).

text: Paradoxical splitting of S2 is heard on {{c1::expiration}} and disappears on inspiration.
extraInfo: Inspiration delays P2, moving it closer to the already delayed A2.

text: The Carvallo sign refers to the increase in intensity of a {{c1::tricuspid regurgitation}} murmur during inspiration.
extraInfo: Helps distinguish TR from MR.

text: In Mitral Valve Prolapse, maneuvers that decrease preload (standing/valsalva) cause the click to occur {{c1::earlier}} in systole.
extraInfo: A smaller LV volume allows the valve to prolapse sooner.

text: Tricuspid regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur that {{c1::increases}} in intensity with inspiration.
extraInfo: Often seen in IV drug users due to endocarditis.

text: A Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) produces a {{c1::continuous machine-like}} murmur.
extraInfo: Loudest at S2; best heard at the left infraclavicular area.

text: {{c1::Wide}} splitting of S2 occurs in conditions that delay RV emptying, such as Pulmonic Stenosis or RBBB.
extraInfo: The split is present during expiration and widens during inspiration.

text: Rapid squatting increases both {{c1::preload}} and {{c2::afterload}}.
extraInfo: This decreases the intensity of HOCM and MVP, while increasing most other murmurs (AS, MR, AR).

text: {{c1::Aortic stenosis}} is a {{c2::crescendo-decrescendo}} systolic ejection murmur that follows an ejection click.
extraInfo: It is often caused by age-related calcification or a bicuspid aortic valve.

text: The murmur of aortic stenosis typically radiates to the {{c1::carotids}}.
extraInfo: Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed pulses) is also a classic finding.

text: Mitral regurgitation is a {{c1::holosystolic}}, high-pitched, "blowing" murmur.
extraInfo: It is often caused by ischemic heart disease (post-MI), MVP, or LV dilatation.

text: The murmur of mitral regurgitation classically radiates to the {{c1::axilla}}.
extraInfo: The murmur is best heard at the apex.

text: Tricuspid regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur that {{c1::increases}} in intensity with inspiration.
extraInfo: This increase with inspiration is known as Carvallo sign, which distinguishes it from Mitral Regurgitation.

text: Mitral valve prolapse is characterized by a {{c1::midsystolic click}} followed by a late systolic murmur.
extraInfo: The click is due to sudden tensing of chordae tendineae.

text: VSD presents as a {{c1::holosystolic}}, harsh-sounding murmur loudest at the {{c2::left lower sternal border}}.
extraInfo: Smaller VSDs typically produce louder murmurs than larger ones.

text: Aortic regurgitation is a high-pitched, "blowing" {{c1::early diastolic}} decrescendo murmur.
extraInfo: Often associated with a wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses.

text: The murmur of AR is best heard at the left sternal border with the patient {{c1::leaning forward}} and at end-{{c2::expiration}}.
extraInfo: Common causes include aortic root dilation, bicuspid valve, and endocarditis.

text: Mitral stenosis is characterized by an {{c1::opening snap}} followed by a mid-to-late diastolic rumble.
extraInfo: The opening snap is due to the abrupt halt in leafet motion after the valve opens.

text: In Mitral Stenosis, a {{c1::shorter}} interval between the S2 heart sound and the opening snap indicates more severe disease.
extraInfo: A shorter S2-OS interval reflects higher left atrial pressure.

text: PDA presents as a continuous {{c1::machine-like}} murmur.
extraInfo: It is best heard at the left infraclavicular area and is often associated with congenital rubella.

text: The PDA murmur is loudest at the time of the {{c1::S2}} heart sound.
extraInfo: Because the pressure gradient between the aorta and pulmonary artery is highest at that point.

text: Inspiration increases the intensity of {{c1::right-sided}} heart murmurs.
extraInfo: Inspiration increases venous return to the right atrium.

text: The handgrip maneuver increases {{c1::afterload}}, which increases the intensity of {{c2::MR, AR, and VSD}} murmurs.
extraInfo: Increased systemic vascular resistance forces more blood back through the regurgitant or shunted opening.

text: Handgrip decreases the intensity of {{c1::Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)}} and {{c2::Aortic stenosis}} murmurs.
extraInfo: Increased afterload increases LV volume, reducing the obstruction in HCM and decreasing the pressure gradient in AS.

text: Valsalva and standing {{c1::decrease}} preload by decreasing venous return.
extraInfo: Most murmurs decrease in intensity during these maneuvers, except HCM and MVP.

text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and {{c1::MVP}} are the only murmurs that increase in intensity with decreased preload.
extraInfo: Decreased LV volume increases the outflow obstruction in HCM and causes earlier prolapse in MVP.

text: Rapid squatting increases both {{c1::preload}} and {{c2::afterload}}.
extraInfo: This increases LV volume and decreases the HCM murmur.

text: HCM is a {{c1::systolic}} crescendo-decrescendo murmur that {{c2::decreases}} with squatting.
extraInfo: Increased preload/afterload from squatting increases LV chamber size, moving the septum away from the mitral valve.

text: {{c1::Rheumatic fever}} is the most common cause of mitral stenosis worldwide.
extraInfo: Chronic rheumatic heart disease leads to commissural fusion of the mitral valve.

text: The classic triad of symptoms for Aortic Stenosis includes: {{c1::Syncope}}, {{c2::Angina}}, and {{c3::Dyspnea}} (SAD).
extraInfo: The onset of these symptoms indicates a significantly decreased survival rate without valve replacement.

text: Aortic regurgitation is associated with a {{c1::wide}} pulse pressure.
extraInfo: Pulse pressure = Systolic BP - Diastolic BP.

text: Chronic Mitral Regurgitation can lead to {{c1::left atrial}} enlargement, which increases the risk of atrial fibrillation.
extraInfo: Enlargement results from chronic volume overload.

text: ASD presents with a mid-systolic flow murmur and a {{c1::fixed split S2}}.
extraInfo: The fixed split is due to delayed closure of the pulmonic valve, independent of respiration.

text: Pulmonary stenosis is a {{c1::systolic}} ejection murmur that increases with {{c2::inspiration}}.
extraInfo: It is best heard at the left second intercostal space.

text: An {{c1::Austin Flint}} murmur is a mid-diastolic rumble heard in severe aortic regurgitation.
extraInfo: It is caused by the regurgitant jet from the aorta impinging on the anterior mitral valve leaflet.

text: Mitral valve prolapse is the most common cause of {{c1::mitral regurgitation}} in developed countries.
extraInfo: It is often associated with connective tissue disorders like Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

text: The {{c1::Graham Steell}} murmur is a high-pitched diastolic decrescendo murmur caused by pulmonary regurgitation.
extraInfo: It is usually associated with pulmonary hypertension.

text: Phase {{c1::0}} of the ventricular action potential is characterized by rapid depolarization due to the opening of {{c2::voltage-gated Na+ channels}}.
extraInfo: This phase corresponds to the QRS complex on the ECG.

text: In Phase {{c1::1}} of the myocardial action potential, there is initial repolarization caused by the inactivation of {{c2::Na+ channels}} and the activation of transient {{c3::K+}} efflux.
extraInfo: This is a brief downward notch before the plateau.

text: Phase 2 of the myocardial action potential is the {{c1::plateau}} phase, where {{c2::Ca2+}} influx through {{c3::L-type}} channels balances K+ efflux.
extraInfo: This calcium entry triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

text: The rapid repolarization in Phase {{c1::3}} of the myocardial action potential is primarily due to the massive efflux of {{c2::K+}} through voltage-gated channels.
extraInfo: Phase 3 corresponds to the T wave on the ECG.

text: Phase 4 of the myocardial action potential is the resting potential, where the membrane is most permeable to {{c1::K+}} ions via leak channels.
extraInfo: High K+ permeability keeps the resting potential near -90 mV.

text: Brugada syndrome is an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} disorder most commonly caused by a {{c2::loss-of-function}} mutation in {{c3::Na+}} channels.
extraInfo: Commonly seen in Asian males; increases risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD).

text: Congenital long QT syndrome is most commonly due to loss-of-function mutations in {{c1::K+}} channels, which affects the {{c2::repolarization (Phase 3)}} phase of the action potential.
extraInfo: The delay in K+ efflux leads to a prolonged QT interval.

text: {{c1::Romano-Ward}} syndrome is an autosomal dominant congenital long QT syndrome with a pure cardiac phenotype.
extraInfo: Unlike Jervell and Lange-Nielsen, it does not involve deafness.

text: {{c1::Jervell and Lange-Nielsen}} syndrome is an autosomal recessive congenital long QT syndrome associated with {{c2::sensorineural deafness}}.
extraInfo: The recessive inheritance pattern and deafness distinguish it from Romano-Ward.

text: The ECG pattern in Brugada syndrome shows a pseudo-{{c1::right bundle branch block}} and ST-segment elevations in leads {{c2::V1–V2}}.
extraInfo: Treatment involves prevention of SCD with an ICD.

text: In myocardial cells, {{c1::calcium}}-induced {{c2::calcium}} release occurs specifically during Phase {{c3::2}} of the action potential.
extraInfo: Calcium enters through L-type channels and triggers the ryanodine receptors (RyR2).

text: Unlike ventricular myocytes, the Phase 0 upstroke in the SA and AV nodes is mediated by {{c1::Ca2+}} influx, not Na+.
extraInfo: This accounts for the slower conduction speed in the AV node.

text: The {{c1::effective refractory period (ERP)}} is the interval during which a new action potential cannot be triggered, lasting from Phase 0 to the middle of Phase {{c2::3}}.
extraInfo: This prevents tetany and ensures rhythmic contraction.

text: {{c1::Class III}} antiarrhythmics work by blocking Phase 3 {{c2::K+}} channels, thereby prolonging the action potential duration.
extraInfo: Examples include amiodarone, sotalol, and dofetilide.

text: The QT interval on an ECG provides a clinical measurement of the total duration of the ventricular {{c1::action potential}}.
extraInfo: A prolonged QT interval indicates delayed ventricular repolarization.

text: The T wave on an ECG corresponds to Phase {{c1::3}} (repolarization) of the ventricular action potential.
extraInfo: Inversion of the T wave can indicate ischemia or recent infarction.

text: Myocardial cells are electrically coupled to one another via {{c1::gap junctions}}, which allow the heart to function as a functional {{c2::syncytium}}.
extraInfo: This allows for rapid, coordinated depolarization.

text: Conduction velocity is fastest in the {{c1::Purkinje system}} and slowest in the {{c2::AV node}}.
extraInfo: He Is At Ventricle: His-Purkinje > Atria > Ventricles > AV node.

text: In Phase 4 of the pacemaker action potential, the "funny current" (If) consists of a slow influx of {{c1::Na+}} that determines the heart rate.
extraInfo: This is the target of the drug ivabradine.

text: Hyperkalemia causes the resting membrane potential (Phase 4) to become {{c1::less negative (depolarized)}}, which can eventually lead to cardiac arrest.
extraInfo: On ECG, this manifests as peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes.

text: {{c1::Sick sinus syndrome}} is characterized by age-related degeneration of the SA node, resulting in bradycardia, sinus pauses, or {{c2::sinus arrest}}.
extraInfo: Escape beats (junctional or ventricular) may occur.

text: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block is characterized by progressive lengthening of the {{c1::PR interval}} until a beat is dropped.
extraInfo: This is usually benign and localized to the AV node.

text: In {{c1::Mobitz Type II}} second-degree AV block, there are dropped beats (missing QRS) that are {{c2::not}} preceded by changes in the PR interval.
extraInfo: This often indicates structural disease (e.g., bundle branch block) and requires a pacemaker.

text: Third-degree (complete) AV block is characterized by total dissociation between {{c1::P waves}} and {{c2::QRS complexes}}.
extraInfo: The atrial rate is typically faster than the ventricular escape rate.

text: A premature ventricular contraction (PVC) is an ectopic beat that results in a {{c1::wide}} QRS complex because it bypasses the normal {{c2::His-Purkinje}} system.
extraInfo: The slow myocyte-to-myocyte conduction results in the widened complex.

text: Loss-of-function mutations in $Na^+$ channels (Brugada syndrome) primarily affect the Phase {{c1::0}} upstroke of the action potential.
extraInfo: This results in the characteristic ECG changes in V1-V2.

text: Ventricular fibrillation is a disorganized rhythm with no identifiable waves and is fatal without immediate {{c1::CPR}} and {{c2::defibrillation}}.
extraInfo: This is a common cause of sudden cardiac death following an MI.

text: The duration of the myocardial action potential is much longer than in skeletal muscle, mainly due to the presence of the {{c1::Phase 2 plateau}}.
extraInfo: This prevents mechanical summation and tetany in cardiac muscle.

text: The slope of Phase 0 in the myocardial action potential represents the {{c1::conduction velocity}} through the tissue.
extraInfo: Faster Na+ channel opening leads to a steeper slope and faster conduction.

text: The pacemaker action potential occurs primarily in the {{c1::SA and AV}} nodes.
extraInfo: Unlike myocytes, pacemaker cells lack a stable resting membrane potential.

text: The pacemaker action potential lacks phases {{c1::1 and 2}} which are present in the ventricular action potential.
extraInfo: This accounts for the different morphology of the electrical tracing.

text: Phase 0 of the pacemaker action potential is characterized by the upstroke caused by the opening of voltage-gated {{c1::Ca2+}} channels.
extraInfo: In contrast, phase 0 in myocytes is caused by voltage-gated Na+ channels.

text: Phase 3 in pacemaker cells is the {{c1::repolarization}} phase.
extraInfo: This occurs after the Ca2+ channels close.

text: Repolarization (Phase 3) in pacemaker cells is driven by the opening of voltage-gated {{c1::K+}} channels and the efflux of K+.
extraInfo: This is similar to the repolarization phase in ventricular myocytes.

text: Phase 4 is known as {{c1::spontaneous diastolic depolarization}}.
extraInfo: This phase accounts for the automaticity of nodal cells.

text: The {{c1::slope}} of Phase 4 in the SA node determines the heart rate.
extraInfo: A steeper slope leads to a faster heart rate.

text: Phase 4 depolarization is primarily driven by the {{c1::funny current (If)}}.
extraInfo: If is a mixed inward Na+/K+ current.

text: The funny current ($I_f$) flows through {{c1::HCN}} channels.
extraInfo: HCN stands for Hyperpolarization-activated Cyclic Nucleotide-gated channels.

text: HCN channels are activated by {{c1::hyperpolarization}} during the end of the previous repolarization.
extraInfo: This ensures the cycle repeats automatically.

text: Sympathetic stimulation (via beta-1 receptors) increases the slope of Phase 4 by increasing {{c1::cAMP}}.
extraInfo: This increases the probability that $I_f$ channels are open.

text: Parasympathetic stimulation (ACh) {{c1::decreases}} the slope of Phase 4 and heart rate.
extraInfo: It also hyperpolarizes the cell by increasing K+ conductance.

text: The {{c1::SA node}} is the default pacemaker because it has the fastest rate of Phase 4 depolarization.
extraInfo: It suppresses other potential pacemakers through overdrive suppression.

text: The intrinsic rate of the {{c1::AV node}} is 40-60 bpm, which is slower than the SA node.
extraInfo: The AV node takes over if the SA node fails.

text: {{c1::Adenosine}} and Acetylcholine decrease the heart rate by decreasing the slope of phase 4.
extraInfo: They also increase K+ efflux, hyperpolarizing the cell.

text: The threshold for triggering Phase 0 in a pacemaker cell is approximately {{c1::-40}} mV.
extraInfo: Once reached, voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels open.

text: Sympathetic stimulation shifts the action potential threshold to a {{c1::more negative (lower)}} voltage.
extraInfo: This makes it easier and faster to trigger an action potential.

text: The drug {{c1::Ivabradine}} selectively inhibits the funny current ($I_f$).
extraInfo: It is used to reduce heart rate without affecting contractility.

text: Conduction velocity is {{c1::slowest}} in the AV node.
extraInfo: This allows for a delay to ensure ventricular filling.

text: Conduction velocity is {{c1::fastest}} in the Purkinje system.
extraInfo: This ensures nearly simultaneous contraction of the ventricles.

text: The correct order of conduction velocity from fastest to slowest is {{c1::Purkinje > Atria > Ventricles > AV node}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: He Park At Venture Avenue.

text: The SA node is located at the junction of the {{c1::superior vena cava}} and the right atrium.
extraInfo: It is usually supplied by the SA nodal artery.

text: The AV node is located in the posteroinferior part of the {{c1::interatrial septum}}.
extraInfo: It is located within the Triangle of Koch.

text: Calcium channel blockers (like Verapamil) {{c1::decrease}} the slope of Phase 0 and Phase 4 in nodal cells.
extraInfo: This slows the heart rate and conduction velocity (negative chronotropy and dromotropy).

text: In pacemaker cells, Phase 0 has a {{c1::slower}} upstroke compared to the rapid Na+-driven upstroke in myocytes.
extraInfo: Calcium channels open more slowly than sodium channels.

text: The maximal diastolic potential (the most negative point) in a pacemaker cell is about {{c1::-60}} mV.
extraInfo: There is no true resting membrane potential.

text: Beta-blockers decrease heart rate by {{c1::decreasing}} the slope of phase 4.
extraInfo: This is particularly useful for controlling the rate in atrial fibrillation.

text: ACh decreases the heart rate by decreasing the slope of Phase 4 and increasing {{c1::K+}} conductance.
extraInfo: The increased K+ efflux hyperpolarizes the cell.

text: The intrinsic pacemaker rate of the Purkinje fibers is {{c1::15-40}} bpm.
extraInfo: This is the slowest intrinsic rate in the heart.

text: The SA node is the default pacemaker of the heart because it has the {{c1::fastest}} rate of spontaneous depolarization.
extraInfo: The rate of SA node discharge is roughly 60-100 bpm.

text: The SA node is located at the junction of the {{c1::superior vena cava}} and the {{c2::right atrium}}.
extraInfo: It is located in the upper portion of the sulcus terminalis.

text: The AV node delay (represented by the PR interval) allows time for {{c1::ventricular filling}}.
extraInfo: This delay ensures the atria contract before the ventricles.

text: The AV node is located in the {{c1::posteroinferior}} part of the interatrial septum.
extraInfo: It is located near the opening of the coronary sinus in the Koch triangle.

text: The conduction speed order from fastest to slowest is: {{c1::Purkinje}} > Atria > Ventricles > {{c2::AV node}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: He ParkS At Venture (His-Purkinje, Atria, Ventricles, AV node).

text: The hierarchy of pacemaker rates is: {{c1::SA node}} > {{c2::AV node}} > {{c3::Bundle of His/Purkinje}}.
extraInfo: SA node: 60-100; AV node: 40-60; His/Purkinje: 20-40 bpm.

text: The P wave on an ECG represents {{c1::atrial depolarization}}.
extraInfo: Atrial repolarization is normally not seen as it is buried in the QRS complex.

text: Atrial repolarization is typically not visible on an ECG because it is masked by the {{c1::QRS complex}}.
extraInfo: The QRS signal is much stronger than the atrial repolarization signal.

text: A normal PR interval lasts between {{c1::0.12 and 0.20}} seconds.
extraInfo: This corresponds to 3-5 small boxes on ECG paper.

text: The QRS complex represents {{c1::ventricular depolarization}}.
extraInfo: Its duration is typically < 120 ms.

text: A widened QRS complex ( > 120 ms) suggests {{c1::Bundle Branch Block}} or a ventricular origin of the beat.
extraInfo: Normally, ventricular depolarization occurs rapidly via the His-Purkinje system.

text: The T wave on an ECG represents {{c1::ventricular repolarization}}.
extraInfo: T wave inversion can be a sign of ischemia or recent MI.

text: T wave inversion on an ECG can be indicative of {{c1::ischemia}} or recent myocardial infarction.
extraInfo: It can also be seen in ventricular hypertrophy.

text: The QT interval represents the time required for ventricular {{c1::depolarization and repolarization}}.
extraInfo: A prolonged QT interval increases the risk of sudden cardiac death.

text: The {{c1::ST segment}} is the isoelectric period when both ventricles are completely depolarized.
extraInfo: Deviations from the isoelectric line indicate pathology like STEMI or ischemia.

text: A prominent U wave on an ECG is classically associated with {{c1::hypokalemia}}.
extraInfo: It can also be seen in bradycardia.

text: The J point is the junction between the end of the {{c1::QRS complex}} and the start of the {{c2::ST segment}}.
extraInfo: Elevated J points can be seen in early repolarization or STEMI.

text: Prolongation of the {{c1::QT interval}} predisposes patients to Torsades de Pointes.
extraInfo: Certain drugs (ABCDE: Antiarrhythmics, Antibiotics, 'C'ychotics, Diuretics, Emesis) can cause this.

text: In the majority of people, the SA node is supplied by the {{c1::right coronary artery (RCA)}}.
extraInfo: The nodal artery usually branches from the RCA.

text: In right-dominant hearts, the AV node is supplied by the {{c1::right coronary artery (RCA)}}.
extraInfo: It arises from the posterior descending artery (PDA).

text: The {{c1::delta wave}} is a characteristic ECG finding in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome.
extraInfo: It represents early ventricular depolarization through an accessory pathway.

text: In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, the electrical impulse bypasses the AV node via the {{c1::Bundle of Kent}}.
extraInfo: This accessory pathway allows for pre-excitation of the ventricles.

text: A shortened PR interval and a widened QRS with a slurred upstroke are signs of {{c1::Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW)}} syndrome.
extraInfo: The 'slurred upstroke' is the delta wave.

text: Peaked T waves on an ECG are a classic sign of {{c1::hyperkalemia}}.
extraInfo: This is often the earliest ECG change seen in high potassium levels.

text: ST-segment elevation indicates {{c1::transmural}} ischemia or infarction.
extraInfo: This is the hallmark of a STEMI (ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction).

text: ST-segment depression generally indicates {{c1::subendocardial}} ischemia.
extraInfo: It is often seen in NSTEMI or stable/unstable angina during exercise.

text: The PR interval is shortened in {{c1::Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW)}} syndrome due to pre-excitation.
extraInfo: The accessory pathway bypasses the normal AV node delay.

text: The {{c1::Purkinje fibers}} have the highest conduction velocity in the cardiac conduction system.
extraInfo: This allows for simultaneous contraction of the entire ventricular mass.

text: The {{c1::AV node}} has the slowest conduction velocity in the heart's conduction system.
extraInfo: This slow conduction is what creates the physiological PR delay.

text: {{c1::Atrial}} natriuretic peptide is released from atrial myocytes in response to increased {{c2::blood volume}} and atrial pressure.
extraInfo: ANP acts as a check on the RAAS system.

text: {{c1::B-type}} (ventricular) natriuretic peptide is released from {{c2::ventricular}} myocytes in response to increased tension.
extraInfo: Despite its name, BNP was originally identified in pig brain, but is physiologically significant in the heart.

text: ANP and BNP both act via {{c1::cGMP}} as a second messenger.
extraInfo: They activate membrane-bound guanylyl cyclase.

text: Natriuretic peptides lead to {{c1::vasodilation}} and {{c2::decreased}} Na+ reabsorption at the renal tubule.
extraInfo: This results in decreased peripheral resistance and increased sodium excretion (natriuresis).

text: ANP and BNP {{c1::dilate}} the afferent renal arterioles and {{c2::constrict}} the efferent renal arterioles.
extraInfo: This mechanism increases the GFR.

text: The net effect of ANP/BNP on the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is an {{c1::increase}}.
extraInfo: This contributes to the natriuretic effect by increasing the filtered load of sodium.

text: ANP/BNP decrease Na+ reabsorption in the {{c1::medullary collecting duct}}.
extraInfo: This is a direct inhibitory effect on sodium transport in the distal nephron.

text: ANP/BNP {{c1::inhibit}} the secretion of renin.
extraInfo: This helps shut down the RAAS pathway.

text: ANP/BNP {{c1::inhibit}} the secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex.
extraInfo: Specifically, they act on the zona glomerulosa.

text: BNP is a blood test used to diagnose {{c1::heart failure}} because it has a high {{c2::negative predictive value}}.
extraInfo: If BNP is low, heart failure is very unlikely to be the cause of dyspnea.

text: {{c1::Nesiritide}} is a recombinant form of BNP used in the treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
extraInfo: It causes vasodilation and diuresis.

text: The enzyme {{c1::neprilysin}} is responsible for the degradation of ANP and BNP.
extraInfo: Neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II and bradykinin.

text: {{c1::Sacubitril}} is a drug that acts as a neprilysin inhibitor.
extraInfo: By inhibiting neprilysin, it increases the levels of beneficial natriuretic peptides.

text: Sacubitril is combined with {{c1::valsartan}} to treat heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).
extraInfo: This combination is known as an ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor).

text: Sacubitril must be used with an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor to prevent {{c1::angioedema}}.
extraInfo: Both ACE inhibitors and neprilysin inhibitors increase bradykinin levels.

text: ANP/BNP are responsible for the '{{c1::aldosterone escape}}' phenomenon in Primary Hyperaldosteronism.
extraInfo: This prevents the development of overt hypernatremia and significant edema despite high aldosterone.

text: In Primary Hyperaldosteronism, patients do not develop {{c1::pitting edema}} due to the effects of ANP/BNP.
extraInfo: Pressure natriuresis and ANP release maintain a relatively stable volume state.

text: ANP/BNP promote {{c1::natriuresis}} and {{c2::diuresis}}.
extraInfo: Natriuresis is the excretion of sodium; diuresis is the excretion of water.

text: The second messenger cGMP activated by ANP leads to the relaxation of {{c1::vascular smooth muscle}}.
extraInfo: This is similar to the mechanism of Nitric Oxide (which uses soluble guanylyl cyclase).

text: ANP is released specifically in response to {{c1::atrial stretch}}.
extraInfo: This occurs in states of volume overload (e.g., HF, renal failure).

text: High levels of BNP can be seen in {{c1::chronic kidney disease}} due to reduced renal clearance.
extraInfo: Context is important when interpreting BNP levels in patients with renal dysfunction.

text: Natriuretic peptides essentially act as physiological {{c1::antagonists}} to the RAAS system.
extraInfo: They work to lower blood pressure and volume while RAAS works to raise them.

text: ANP and BNP lead to decreased {{c1::systemic vascular resistance (SVR)}}.
extraInfo: This is achieved through direct vasodilation of peripheral arteries and veins.

text: BNP is synthesized as a pro-hormone called {{c1::proBNP}}.
extraInfo: It is cleaved into active BNP and the inactive NT-proBNP.

text: The inactive fragment {{c1::NT-proBNP}} can also be measured clinically to assess for heart failure.
extraInfo: It has a longer half-life than active BNP.

text: ANP and BNP contribute to the decrease in {{c1::preload}} and {{c2::afterload}} on the heart.
extraInfo: Vasodilation decreases afterload; natriuresis/diuresis decreases preload.

text: The primary trigger for BNP release is ventricular {{c1::wall stress}}.
extraInfo: This stress is often caused by increased end-diastolic pressure.

text: ANP/BNP directly inhibit the {{c1::sympathetic}} nervous system's outflow.
extraInfo: This further aids in reducing blood pressure and heart rate.

text: During an acute MI, BNP levels {{c1::increase}} due to ventricular wall stress and ischemia.
extraInfo: Elevated BNP following MI is a marker of poor prognosis.

text: The carotid sinus baroreceptor transmits afferent signals via the {{c1::glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)}} to the medulla.
extraInfo: The carotid sinus is located at the bifurcation of the carotid arteries.

text: The aortic arch baroreceptor transmits afferent signals via the {{c1::vagus nerve (CN X)}} to the medulla.
extraInfo: The aortic arch primarily responds to changes in high blood pressure.

text: Afferent signals from both baroreceptors and chemoreceptors terminate in the {{c1::nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)}} of the medulla.
extraInfo: The NTS is the sensory integration center for cardiovascular control.

text: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) are stimulated by a PO2 of less than {{c1::60}} mm Hg.
extraInfo: They also respond to increased PCO2 and decreased pH of the blood.

text: Central chemoreceptors are stimulated by changes in the pH and PCO2 of the {{c1::brain interstitial fluid}}.
extraInfo: Central chemoreceptors do not directly respond to PO2.

text: In the central chemoreceptor response, {{c1::CO2}} can cross the blood-brain barrier, while H+ cannot.
extraInfo: Once CO2 crosses, it reacts with water to form H+, which then stimulates the receptors.

text: In patients with chronic hypercapnia (e.g., COPD), central chemoreceptors become {{c1::less}} responsive to PCO2.
extraInfo: This leads to a dependence on peripheral chemoreceptors to drive respiration via O2 sensing.

text: In chronic hypercapnia, the body relies on {{c1::peripheral}} chemoreceptors to detect low O2 levels to drive respiration.
extraInfo: This is known as the hypoxic drive.

text: Hypotension results in {{c1::decreased}} stretch of the baroreceptors, which {{c2::decreases}} their afferent firing rate.
extraInfo: Decreased firing leads to compensatory sympathetic activation.

text: Decreased afferent baroreceptor firing causes a(n) {{c1::increase}} in efferent sympathetic firing.
extraInfo: This results in vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and increased contractility.

text: Decreased afferent baroreceptor firing causes a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in efferent parasympathetic stimulation.
extraInfo: This helps to increase the heart rate.

text: The baroreceptor reflex is an essential component of the body's response to {{c1::hypovolemic}} shock.
extraInfo: It attempts to maintain blood pressure through vasoconstriction and tachycardia.

text: Carotid sinus massage increases {{c1::pressure/stretch}} on the carotid sinus, causing the brain to perceive high blood pressure.
extraInfo: This triggers a reflex to lower blood pressure and heart rate.

text: Carotid massage increases the {{c1::AV node}} refractory period, which decreases the heart rate.
extraInfo: This can be used to terminate certain supraventricular tachycardias.

text: The Cushing reflex triad consists of hypertension, bradycardia, and {{c1::respiratory depression}}.
extraInfo: This triad indicates severely increased intracranial pressure (ICP).

text: In the Cushing reflex, increased intracranial pressure leads to {{c1::cerebral ischemia}}.
extraInfo: The ischemia results in an accumulation of CO2 and a decrease in pH.

text: In the Cushing reflex, the sympathetic nervous system is activated to increase {{c1::perfusion pressure}} (hypertension).
extraInfo: This is an attempt to overcome the high ICP and restore cerebral blood flow.

text: The bradycardia in the Cushing reflex is a {{c1::baroreceptor}}-mediated reflex to the high blood pressure.
extraInfo: Increased BP increases stretch, leading to increased vagal tone.

text: The {{c1::carotid body}} is a peripheral chemoreceptor, whereas the {{c2::carotid sinus}} is a baroreceptor.
extraInfo: Both are located near the carotid bifurcation but serve different sensory functions.

text: Central chemoreceptors are {{c1::not}} directly responsive to PO2 levels.
extraInfo: They only sense changes in CO2 and pH.

text: Efferent parasympathetic signals to the heart are carried by the {{c1::vagus nerve}}.
extraInfo: The vagus nerve specifically acts on the SA and AV nodes.

text: Aortic arch baroreceptors transmit afferent information via the {{c1::vagus}} nerve, which then travels to the medulla.
extraInfo: Note that CN X serves as both afferent for the aortic arch and efferent for the heart.

text: Carotid sinus massage can lead to peripheral {{c1::vasodilation}}.
extraInfo: This contributes to the drop in blood pressure and potential syncope.

text: Exaggerated responses to carotid sinus pressure are more common in older patients with {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
extraInfo: Atherosclerotic plaques can increase the sensitivity of the baroreceptors.

text: The aortic body peripheral chemoreceptor transmits afferent signals via the {{c1::vagus nerve (CN X)}}.
extraInfo: The aortic body is located on the aortic arch.

text: The carotid body peripheral chemoreceptor transmits afferent signals via the {{c1::glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)}}.
extraInfo: It detects changes in arterial O2, CO2, and pH.

text: In the Cushing reflex, high ICP constricts {{c1::arterioles}} in the brain, leading to ischemia.
extraInfo: This triggers the sympathetic surge to raise systemic MAP.

text: Unlike other organs, hypoxia in the lungs causes {{c1::vasoconstriction}}.
extraInfo: This is known as hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which shunts blood to better-ventilated alveoli.

text: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond specifically to the {{c1::partial pressure}} of oxygen (PO2).
extraInfo: They do not respond to oxygen content (e.g., anemia or CO poisoning).

text: The normal mean {{c1::right atrial}} pressure is {{c2::< 5}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Measured as Central Venous Pressure (CVP).

text: Normal right ventricular systolic pressure is approximately {{c1::25}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Matches the systolic pressure of the pulmonary artery.

text: Normal right ventricular diastolic pressure is approximately {{c1::5}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Significantly lower than left ventricular diastolic pressure.

text: Normal pulmonary artery systolic pressure is approximately {{c1::25}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Elevated in pulmonary hypertension.

text: Normal pulmonary artery diastolic pressure is approximately {{c1::10}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Higher than RV diastolic pressure due to pulmonic valve closure.

text: The {{c1::PCWP}} is a clinical proxy for {{c2::left atrial}} pressure.
extraInfo: Measured using a Swan-Ganz catheter.

text: Normal Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) is less than {{c1::12}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Elevated in left-sided heart failure.

text: Normal left ventricular systolic pressure is approximately {{c1::130}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Should equal aortic systolic pressure in the absence of stenosis.

text: Normal left ventricular diastolic pressure is approximately {{c1::10}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Measured as LVEDP at the end of diastole.

text: Normal aortic systolic pressure is approximately {{c1::130}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Peak pressure during ventricular contraction.

text: Normal aortic diastolic pressure is approximately {{c1::90}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Maintained by the elastic recoil of the large arteries.

text: Pulmonary artery systolic pressure is normally {{c1::equal}} to right ventricular systolic pressure.
extraInfo: A gradient suggests pulmonic valve stenosis.

text: Aortic systolic pressure is normally {{c1::equal}} to left ventricular systolic pressure.
extraInfo: A gradient suggests aortic valve stenosis.

text: During diastole, aortic pressure is much {{c1::higher}} than left ventricular pressure.
extraInfo: The aortic valve is closed, preventing backflow while the LV relaxes.

text: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) is calculated as {{c1::1/3}} (Systolic BP) + {{c2::2/3}} (Diastolic BP).
extraInfo: Alternatively: MAP = CO x SVR.

text: {{c1::Pulse pressure}} is defined as the difference between the systolic and diastolic blood pressures.
extraInfo: Proportional to stroke volume; inversely proportional to arterial compliance.

text: A PCWP greater than {{c1::18}} mmHg strongly suggests {{c2::cardiogenic pulmonary edema}}.
extraInfo: Reflects high back-pressure from the left heart.

text: In the absence of mitral valve disease, PCWP is a reliable estimate of {{c1::Left Ventricular End-Diastolic Pressure (LVEDP)}}.
extraInfo: Mitral stenosis would cause PCWP to be higher than LVEDP.

text: The lowest pressure in the entire systemic circulatory circuit is found in the {{c1::right atrium}}.
extraInfo: Facilitates venous return.

text: The {{c1::Swan-Ganz}} catheter is a balloon-tipped catheter used to measure {{c2::PCWP}}.
extraInfo: Also called a pulmonary artery catheter.

text: Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) > {{c1::20}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Defined at rest; updated clinical guidelines.

text: {{c1::Central Venous Pressure (CVP)}} is equivalent to the pressure in the right atrium.
extraInfo: Reflects fluid status and right-heart function.

text: The greatest pressure drop in the vascular system occurs across the {{c1::arterioles}}.
extraInfo: These are the primary resistance vessels.

text: The formula for SVR is ({{c1::MAP}} - {{c2::CVP}}) / {{c3::CO}}.
extraInfo: Analogous to Ohm's Law (R = V/I).

text: The formula for PVR is ({{c1::mPAP}} - {{c2::PCWP}}) / {{c3::CO}}.
extraInfo: mPAP = mean pulmonary artery pressure.

text: Oxygen saturation in the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary artery is normally about {{c1::75%}}.
extraInfo: Mixed venous oxygen saturation.

text: In a normal heart, left atrial pressure is slightly {{c1::higher}} than right atrial pressure.
extraInfo: Ensures closure of the foramen ovale after birth.

text: A significant oxygen step-up from the right atrium to the {{c1::right ventricle}} suggests a {{c2::Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)}}.
extraInfo: Left-to-right shunt increases O2 content in the RV.

text: A significant oxygen step-up from the right ventricle to the {{c1::pulmonary artery}} suggests a {{c2::Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)}}.
extraInfo: Oxygenated blood from the aorta enters the pulmonary artery.

text: The primary local factors regulating coronary blood flow are {{c1::adenosine}}, {{c2::NO}}, and CO2.
extraInfo: Adenosine is a byproduct of ATP breakdown and is a potent vasodilator.

text: The most important factor for cerebral blood flow autoregulation is {{c1::PCO2}} (or pH).
extraInfo: Hypercapnia (high CO2) causes vasodilation to increase blood flow and wash out CO2.

text: Kidney autoregulation is maintained by the {{c1::myogenic mechanism}} and {{c2::tubuloglomerular feedback}}.
extraInfo: This keeps GFR and RPF constant over a wide range of blood pressures.

text: In the lungs, hypoxia causes {{c1::vasoconstriction}}.
extraInfo: This is unique (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) and shunts blood to well-ventilated areas.

text: During exercise, skeletal muscle blood flow is regulated by {{c1::local metabolites}} (CHAL: CO2, H+, Adenosine, Lactate, K+).
extraInfo: Metabolic demand dictates flow during activity, overriding sympathetic tone.

text: At rest, skeletal muscle blood flow is primarily controlled by {{c1::sympathetic tone}}.
extraInfo: Alpha-1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction at rest.

text: Skin blood flow is primarily regulated by the {{c1::sympathetic nervous system}} for the purpose of {{c2::thermoregulation}}.
extraInfo: The skin has very little metabolic autoregulation.

text: Most coronary blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during {{c1::diastole}}.
extraInfo: During systole, the high intramyocardial pressure compresses the coronary vessels.

text: The myogenic mechanism involves vascular smooth muscle {{c1::constriction}} in response to increased wall stretch.
extraInfo: This is mediated by pressure-sensitive Ca2+ channels.

text: Cerebral blood flow is constant between a Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) of {{c1::60}} and {{c2::150}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Outside this range, the brain is at risk for ischemia (low MAP) or edema/hemorrhage (high MAP).

text: In the brain, blood flow increases significantly only when PaO2 drops below {{c1::60}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Severe hypoxia is a potent stimulus for cerebral vasodilation.

text: The {{c1::subendocardium}} is the most vulnerable region of the heart to ischemia.
extraInfo: It experiences the highest pressure during systole, which limits blood flow.

text: In TGF, the macula densa senses an increase in {{c1::NaCl}} delivery and causes afferent arteriole constriction.
extraInfo: This protects the kidney from high pressure and prevents excessive salt loss.

text: Autoregulation in the kidney primarily acts by changing the resistance of the {{c1::afferent}} arteriole.
extraInfo: The efferent arteriole is more sensitive to Angiotensin II.

text: Therapeutic {{c1::hyperventilation}} is used to reduce ICP by causing cerebral vasoconstriction.
extraInfo: Decreasing PCO2 leads to vasoconstriction, decreasing cerebral blood volume.

text: The coronary vasodilator Nitric Oxide (NO) is produced by {{c1::endothelial cells}} in response to shear stress.
extraInfo: NO stimulates guanylate cyclase to increase cGMP, causing smooth muscle relaxation.

text: The heart has a very high baseline O2 extraction of approximately {{c1::75}}%.
extraInfo: Because extraction is already near-maximal, oxygen delivery to the heart must be increased by increasing blood flow.

text: The {{c1::hepatic arterial buffer response}} describes the increase in hepatic artery flow when portal vein flow decreases.
extraInfo: This is mediated by adenosine washout in the space of Mall.

text: Autoregulation is the ability of an organ to maintain constant blood flow despite changes in {{c1::perfusion pressure}}.
extraInfo: Flow = Pressure / Resistance; as pressure rises, resistance rises to keep flow stable.

text: Adenosine causes vasodilation in the heart by binding to {{c1::A2}} receptors on vascular smooth muscle.
extraInfo: This increases cAMP, leading to relaxation.

text: During the onset of exercise, {{c1::K+}} ions released during muscle action potentials act as an early vasodilator.
extraInfo: This contributes to 'active hyperemia'.

text: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) serves to optimize {{c1::ventilation-perfusion (V/Q)}} matching.
extraInfo: It prevents 'wasted' perfusion to areas of the lung that are not ventilated.

text: In skeletal muscle, epinephrine at low doses causes vasodilation via {{c1::beta-2}} receptors.
extraInfo: At higher doses, the alpha-1 effect (vasoconstriction) may dominate.

text: Stretch-activated ion channels in the myogenic mechanism allow the influx of {{c1::Calcium (Ca2+)}}.
extraInfo: Calcium binds to calmodulin, activating MLCK to cause contraction.

text: Autoregulation in the kidney ensures that {{c1::GFR}} and {{c2::RPF}} remain stable during fluctuations in MAP.
extraInfo: MAP range for renal autoregulation is typically 80-180 mmHg.

text: Heat loss in the skin is regulated by {{c1::arteriovenous (AV) anastomoses}} in the fingertips and nose.
extraInfo: Sympathetic withdrawal allows blood to bypass the shunts and fill the venous plexuses for cooling.

text: The most important determinant of coronary blood flow is myocardial {{c1::oxygen demand (MVO2)}}.
extraInfo: Flow is 'pulled' by metabolic need rather than 'pushed' by pressure.

text: Increased arterial PCO2 leads to a decrease in perivascular {{c1::pH}}, which triggers cerebral vasodilation.
extraInfo: Protons (H+) are thought to be the direct mediators of the vessel relaxation.

text: The JGA senses blood pressure drops via the baroreceptors in the {{c1::afferent}} arteriole, triggering renin release.
extraInfo: This is distinct from the macula densa's role in tubuloglomerular feedback.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: The Starling equation for net fluid flux ($J_v$) is: $J_v = {{c1::K_f}} [(P_c - P_i) - σ(π_c - π_i)]$.
extraInfo: K_f is the filtration coefficient, representing capillary permeability and surface area.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: The primary force favoring filtration (movement out of the capillary) is {{c1::capillary hydrostatic pressure ($P_c$)}}.
extraInfo: P_c is determined by arterial and venous pressures and resistances.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: The primary force opposing filtration (favoring absorption) is {{c1::capillary oncotic pressure (π_c)}}.
extraInfo: Capillary oncotic pressure is primarily determined by the concentration of plasma proteins, mainly albumin.
