topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: In the Starling equation, the term σ represents the {{c1::reflection coefficient}}, which measures the capillary's permeability to {{c2::proteins}}.
extraInfo: A reflection coefficient of 1 means the membrane is impermeable to proteins; 0 means it is fully permeable.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Edema in heart failure is primarily caused by an {{c1::increase}} in {{c2::capillary hydrostatic pressure ($P_c$)}}.
extraInfo: Backward failure leads to increased venous pressure, which increases P_c.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Nephrotic syndrome causes edema by {{c1::decreasing}} the {{c2::capillary oncotic pressure (π_c)}}.
extraInfo: This is due to the loss of albumin in the urine (proteinuria).

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Liver failure (cirrhosis) leads to edema/ascites by {{c1::decreasing}} the production of {{c2::albumin}}, which lowers π_c.
extraInfo: Decreased protein synthesis results in reduced plasma oncotic pressure.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: In inflammation, edema is caused by an increase in {{c1::capillary permeability}} ($K_f$).
extraInfo: Inflammatory mediators like histamine cause endothelial contraction and widening of intercellular clefts.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Lymphatic obstruction leads to edema by increasing the {{c1::interstitial oncotic pressure (π_i)}}.
extraInfo: Failure to remove proteins from the interstitium increases the local oncotic pressure, favoring filtration.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Normally, there is a net {{c1::filtration}} of fluid at the arterial end and a net {{c2::absorption}} at the venous end.
extraInfo: Small amounts of fluid not reabsorbed at the venous end are returned via the lymphatics.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: The interstitial hydrostatic pressure ($P_i$) is typically close to {{c1::zero}} or slightly {{c2::negative}}.
extraInfo: This favors filtration into the interstitial space.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Arteriolar {{c1::constriction}} decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure ($P_c$), whereas arteriolar {{c2::dilation}} increases it.
extraInfo: Think of the arteriole as a faucet; closing it drops the pressure downstream in the capillary.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Venous {{c1::constriction}} or obstruction leads to an {{c2::increase}} in capillary hydrostatic pressure ($P_c$).
extraInfo: This is a common mechanism for localized edema in Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT).

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: The $K_f$ (filtration coefficient) is a product of capillary {{c1::permeability}} and {{c2::surface area}}.
extraInfo: Conditions that increase surface area (recruitment) or permeability (burns/toxins) increase K_f.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: A reflection coefficient (σ) of {{c1::1.0}} indicates a membrane that is totally impermeable to solutes (e.g., the blood-brain barrier).
extraInfo: In this state, the full osmotic pressure gradient is realized.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: An exudate is an edema fluid characterized by {{c1::high}} protein content, usually resulting from {{c2::increased capillary permeability}}.
extraInfo: Contrast this with transudate, which has low protein content.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Transudate is characterized by {{c1::low}} protein content and results from {{c2::hydrostatic}} or {{c2::oncotic}} pressure changes.
extraInfo: Common in CHF or Cirrhosis.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Pulmonary edema in left-sided heart failure is caused by an increase in {{c1::pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure}}.
extraInfo: Backup from the left atrium into pulmonary veins increases P_c in the lungs.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: The Starling force that changes the most as blood moves from the arterial to the venous end of the capillary is {{c1::capillary hydrostatic pressure ($P_c$)}}.
extraInfo: P_c drops along the length of the capillary due to resistance.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Severe burns cause massive edema by increasing {{c1::capillary permeability ($K_f$)}} and decreasing {{c2::capillary oncotic pressure (π_c)}}.
extraInfo: Endothelial damage increases permeability, and loss of plasma proteins lowers oncotic pressure.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Standing for long periods increases edema in the lower extremities due to an increase in {{c1::venous pressure}} leading to increased {{c2::P_c}}.
extraInfo: Gravity increases the hydrostatic pressure column in the veins and capillaries.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Kwashiorkor (malnutrition) causes edema due to a deficiency in {{c1::protein}} intake, which leads to decreased {{c2::π_c}}.
extraInfo: Reduced albumin synthesis is the driving factor.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Lymphatic drainage {{c1::decreases}} the interstitial hydrostatic pressure ($P_i$) and {{c2::decreases}} the interstitial oncotic pressure (π_i).
extraInfo: By removing fluid and escaped proteins, lymphatics prevent edema.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: If the net driving force is positive, {{c1::filtration}} occurs; if negative, {{c2::absorption}} occurs.
extraInfo: Net Driving Force = (P_c - P_i) - σ(π_c - π_i).

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: A reflection coefficient (σ) of {{c1::0}} means the membrane is completely permeable to protein, meaning protein exerts {{c2::no}} effective osmotic pressure.
extraInfo: In this scenario, π_c and π_i would eventually equalize.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Myxedema in hypothyroidism is caused by the accumulation of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans}} in the interstitium, which increases {{c2::interstitial oncotic pressure (π_i)}}.
extraInfo: This 'traps' water in the skin, causing non-pitting edema.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: During exercise, $K_f$ increases because of {{c1::capillary recruitment}}, which increases the total {{c2::surface area}} available for exchange.
extraInfo: More open capillaries = higher surface area = higher K_f.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: Increased venous resistance {{c1::increases}} capillary hydrostatic pressure ($P_c$), while increased arteriolar resistance {{c2::decreases}} $P_c$.
extraInfo: Resistance upstream (arteriole) protects the capillary from pressure; resistance downstream (vein) backs it up.

topic: Capillary fluid exchange and Starling forces
text: The Starling force that 'sucks' fluid into the capillary is {{c1::capillary oncotic pressure (π_c)}}.
extraInfo: Often called 'colloid osmotic pressure'.

text: Right-to-left shunts cause early {{c1::cyanosis}} because deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs and enters the systemic circulation.
extraInfo: Commonly referred to as "blue babies."

text: The five common causes of right-to-left shunts all start with the letter {{c1::T}}.
extraInfo: 1. Truncus arteriosus, 2. Transposition, 3. Tricuspid atresia, 4. Tetralogy of Fallot, 5. TAPVR.

text: {{c1::Persistent truncus arteriosus}} occurs when the truncus fails to divide into the pulmonary artery and the aorta.
extraInfo: This is due to failure of aorticopulmonary septum formation.

text: Persistent truncus arteriosus is most commonly associated with {{c1::DiGeorge (22q11 deletion)}} syndrome.
extraInfo: Requires a VSD to be present to function.

text: In Transposition of the Great Vessels (TGA), the aorta leaves the {{c1::right ventricle}} and the pulmonary artery leaves the {{c2::left ventricle}}.
extraInfo: This results in two separate, parallel circuits.

text: Transposition of the Great Vessels is due to a failure of the {{c1::aorticopulmonary septum}} to spiral.
extraInfo: It is incompatible with life unless a shunt (VSD, ASD, or PDA) is present.

text: Transposition of the Great Vessels is strongly associated with maternal {{c1::diabetes}}.
extraInfo: Infants often present with cyanosis immediately after birth.

text: The classic X-ray finding for Transposition of the Great Vessels is an "{{c1::egg on a string}}" appearance.
extraInfo: The narrow mediastinum represents the aorta and pulmonary artery being parallel.

text: In cases of Transposition of the Great Vessels, {{c1::Prostaglandin E1}} is administered to keep the PDA open.
extraInfo: This allows for blood mixing until surgical intervention can occur.

text: Tricuspid atresia is characterized by the absence of the tricuspid valve, leading to a hypoplastic {{c1::right}} ventricle.
extraInfo: Requires both an ASD and a VSD for viability.

text: The four classic findings of Tetralogy of Fallot are: 1. Pulmonary infundibular stenosis, 2. {{c1::Right ventricular hypertrophy}}, 3. {{c2::Overriding aorta}}, and 4. {{c3::VSD}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: PROV.

text: The single most important determinant for the degree of cyanosis in Tetralogy of Fallot is {{c1::pulmonary infundibular stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Increased obstruction forces more deoxygenated blood through the VSD into the aorta.

text: The classic X-ray finding for Tetralogy of Fallot is a {{c1::boot-shaped}} heart.
extraInfo: Caused by right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) elevating the apex.

text: Patients with Tetralogy of Fallot experience "tet spells" and often squat to increase {{c1::systemic vascular resistance (SVR)}}.
extraInfo: Increasing SVR reduces the right-to-left shunt across the VSD, improving oxygenation.

text: Tetralogy of Fallot is caused by an {{c1::anterosuperior}} displacement of the infundibular septum.
extraInfo: This displacement leads to the four characteristic defects.

text: In Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return (TAPVR), the pulmonary veins drain into the {{c1::right heart (e.g., SVC or coronary sinus)}}.
extraInfo: Requires an ASD (and sometimes a PDA) to allow blood to reach the left side of the heart.

text: The classic X-ray finding associated with TAPVR is the "{{c1::snowman}}" sign.
extraInfo: Represented by a dilated vertical vein and SVC.

text: Ebstein anomaly involves the displacement of the {{c1::tricuspid}} valve leaflets down into the right ventricle.
extraInfo: This results in "atrialization" of the right ventricle.

text: Ebstein anomaly is classically associated with maternal {{c1::lithium}} exposure during pregnancy.
extraInfo: It often leads to severe tricuspid regurgitation and right heart failure.

text: Ebstein anomaly is highly associated with which pre-excitation syndrome? {{c1::Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW)}}.
extraInfo: Patients may present with SVT.

text: Eisenmenger syndrome occurs when a chronic {{c1::left-to-right}} shunt leads to pulmonary hypertension, eventually reversing the shunt.
extraInfo: This results in late-onset cyanosis.

text: The primary mechanism of Eisenmenger syndrome is increased pulmonary resistance caused by {{c1::pulmonary vascular remodeling}}.
extraInfo: Right ventricular pressure eventually exceeds left ventricular pressure.

text: Clinical features of Eisenmenger syndrome include cyanosis, {{c1::clubbing}}, and polycythemia.
extraInfo: Polycythemia occurs as a compensatory response to chronic hypoxemia.

text: Persistent truncus arteriosus is the result of the failure of {{c1::neural crest}} cells to migrate and form the septum.
extraInfo: Neural crest cells are essential for truncal and bulbar ridge formation.

text: In Tetralogy of Fallot, the murmur heard is typically a {{c1::harsh systolic ejection}} murmur.
extraInfo: The murmur is actually from the pulmonary stenosis, not the VSD.

text: While most R-to-L shunts cause cyanosis at birth, Eisenmenger syndrome causes {{c1::late}} cyanosis.
extraInfo: It typically presents in late childhood or adulthood.

text: A right-to-left shunt can allow an embolus from the venous system to enter the systemic arterial circulation, known as a {{c1::paradoxical}} embolism.
extraInfo: This can result in a stroke (brain infarct) from a DVT.

text: Tricuspid atresia results in a right-to-left shunt at the level of the {{c1::atria}}.
extraInfo: An ASD is necessary for blood to exit the right atrium.

text: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) is often associated with a {{c1::supracardiac}} drainage into the innominate vein or SVC.
extraInfo: This leads to the dilated appearance on X-ray.

text: The three most common congenital left-to-right shunts are {{c1::VSD}}, {{c2::ASD}}, and {{c3::PDA}}.
extraInfo: These are initially acyanotic because oxygenated blood from the left heart flows into the right heart.

text: Left-to-right shunts are initially {{c1::acyanotic}}.
extraInfo: Cyanosis only occurs later if Eisenmenger syndrome develops (late cyanosis).

text: The most common congenital cardiac anomaly is {{c1::VSD}}.
extraInfo: Specifically, membranous VSD is the most common type.

text: VSD presents as a {{c1::holosystolic}} murmur, loudest at the {{c2::left lower sternal border}}.
extraInfo: Smaller VSDs typically produce louder murmurs due to higher turbulence.

text: Small VSDs are often {{c1::asymptomatic}} and may {{c2::close spontaneously}}.
extraInfo: Large VSDs require surgical repair to prevent pulmonary hypertension.

text: The classic auscultatory finding in ASD is a {{c1::fixed split S2}}.
extraInfo: This occurs because the increased volume in the right heart delays the closing of the pulmonic valve regardless of breath cycle.

text: The most common type of ASD is the {{c1::ostium secundum}} defect.
extraInfo: Ostium secundum occurs near the center of the interatrial septum.

text: The {{c1::ostium primum}} type of ASD is commonly associated with Down syndrome.
extraInfo: This is often part of a larger endocardial cushion defect.

text: In ASD, the systolic ejection murmur heard is actually due to increased flow across the {{c1::pulmonic}} valve.
extraInfo: The shunt itself does not produce a murmur because the pressure gradient between the atria is low.

text: A potential complication of ASD is a(n) {{c1::paradoxical embolus}}, where a DVT travels to the systemic circulation.
extraInfo: The embolus crosses from the right atrium to the left atrium through the defect.

text: PDA is a persistent connection between the {{c1::aorta}} and the {{c2::pulmonary artery}}.
extraInfo: In utero, the ductus arteriosus shunts blood away from the lungs.

text: The murmur of a PDA is described as {{c1::continuous machine-like}}, loudest at the {{c2::left infraclavicular}} area.
extraInfo: The murmur persists through both systole and diastole.

text: PDA is classically associated with maternal infection by {{c1::Congenital Rubella}}.
extraInfo: One of the 'classic triad' along with cataracts and sensorineural deafness.

text: The ductus arteriosus is kept open in utero by high levels of {{c1::Prostaglandin E2}}.
extraInfo: Prostaglandin levels drop after birth as the lungs begin to clear them.

text: To close a PDA in a neonate, {{c1::Indomethacin}} (an NSAID) is administered.
extraInfo: Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin synthesis.

text: To maintain a PDA (e.g., in transposition of great vessels), {{c1::Alprostadil}} (PGE1) is administered.
extraInfo: Remember: 'kEEp' it open with Prostaglandin E.

text: Eisenmenger syndrome is the {{c1::reversal}} of a left-to-right shunt once {{c2::pulmonary hypertension}} develops.
extraInfo: The chronic high pressure in the pulmonary circuit causes vascular remodeling.

text: Once a shunt reverses in Eisenmenger syndrome, it becomes a {{c1::right-to-left}} shunt.
extraInfo: This results in 'late cyanosis' in an infant/child who was previously acyanotic.

text: The clinical triad of Eisenmenger syndrome includes cyanosis, {{c1::clubbing}}, and {{c2::polycythemia}}.
extraInfo: Polycythemia is a compensatory response to chronic hypoxemia.

text: PDA Eisenmenger results in {{c1::differential cyanosis}}, where cyanosis is seen in the {{c2::lower}} extremities only.
extraInfo: This is because the PDA delivers deoxygenated blood distal to the left subclavian artery.

text: Clinical signs of a PDA include {{c1::bounding}} pulses and a wide pulse pressure.
extraInfo: Blood leaks from the aorta into the pulmonary artery during diastole, lowering diastolic pressure.

text: Chronic left-to-right shunting causes {{c1::RVH (Right Ventricular Hypertrophy)}} due to increased pressure/volume overload.
extraInfo: This eventually leads to the reversal of the shunt.

text: VSD is associated with {{c1::Fetal Alcohol Syndrome}} and Down syndrome.
extraInfo: Most VSDs are isolated, but these associations are high-yield.

text: The underlying pathology of Eisenmenger syndrome is pulmonary vascular {{c1::remodeling}} (intimal fibrosis and medial hypertrophy).
extraInfo: This process is generally irreversible once it reaches a certain stage.

text: ASD results in volume overload of the {{c1::Right}} atrium and {{c2::Right}} ventricle.
extraInfo: In contrast, VSD and PDA primarily cause volume overload of the left heart initially.

text: In a VSD, blood is shunted from the {{c1::Left Ventricle}} to the {{c2::Right Ventricle}} during systole.
extraInfo: This increases pulmonary blood flow.

text: ASD is distinct from Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) because ASD involves a {{c1::missing}} septum, whereas PFO is a failure of the septum to {{c2::fuse}}.
extraInfo: ASD is a true deficiency of tissue.

text: Large left-to-right shunts can lead to symptoms of {{c1::heart failure}} in infancy (e.g., poor feeding, failure to thrive).
extraInfo: This is due to pulmonary overcirculation and systemic underperfusion.

text: Once Eisenmenger syndrome occurs, surgical repair of the defect is {{c1::contraindicated}}.
extraInfo: Closing the defect would cause acute right heart failure because the right ventricle has no outlet for the high pulmonary pressures.

text: Eisenmenger syndrome occurs when a chronic {{c1::left-to-right}} shunt reverses to a {{c2::right-to-left}} shunt.
extraInfo: This reversal is due to the development of pulmonary hypertension.

text: The initial step in Eisenmenger syndrome is increased {{c1::pulmonary blood flow}}, which leads to pathologic remodeling of the vasculature.
extraInfo: The remodeling causes a significant increase in pulmonary vascular resistance.

text: In Eisenmenger syndrome, pulmonary arterial hypertension leads to the development of {{c1::right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)}} as a compensatory mechanism.
extraInfo: The RV must pump against higher pressures to overcome pulmonary resistance.

text: The shunt reversal in Eisenmenger syndrome occurs specifically when {{c1::RV}} pressure exceeds {{c2::LV}} pressure.
extraInfo: Once RV > LV pressure, deoxygenated blood is pushed into the systemic circulation.

text: Eisenmenger syndrome is characterized by {{c1::late}} cyanosis, distinguishing it from defects that are cyanotic at birth.
extraInfo: Cyanosis only appears after the shunt has reversed.

text: Three classic clinical findings in Eisenmenger syndrome include cyanosis, {{c1::clubbing}}, and polycythemia.
extraInfo: These result from chronic hypoxemia.

text: In Eisenmenger syndrome, {{c1::polycythemia}} occurs as a result of increased erythropoietin production in response to chronic hypoxemia.
extraInfo: The body attempts to increase oxygen-carrying capacity.

text: The age of onset for Eisenmenger syndrome varies depending on the {{c1::size}} and severity of the initial left-to-right shunt.
extraInfo: Larger defects generally lead to earlier syndrome onset.

text: Common congenital defects that can progress to Eisenmenger syndrome include VSD, ASD, and {{c1::PDA}}.
extraInfo: VSD is the most common cause.

text: The pathologic remodeling of pulmonary vasculature in Eisenmenger syndrome eventually becomes {{c1::irreversible}}.
extraInfo: This is why surgical closure of the defect is contraindicated once the shunt reverses.

text: A PDA-associated Eisenmenger syndrome can present with {{c1::differential}} cyanosis.
extraInfo: Cyanosis is seen in the lower extremities but not the upper extremities.

text: The increase in {{c1::pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR)}} is the primary driver of shunt reversal in Eisenmenger syndrome.
extraInfo: PVR eventually exceeds systemic vascular resistance (SVR).

text: Eisenmenger syndrome leads to {{c1::right-sided}} heart failure as the right ventricle fails to pump against extreme pulmonary pressures.
extraInfo: This is a late-stage complication.

text: On physical exam, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound (P2) in Eisenmenger syndrome is typically {{c1::loud/accentuated}}.
extraInfo: This reflects the high pressure in the pulmonary artery.

text: Patients with Eisenmenger syndrome are at a significantly increased risk of maternal mortality during {{c1::pregnancy}}.
extraInfo: The physiological changes of pregnancy are poorly tolerated.

text: In Eisenmenger syndrome, {{c1::central}} cyanosis occurs because deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs.
extraInfo: It is not due to peripheral vasoconstriction.

text: The long-term polycythemia in Eisenmenger syndrome increases the risk of {{c1::thrombosis}} or strokes.
extraInfo: Hyperviscosity of the blood is the underlying mechanism.

text: Once the shunt becomes right-to-left, the patient's oxygen saturation will be {{c1::lower}} in the systemic arteries.
extraInfo: Deoxygenated blood mixes with oxygenated blood in the left heart/aorta.

text: Pathologically, Eisenmenger syndrome involves {{c1::intimal hyperplasia}} and fibrosis of the pulmonary arterioles.
extraInfo: This leads to the narrowing of the vessel lumen.

text: Prior to shunt reversal, a VSD or ASD is considered a(n) {{c1::acyanotic}} congenital heart disease.
extraInfo: Oxygenated blood is moving to the lungs.

text: Management of end-stage Eisenmenger syndrome may require a {{c1::heart-lung}} transplant.
extraInfo: Repairing the heart defect alone is insufficient due to permanent lung damage.

text: In the context of Eisenmenger syndrome, digital clubbing is a sign of {{c1::chronic hypoxemia}}.
extraInfo: Clubbing is the rounding/swelling of the nail bed.

text: The initial left-to-right shunt in Eisenmenger syndrome causes pulmonary {{c1::overcirculation}}.
extraInfo: This excess flow triggers the vascular remodeling process.

text: Eisenmenger syndrome is a potential complication of {{c1::unrepaired}} congenital heart defects.
extraInfo: Early surgical correction can prevent the syndrome.

text: The transition from a left-to-right shunt to a right-to-left shunt is often {{c1::gradual}} rather than sudden.
extraInfo: It occurs as pulmonary pressures slowly climb over years.

text: In Eisenmenger syndrome, the chest X-ray may show enlarged {{c1::central pulmonary arteries}}.
extraInfo: This is a sign of long-standing pulmonary hypertension.

text: Echocardiography with a bubble study in Eisenmenger syndrome would show bubbles moving from the {{c1::right}} atrium/ventricle to the {{c2::left}} side.
extraInfo: This confirms the right-to-left direction of the shunt.

text: A paradoxical embolism is a risk in Eisenmenger syndrome because the shunt allows clots to bypass the {{c1::lungs}}.
extraInfo: Clots from the venous system can enter the systemic arterial system.

text: The polycythemia in Eisenmenger syndrome can lead to {{c1::hyperuricemia}} and secondary gout.
extraInfo: Increased red blood cell turnover increases urate production.

text: Coarctation of the aorta is a narrowing of the aortic lumen, most commonly found near the {{c1::ductus arteriosus}} or ligamentum arteriosum.
extraInfo: The narrowing is usually distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.

text: In patients with Turner syndrome (45,XO), {{c1::coarctation of the aorta}} is a characteristic cardiovascular finding.
extraInfo: Turner syndrome is also associated with bicuspid aortic valve.

text: A key physical exam finding in coarctation of the aorta is {{c1::brachial-femoral}} pulse delay.
extraInfo: This is caused by the obstruction to blood flow to the lower body.

text: Patients with coarctation of the aorta typically have {{c1::higher}} blood pressure in the arms compared to the legs.
extraInfo: This disparity is a hallmark of the 'adult-type' or postductal coarctation.

text: The 'adult type' of coarctation is usually located {{c1::distal}} to the ligamentum arteriosum.
extraInfo: This results in hypertension in the upper extremities and hypotension in the lower extremities.

text: The 'infantile type' (preductal) of coarctation is usually located {{c1::proximal}} to the ductus arteriosus.
extraInfo: It is often associated with Turner syndrome and early-onset heart failure.

text: On chest X-ray, coarctation of the aorta can cause {{c1::rib notching}} due to collateral circulation.
extraInfo: Collateral flow occurs via the intercostal arteries.

text: The {{c1::'3' sign}} on a chest X-ray is characteristic of coarctation of the aorta.
extraInfo: It is formed by the pre-stenotic dilation, the coarctation itself, and the post-stenotic dilation.

text: The most common congenital heart defect associated with coarctation of the aorta is a {{c1::bicuspid aortic valve}}.
extraInfo: This occurs in up to 50% of cases.

text: Coarctation of the aorta increases the risk of {{c1::berry (saccular)}} aneurysms in the circle of Willis.
extraInfo: Upper body hypertension predisposes patients to these aneurysms and subsequent subarachnoid hemorrhage.

text: In coarctation of the aorta, collateral circulation develops through the {{c1::intercostal}} arteries to bypass the obstruction.
extraInfo: Pressure from these enlarged arteries erodes the ribs, causing notching.

text: In patients with coarctation of the aorta, femoral pulses are typically {{c1::weak}} compared to brachial pulses.
extraInfo: This is a high-yield physical exam finding for USMLE.

text: Lower extremity cyanosis in an infant can be a sign of {{c1::preductal}} coarctation of the aorta.
extraInfo: Deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery enters the aorta via the ductus arteriosus.

text: Erosion of the lower borders of ribs 3-8 seen on X-ray in coarctation is called {{c1::rib notching}}.
extraInfo: This is usually not seen in infants because collaterals take time to develop.

text: Coarctation of the aorta can lead to {{c1::left ventricular}} hypertrophy due to increased afterload.
extraInfo: The heart must pump against the high pressure caused by the narrowing.

text: In adults, coarctation of the aorta often presents as asymptomatic {{c1::hypertension}}.
extraInfo: Often discovered during routine blood pressure screening.

text: Congestive heart failure in the first few weeks of life can be caused by {{c1::preductal (infantile)}} coarctation.
extraInfo: Symptoms appear when the ductus arteriosus begins to close.

text: Infantile (preductal) coarctation is strongly associated with {{c1::Turner syndrome}}.
extraInfo: 45,XO females should always be screened for this condition.

text: Postductal coarctation is also known as the {{c1::adult}} type.
extraInfo: It typically presents later in life with upper extremity hypertension.

text: Rib notching occurs because of high pressure and flow in the internal thoracic and {{c1::intercostal}} arteries.
extraInfo: These vessels act as a bypass for the aortic narrowing.

text: Excluding Turner syndrome, coarctation of the aorta is more common in {{c1::males}}.
extraInfo: Male-to-female ratio is approximately 2:1.

text: A systolic murmur may be heard over the {{c1::left back (infrascapular)}} area in coarctation.
extraInfo: This represents the site of turbulent flow through the narrowed aorta.

text: Patients with coarctation of the aorta are at increased risk for {{c1::infective endocarditis}}.
extraInfo: Turbulent flow damages the endothelium, providing a site for bacterial attachment.

text: Untreated coarctation of the aorta can lead to {{c1::aortic dissection}}.
extraInfo: This is due to chronic high pressure in the proximal aorta.

text: Adult coarctation presents with {{c1::claudication}} of the lower extremities during exercise.
extraInfo: Due to insufficient blood flow to the leg muscles.

text: Coarctation of the aorta is a narrowing of the {{c1::descending}} aorta.
extraInfo: Specifically, it is almost always located at the aortic isthmus.

text: The presence of a bicuspid aortic valve in a patient with coarctation increases the risk of {{c1::aortic stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Aortic stenosis adds to the pressure load on the left ventricle.

text: Intercostal artery engorgement in coarctation results in the {{c1::rib notching}} sign on X-ray.
extraInfo: It primarily affects the posterior aspects of the ribs.

text: In coarctation, blood pressure is {{c1::decreased}} in the lower extremities.
extraInfo: This is relative to the hypertensive readings in the upper extremities.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: {{c1::Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)}} is the failure of the normal decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth.
extraInfo: In utero, PVR is high; at birth, it normally drops to allow for pulmonary gas exchange.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: PPHN results in a {{c1::right-to-left}} shunt through the patent foramen ovale or ductus arteriosus.
extraInfo: This leads to severe hypoxemia as deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: PPHN is most commonly seen in infants who are {{c1::term}} or {{c2::post-term}}.
extraInfo: It is less common in preterm infants, though it can occur with RDS.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: The most common underlying cause of PPHN is {{c1::meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)}}.
extraInfo: Meconium causes airway obstruction and chemical pneumonitis, leading to V/Q mismatch and hypoxia.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Maternal use of {{c1::SSRIs}} (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors) after 20 weeks gestation is a known risk factor for PPHN.
extraInfo: Fluoxetine and paroxetine are frequently cited in associations with neonatal PPHN.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Prenatal exposure to {{c1::NSAIDs}} (e.g., indomethacin) can cause PPHN by inducing premature closure of the {{c2::ductus arteriosus}}.
extraInfo: Ductal closure in utero increases pulmonary pressure and arterial muscularization.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Severe {{c1::pulmonary hypoplasia}}, often seen in {{c2::congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH)}}, is a major cause of PPHN.
extraInfo: The lack of lung development leads to fewer and thicker pulmonary vessels.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Cardiac auscultation in PPHN often reveals a {{c1::loud, single S2}}.
extraInfo: This is due to the increased pressure causing forceful closure of the pulmonary valve.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: A difference in oxygen saturation (SpO2) of >{{c1::10}}% between the {{c2::right hand}} and the {{c3::lower extremities}} suggests PPHN.
extraInfo: The right hand is pre-ductal; the feet are post-ductal.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: A pre-ductal to post-ductal {{c1::PaO2}} difference of >{{c2::15}} mmHg indicates significant right-to-left shunting across the ductus arteriosus.
extraInfo: PaO2 is measured via arterial blood gas (ABG) from the right radial artery vs. umbilical/pedal artery.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: The gold standard for diagnosing PPHN and excluding structural heart disease is {{c1::echocardiography}}.
extraInfo: Echo confirms pulmonary hypertension and right-to-left shunting.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: On echocardiography, PPHN is characterized by {{c1::flattening or bowing of the interventricular septum}} toward the left ventricle.
extraInfo: This occurs because right ventricular pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: The specific pulmonary vasodilator used as first-line medical therapy for PPHN is {{c1::inhaled nitric oxide (iNO)}}.
extraInfo: iNO selectively dilates pulmonary vasculature without affecting systemic blood pressure.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: The mechanism of action of Inhaled Nitric Oxide (iNO) involves increasing {{c1::cGMP}} in vascular smooth muscle cells.
extraInfo: This leads to smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: If a neonate with PPHN fails medical management (iNO, ventilation), the next step in therapy is {{c1::ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation)}}.
extraInfo: ECMO provides temporary heart-lung bypass to allow the pulmonary vasculature to relax.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: {{c1::High-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV)}} is often used in PPHN to improve lung recruitment while minimizing barotrauma.
extraInfo: Proper lung expansion helps lower pulmonary vascular resistance.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: PPHN typically presents within the first {{c1::24}} hours of life with {{c2::cyanosis}} and respiratory distress.
extraInfo: Affected infants are often profoundly hypoxemic.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Hypoxia and {{c1::acidosis}} are potent triggers for pulmonary vasoconstriction, which worsens PPHN.
extraInfo: Maintaining adequate oxygenation and pH is critical in management.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: A systolic murmur heard at the lower left sternal border in PPHN is often due to {{c1::tricuspid regurgitation}}.
extraInfo: High right ventricular pressures cause the tricuspid valve to leak.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: In idiopathic PPHN, the chest X-ray may show {{c1::clear lung fields}} with {{c2::decreased}} pulmonary vascular markings.
extraInfo: This helps distinguish it from MAS or pneumonia, which have opacities.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Initial stabilization of PPHN includes maintaining systemic blood pressure at {{c1::normal or high-normal}} levels.
extraInfo: Using vasopressors (e.g., dopamine) can help reduce the right-to-left shunt by making systemic pressure higher than pulmonary pressure.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: A significant long-term complication in survivors of PPHN is {{c1::sensorineural hearing loss}}.
extraInfo: Routine hearing screens are mandatory for these infants after discharge.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Histologically, PPHN involves increased {{c1::muscularization}} of the small, non-muscularized distal pulmonary arteries.
extraInfo: The smooth muscle extends further into the vessel tree than normal.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: {{c1::Neonatal sepsis}} (frequently Group B Streptococcus) is a common infectious trigger for PPHN.
extraInfo: Inflammatory mediators can cause intense pulmonary vasoconstriction.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: The 'Hyperoxic Test' involves giving {{c1::100%}} oxygen; if the PaO2 does not rise above {{c2::100}} mmHg, PPHN or cyanotic heart disease is likely.
extraInfo: In lung parenchymal disease, PaO2 usually improves significantly.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: {{c1::Alkali}} therapy (sodium bicarbonate) was historically used in PPHN to induce {{c2::metabolic alkalosis}} and vasodilation, but it is now less common.
extraInfo: Current practice focuses on maintaining normal pH rather than extreme alkalosis.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: {{c1::Milrinone}} is an inodilator (PDE3 inhibitor) that may be used as an adjunct to iNO in PPHN to improve right ventricular function.
extraInfo: It helps by relaxing pulmonary vessels and increasing cardiac contractility.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: Risk factors for PPHN include maternal {{c1::diabetes}}, maternal {{c2::obesity}}, and cesarean delivery.
extraInfo: Cesarean delivery lacks the 'squeeze' that helps clear fetal lung fluid and transition circulation.

topic: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
text: If oxygenation is post-ductally low but pre-ductally normal, the shunt is occurring at the {{c1::ductus arteriosus}}.
extraInfo: This is a classic 'differential cyanosis' pattern seen in PPHN.

text: {{c1::Down syndrome}} is most commonly associated with {{c2::endocardial cushion defects (AVSD)}}.
extraInfo: It is the most common cardiac defect in Trisomy 21.

text: {{c1::Turner syndrome}} is associated with {{c2::bicuspid aortic valve}} and {{c3::coarctation of the aorta}}.
extraInfo: Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common cardiac defect in Turner syndrome.

text: {{c1::Williams syndrome}} is classically associated with {{c2::supravalvular aortic stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Associated with elfin facies and hypercalcemia.

text: {{c1::DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion)}} is associated with {{c2::truncus arteriosus}} and {{c3::tetralogy of Fallot}}.
extraInfo: Results from a failure of neural crest cell migration.

text: {{c1::Congenital rubella}} infection is associated with {{c2::patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)}} and {{c3::pulmonary artery stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Also presents with cataracts and sensorineural deafness.

text: Infant of a {{c1::diabetic mother}} is associated with {{c2::transposition of the great vessels (TGA)}}.
extraInfo: Also associated with VSD and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (asymmetric septal hypertrophy).

text: {{c1::Marfan syndrome}} is associated with {{c2::mitral valve prolapse (MVP)}} and {{c3::aortic root dilation}}.
extraInfo: Aortic root dilation can lead to aortic dissection or regurgitation.

text: {{c1::Friedreich ataxia}} is associated with {{c2::hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)}}.
extraInfo: HCM is the leading cause of death in these patients.

text: {{c1::Fetal alcohol syndrome}} is associated with {{c2::ventricular septal defect (VSD)}} and {{c3::atrial septal defect (ASD)}}.
extraInfo: Also associated with Tetralogy of Fallot.

text: Maternal {{c1::lithium}} use is associated with {{c2::Ebstein anomaly}}.
extraInfo: Characterized by apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets.

text: {{c1::Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)}} and {{c1::Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)}} are both associated with {{c2::VSD}} and {{c3::PDA}}.
extraInfo: VSD is the most common congenital heart defect overall.

text: {{c1::Maternal SLE}} is associated with {{c2::congenital heart block}}.
extraInfo: Caused by placental transfer of anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies.

text: {{c1::Holt-Oram syndrome}} (heart-hand syndrome) is associated with {{c2::ASD (secundum)}}.
extraInfo: Associated with radial ray hypoplasia (e.g., thumb abnormalities).

text: {{c1::Noonan syndrome}} is associated with {{c2::pulmonary valve stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Sometimes called the male version of Turner syndrome; autosomal dominant.

text: {{c1::Tuberous sclerosis}} is associated with {{c2::cardiac rhabdomyoma}}.
extraInfo: These tumors often spontaneously regress.

text: {{c1::Kartagener syndrome}} (primary ciliary dyskinesia) is associated with {{c2::dextrocardia}}.
extraInfo: Part of situs inversus.

text: {{c1::Maternal PKU}} is associated with {{c2::VSD}} and ASD.
extraInfo: Can be prevented if the mother maintains a low-phenylalanine diet.

text: Maternal {{c1::Isotretinoin (Vitamin A)}} use is associated with conotruncal defects like {{c2::TGA}} and {{c3::Tetralogy of Fallot}}.
extraInfo: Due to interference with neural crest cell development.

text: {{c1::Ellis-van Creveld syndrome}} is classically associated with {{c2::atrial septal defects}} or a {{c3::single atrium}}.
extraInfo: Common in Old Order Amish populations; includes polydactyly and dwarfism.

text: {{c1::Ehlers-Danlos syndrome}} is associated with {{c2::mitral valve prolapse (MVP)}} and {{c3::aortic dissection}}.
extraInfo: Due to defective collagen synthesis.

text: {{c1::Osteogenesis imperfecta}} is associated with {{c2::mitral valve prolapse (MVP)}} and aortic root dilation.
extraInfo: Associated with blue sclerae and frequent fractures.

text: In {{c1::Down syndrome}}, the specific type of ASD seen is the {{c2::ostium primum}} type.
extraInfo: Most other ASDs (sporadic) are ostium secundum type.

text: {{c1::Alagille syndrome}} is associated with {{c2::peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Associated with bile duct paucity and butterfly vertebrae.

text: {{c1::Pompe disease}} (GSD Type II) is associated with severe {{c2::hypertrophic cardiomyopathy}}.
extraInfo: Due to lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency.

text: {{c1::Cri-du-chat syndrome}} is associated with {{c2::VSD}}.
extraInfo: Caused by 5p deletion.

text: {{c1::Thalidomide}} exposure in utero is associated with {{c2::phocomelia}} and various {{c3::septal defects}}.
extraInfo: Historically used for morning sickness.

text: Maternal {{c1::cocaine}} use is associated with {{c2::coronary artery abnormalities}} and septal defects.
extraInfo: Due to vasoconstrictive effects.

text: {{c1::Maternal smoking}} is associated with increased risk of {{c2::septal defects}} (VSD/ASD).
extraInfo: Smoking also causes intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR).

text: The most common cardiac abnormality in {{c1::Turner syndrome}} is {{c2::bicuspid aortic valve}}.
extraInfo: Found in about 30% of cases.

text: Xanthomas are skin/tendon manifestations composed of collections of {{c1::lipid-laden macrophages}}.
extraInfo: They are characteristic of various familial dyslipidemias.

text: {{c1::Tendon}} xanthomas are most classically found on the Achilles tendon.
extraInfo: They can also be found on the extensor tendons of the fingers.

text: Tendon xanthomas are highly associated with Familial {{c1::Hypercholesterolemia}} (Type IIa).
extraInfo: This condition involves a defect in LDL receptors.

text: {{c1::Eruptive}} xanthomas appear as crops of small, itchy, yellow-orange papules.
extraInfo: They are typically found on the back, buttocks, and extensor surfaces.

text: Eruptive xanthomas are associated with severe {{c1::hypertriglyceridemia}}.
extraInfo: Usually seen when triglycerides exceed 1000 mg/dL.

text: {{c1::Xanthelasma}} is a yellowish deposit of fat underneath the skin, typically located on the eyelids.
extraInfo: While often associated with high LDL, they can occur in patients with normal lipid levels.

text: Corneal arcus (arcus senilis) is a lipid deposit in the {{c1::cornea}} appearing as a white or gray ring.
extraInfo: It is common in elderly patients but suggests hypercholesterolemia in younger patients.

text: Corneal arcus seen in a patient younger than {{c1::40}} years old is highly suggestive of hyperlipidemia.
extraInfo: It is an important clinical clue for Familial Hypercholesterolemia.

text: {{c1::Palmar}} xanthomas (xanthoma striatum palmare) are yellow deposits in the creases of the hands.
extraInfo: These are pathognomonic for Type III Dysbetalipoproteinemia.

text: Type III Dysbetalipoproteinemia, which presents with palmar xanthomas, is caused by a deficiency in {{c1::ApoE}}.
extraInfo: This leads to an accumulation of chylomicron and VLDL remnants (IDL).

text: Lipemia retinalis presents as {{c1::milky-white}} or cream-colored retinal vessels on fundoscopy.
extraInfo: It occurs when serum triglyceride levels are extremely high (> 2000 mg/dL).

text: {{c1::Tuberous}} xanthomas are firm, painless, reddish-yellow nodules typically found on the elbows and knees.
extraInfo: They are associated with Type II and Type III dyslipidemias.

text: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG > 1000 mg/dL) significantly increases the risk of acute {{c1::pancreatitis}}.
extraInfo: This is often seen in Type I, IV, and V dyslipidemias.

text: Type I dyslipidemia (Hyperchylomicronemia) is characterized by a deficiency in {{c1::Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL)}} or Apo C-II.
extraInfo: It presents with eruptive xanthomas and pancreatitis but does not increase atherosclerosis risk.

text: Hepatosplenomegaly is a physical sign often associated with Type {{c1::I}} Hyperchylomicronemia.
extraInfo: Enlargement occurs due to the uptake of chylomicrons by macrophages in the liver and spleen.

text: High levels of serum {{c1::LDL}} are the primary driver for the formation of tendon xanthomas and xanthelasma.
extraInfo: Associated with Type IIa and IIb dyslipidemias.

text: High levels of serum {{c1::chylomicrons}} are the primary driver for eruptive xanthomas and lipemia retinalis.
extraInfo: Characteristic of Hyperchylomicronemia (Type I).

text: Type IIa dyslipidemia results in high serum {{c1::LDL}} due to defective LDL receptors.
extraInfo: This leads to premature atherosclerosis and tendon xanthomas.

text: Premature {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and myocardial infarction are major risks in patients with Type IIa and Type III dyslipidemia.
extraInfo: Early screening is vital for these patients.

text: The clinical triad of Hyperchylomicronemia (Type I) includes eruptive xanthomas, hepatosplenomegaly, and {{c1::acute pancreatitis}}.
extraInfo: Serum will also show a creamy layer in the supernatant.

text: Type IV Hypertriglyceridemia is characterized by an overproduction of {{c1::VLDL}}.
extraInfo: It is often associated with insulin resistance and can cause pancreatitis.

text: In Type III Dysbetalipoproteinemia, there is a specific elevation of {{c1::IDL}} (remnants).
extraInfo: ApoE is required for the hepatic uptake of these remnants.

text: {{c1::Xanthelasma}} is considered the most common clinical type of xanthoma.
extraInfo: It is often the first physical sign of a lipid disorder noted by patients.

text: Tuberous xanthomas are distinct from eruptive xanthomas because tuberous ones are usually {{c1::larger}} and coalesce into nodules.
extraInfo: They are typically seen over joints.

text: Achilles tendon thickening detected on physical exam or ultrasound can be a subtle sign of {{c1::Familial Hypercholesterolemia}}.
extraInfo: This represents the early stage of a tendon xanthoma.

text: Type IIb dyslipidemia involves elevations in both LDL and {{c1::VLDL}}.
extraInfo: This is known as Familial Combined Hyperlipidemia.

text: Apo {{c1::C-II}} is a necessary cofactor for Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL) activity.
extraInfo: Deficiency leads to Type I dyslipidemia and eruptive xanthomas.

text: Patients with Type V dyslipidemia have elevated levels of both Chylomicrons and {{c1::VLDL}}.
extraInfo: They often present with eruptive xanthomas and severe risk for pancreatitis.

text: Lipid deposits in the skin of the elbow are specifically termed {{c1::tuberous}} xanthomas.
extraInfo: They are yellow-red and often associated with Type III hyperlipidemia.

text: Hypertension is defined as persistent SBP ≥ {{c1::130}} mmHg or DBP ≥ {{c2::80}} mmHg.
extraInfo: Based on ACC/AHA guidelines.

text: 90% of hypertension cases are {{c1::primary (essential)}} and are related to increased CO or TPR.
The most common cause of secondary hypertension is {{c1::renal or renovascular}} disease.
Hypertensive {{c1::urgency}} is defined as BP >180/120 mmHg without acute end-organ damage.
Hypertensive {{c1::emergency}} is defined as BP >180/120 mmHg with acute end-organ damage.
extraInfo: Examples of damage: encephalopathy, stroke, retinal hemorrhages, papilledema, MI, HF, aortic dissection, AKI.

text: Severe hypertension can lead to {{c1::hyperplastic}} arteriolosclerosis, which is characterized by {{c2::onion skinning}} of vessel walls.
{{c1::Hyaline}} arteriolosclerosis is often seen in patients with diabetes or mild-to-moderate hypertension.
Renovascular hypertension in young women is most often due to {{c1::fibromuscular dysplasia}}, which shows a 'string of beads' appearance.
In patients with renal artery stenosis, the affected kidney secretes high levels of {{c1::renin}}.
{{c1::Fenoldopam}} is a dopamine D1 receptor agonist used in hypertensive emergencies to lower BP while maintaining {{c2::renal}} perfusion.
{{c1::Nitroprusside}} can lead to toxic accumulation of {{c2::cyanide}}.
Hypertension in pregnancy is safely managed with the mnemonic 'He Likes My Neonate': {{c1::Hydralazine, Labetalol, Methyldopa, Nifedipine}}.
{{c1::Hydralazine}} can cause a drug-induced {{c2::Lupus-like}} syndrome.
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) presents with hypertension, {{c1::hypokalemia}}, and {{c2::low}} plasma renin.
Pheochromocytoma is a tumor of the {{c1::adrenal medulla}} that causes episodic hypertension.
extraInfo: Diagnosis involves urinary/plasma metanephrines.

text: {{c1::Coarctation}} of the aorta typically presents with high BP in the arms and low BP/weak pulses in the legs.
extraInfo: Associated with rib notching and Turner syndrome.

text: Chronic hypertension causes {{c1::concentric}} left ventricular hypertrophy as the heart pumps against increased afterload.
ACE inhibitors are notorious for causing a dry {{c1::cough}} due to increased levels of {{c2::bradykinin}}.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in patients with {{c1::bilateral renal artery stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Can precipitate acute renal failure.

text: {{c1::Thiazide}} diuretics can lead to hypercalcemia, while {{c2::loop}} diuretics can lead to hypocalcemia.
{{c1::Clevidipine}} is an IV-only, ultra-short-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used in hypertensive emergencies.
Malignant hypertension can cause {{c1::flea-bitten}} kidneys due to pinpoint hemorrhages from necrotizing arteriolitis.
{{c1::Labetalol}} is a combined alpha-1 and nonselective beta-blocker used for hypertensive emergencies and aortic dissection.
{{c1::Methyldopa}} can cause a positive {{c2::Direct Coombs}} test and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
A major complication of hypertensive emergency in the eye is {{c1::papilledema}}.
Hypertension is the most common cause of {{c1::Charcot-Bouchard}} microaneurysms, which can lead to intracerebral hemorrhage.
Renovascular hypertension in the elderly is usually caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}} at the {{c2::ostium}} of the renal artery.
Hypertensive retinopathy can show 'silver wiring' and {{c1::AV nicking}} on fundoscopic exam.
{{c1::Nitroprusside}} works by increasing {{c2::cGMP}} via direct release of nitric oxide.
Atherosclerosis is a disease of {{c1::elastic}} arteries and large- and medium-sized {{c2::muscular}} arteries.
extraInfo: Examples include the aorta, carotid, and iliac (elastic) and coronary and popliteal (muscular).

text: The most common location for atherosclerosis (in descending order) is {{c1::abdominal aorta}} > coronary artery > popliteal artery > carotid artery.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: After Acute Myocardial Infarction, Children Are Small (Aorta, Coronary, Popliteal, Carotid, Circle of Willis).

text: The pathogenesis of atherosclerosis begins with {{c1::endothelial}} cell injury.
extraInfo: Triggers include tobacco smoke, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia.

text: In the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, {{c1::LDL}} accumulates in the intima and undergoes {{c2::oxidation}}.
extraInfo: Oxidized LDL is proinflammatory and is taken up by macrophages via scavenger receptors.

text: Macrophages that ingest oxidized LDL are known as {{c1::foam cells}}.
extraInfo: These cells contribute to the formation of the fatty streak.

text: The earliest visible lesion in atherosclerosis is the {{c1::fatty streak}}.
extraInfo: Fatty streaks can be seen in the aortas of most children regardless of geography or race.

text: Smooth muscle cells migrate from the {{c1::media}} to the {{c2::intima}} during plaque formation.
extraInfo: This transformation from a contractile to a synthetic phenotype is a key step.

text: Smooth muscle cell migration and proliferation are mediated by {{c1::PDGF}} and {{c2::TGF-β}}.
extraInfo: Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF) is released by platelets and macrophages.

text: The fibrous cap of an atherosclerotic plaque consists of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and {{c2::collagen}}.
extraInfo: The strength of this cap determines the stability of the plaque.

text: Atherosclerosis of the abdominal aorta typically leads to the formation of {{c1::aneurysms}}.
extraInfo: This occurs due to ischemia-induced weakening of the underlying media.

text: Symptomatic peripheral artery disease (e.g., claudication) often involves the {{c1::popliteal}} artery.
extraInfo: The popliteal artery is one of the most common sites for atherosclerosis after the aorta and coronaries.

text: Critical stenosis causing stable angina usually occurs when the vessel lumen is narrowed by >{{c1::70}}%.
extraInfo: Below this threshold, blood flow is usually sufficient at rest.

text: Acute plaque {{c1::rupture}} or erosion can lead to thrombosis and subsequent {{c2::myocardial infarction}}.
extraInfo: Rupture exposes the highly thrombogenic necrotic core to the blood.

text: The non-modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis include {{c1::age}}, {{c2::sex}}, and {{c3::family history}}.
extraInfo: Postmenopausal women lose the protective effect of estrogen, increasing their risk to that of men.

text: Major modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis include {{c1::smoking}}, {{c2::hypertension}}, {{c3::hyperlipidemia}}, and {{c4::diabetes}}.
extraInfo: Smoking is the most preventable cause of cardiovascular disease.

text: After the abdominal aorta, the {{c1::coronary}} arteries are the next most common site for atherosclerosis.
extraInfo: Atherosclerosis here leads to ischemic heart disease.

text: Atherosclerosis in the {{c1::carotid}} arteries can lead to TIAs or embolic strokes.
extraInfo: Bruits may be heard on physical exam over the carotid bifurcation.

text: Cholesterol {{c1::emboli}} can occur after invasive vascular procedures, characterized by needle-shaped clefts in small vessels.
extraInfo: Commonly presents with "blue toe syndrome" or renal failure.

text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia is often caused by atherosclerosis of the {{c1::mesenteric}} arteries, presenting as "intestinal angina."
extraInfo: Patients typically present with postprandial abdominal pain and weight loss (fear of eating).

text: High levels of {{c1::homocysteine}} are an independent risk factor for the development of atherosclerosis.
extraInfo: Can be caused by deficiencies in Vitamin B6, B12, or folate.

text: Atherosclerotic plaques often contain a central {{c1::necrotic}} core composed of lipid and debris.
extraInfo: This core is rich in cholesterol crystals and extracellular lipids.

text: Thinning of the {{c1::media}} layer beneath a plaque can lead to the formation of an aneurysm.
extraInfo: The plaque prevents oxygen from diffusing from the lumen to the media, causing atrophy.

text: Endothelial injury leads to the expression of {{c1::VCAM-1}} or other adhesion molecules, allowing monocyte recruitment.
extraInfo: Vascular Cell Adhesion Molecule-1.

text: The "Response to {{c1::Injury}}" hypothesis is the primary model for atherosclerosis pathogenesis.
extraInfo: Emphasizes that chronic inflammatory response is triggered by endothelial damage.

text: A {{c1::thin}} fibrous cap and a {{c2::large}} lipid core are features of an unstable (vulnerable) plaque.
extraInfo: High macrophage content and low smooth muscle cell content also increase rupture risk.

text: Renovascular hypertension can be caused by atherosclerosis of the {{c1::renal artery}}.
extraInfo: Typically occurs at the ostium; common in older men.

text: Calcification of the plaque is common and can be detected on CT, often quantified as a {{c1::coronary calcium score}}.
extraInfo: Higher scores correlate with a higher risk of cardiovascular events.

text: {{c1::Chlamydia pneumoniae}} and CMV have been associated with atherosclerosis, though their causal role is debated.
extraInfo: Chronic infection may contribute to vessel wall inflammation.

text: Unlike atherosclerosis, {{c1::Monckeberg}} arteriosclerosis involves calcification of the media without obstructing blood flow.
extraInfo: Often an incidental finding on X-ray, seen as "pipestem" arteries.

text: Cholesterol emboli syndrome is most frequently triggered by {{c1::invasive vascular procedures}} (e.g., cardiac catheterization or aortography).
extraInfo: Mechanical disruption of atherosclerotic plaques releases cholesterol crystals into the circulation.

text: The source of cholesterol emboli is typically a(n) {{c1::atherosclerotic plaque}} located in a large artery like the aorta.
extraInfo: This is why it is often seen after procedures involving the aorta.

text: A classic cutaneous finding in cholesterol emboli syndrome is {{c1::livedo reticularis}}.
extraInfo: This presents as a lace-like, purplish discoloration of the skin.

text: {{c1::Blue toe syndrome}} refers to the development of cyanotic toes despite intact pedal pulses, often seen in cholesterol embolism.
extraInfo: Intact pulses differentiate this from large-vessel peripheral arterial disease.

text: On histopathology, cholesterol emboli appear as {{c1::biconvex}}, needle-shaped clefts within small arteries.
extraInfo: These are often referred to as 'cholesterol clefts'.

text: The needle-shaped clefts seen on biopsy are empty because {{c1::cholesterol is dissolved}} during the routine histological fixation process.
extraInfo: The solvent used in processing (like alcohol or xylene) removes the lipid.

text: A characteristic laboratory finding in cholesterol emboli syndrome is {{c1::eosinophilia}}.
extraInfo: This is a high-yield pearl for differentiating it from other causes of renal failure.

text: Urinalysis in a patient with cholesterol emboli syndrome may reveal {{c1::eosinophiluria}}.
extraInfo: While not always present, it is highly suggestive when found alongside acute kidney injury.

text: In cholesterol emboli syndrome, serum levels of {{c1::complement (C3/C4)}} are often decreased.
extraInfo: This is thought to be due to activation of the alternative complement pathway by the crystals.

text: {{c1::Hollenhorst plaques}} are bright yellow, refractile crystals seen in retinal arterioles during fundoscopy.
extraInfo: These indicate systemic cholesterol embolization.

text: Cholesterol emboli syndrome typically causes {{c1::acute or subacute}} kidney injury.
extraInfo: It is a major cause of renal failure post-vascular intervention.

text: Unlike contrast-induced nephropathy, renal failure in cholesterol emboli syndrome is often {{c1::delayed}} (occurring days to weeks later).
extraInfo: Contrast nephropathy usually peaks within 3-5 days; cholesterol emboli can take longer to manifest.

text: The most common internal organ involved in cholesterol emboli syndrome is the {{c1::kidney}}.
extraInfo: Renal involvement is present in over 70% of symptomatic cases.

text: Cholesterol emboli syndrome primarily affects {{c1::small}} arteries and arterioles.
extraInfo: Large vessel pulses (like the dorsalis pedis) remain palpable.

text: Major risk factors for cholesterol emboli syndrome include {{c1::advanced age}}, smoking, and hypertension.
extraInfo: These are the same risk factors for generalized atherosclerosis.

text: In cholesterol emboli syndrome, pedal pulses are typically {{c1::palpable (intact)}} because the occlusion occurs in the microvasculature.
extraInfo: This is a key physical exam finding.

text: Gastrointestinal involvement in cholesterol emboli syndrome can present as {{c1::mesenteric ischemia}} or GI bleeding.
extraInfo: This results from emboli to the mesenteric vessels.

text: Management of cholesterol emboli syndrome is primarily {{c1::supportive}}.
extraInfo: There is no specific treatment to 'dissolve' the crystals once they have embolized.

text: Following an episode of cholesterol emboli, {{c1::anticoagulation}} should generally be avoided to prevent further plaque destabilization.
extraInfo: Anticoagulants may prevent the 'healing' of the ulcerated plaque, leading to recurrent emboli.

text: Livedo reticularis has a characteristic {{c1::lace-like}} appearance.
extraInfo: It is caused by swelling of the venules due to obstruction of capillaries by small thrombi or emboli.

text: Pathologically, the 'clefts' found in vessel lumens are known as {{c1::cholesterol clefts}}.
extraInfo: This is a pathognomonic finding on biopsy.

text: Cholesterol emboli syndrome is defined as an {{c1::embolic}} disease, not a primary vasculitis.
extraInfo: However, it can trigger a secondary inflammatory response in the vessel wall.

text: A patient presenting with acute renal failure and blue toes after a {{c1::cardiac catheterization}} most likely has cholesterol emboli syndrome.
extraInfo: This is the classic USMLE clinical vignette.

text: The fundamental pathophysiology of this syndrome involves the {{c1::mechanical disruption}} of a friable atherosclerotic plaque.
extraInfo: Can be spontaneous, but most are iatrogenic.

text: Embolization to the CNS can result in {{c1::stroke}} or transient ischemic attacks (TIAs).
extraInfo: Neurologic deficits may be focal or diffuse (confusion/delirium).

text: The biopsy finding is specifically described as {{c1::needle-shaped}} clefts.
extraInfo: This description is high-yield for pathology questions.

text: A key clinical differentiator from other renal pathologies is the presence of {{c1::extra-renal}} manifestations (skin, eye, or GI).
extraInfo: Multisystem involvement after a procedure points toward emboli.

text: The vascular occlusion by crystals is often followed by a(n) {{c1::inflammatory}} response with giant cells and fibrosis.
extraInfo: This secondary reaction contributes to the permanent vessel narrowing.

text: The rise in serum creatinine in cholesterol emboli syndrome is typically {{c1::gradual}} or stepwise.
extraInfo: This contrasts with the rapid rise and fall seen in contrast-induced nephropathy.

text: Arteriolosclerosis is a disease of {{c1::small arteries}} and {{c1::arterioles}}.
extraInfo: In contrast, atherosclerosis affects large and medium-sized arteries.

text: {{c1::Hyaline}} arteriolosclerosis is associated with essential hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
extraInfo: Hyaline refers to the pink, glassy appearance on H&E stain.

text: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is caused by the leakage of {{c1::plasma proteins}} into the vessel wall.
extraInfo: The increased pressure (HTN) or damage (DM) pushes proteins into the media.

text: In diabetes mellitus, hyaline arteriolosclerosis is caused by {{c1::nonenzymatic glycosylation}} of the basement membrane.
extraInfo: This makes the vessel wall leaky to plasma proteins.

text: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis on histology shows {{c1::pink hyaline}} thickening of the arteriolar walls.
extraInfo: This results in luminal narrowing and downstream ischemia.

text: In the kidney, hyaline arteriolosclerosis leads to {{c1::benign nephrosclerosis}}.
extraInfo: Grossly, the kidney appears shrunken with a granular surface ('grainy leather').

text: {{c1::Hyperplastic}} arteriolosclerosis is associated with severe (malignant) hypertension.
extraInfo: Malignant hypertension is typically defined as BP > 180/120 mmHg.

text: The classic histological finding in hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is {{c1::onion skinning}}.
extraInfo: This refers to concentric laminations of the vessel wall.

text: The 'onion skin' layers in hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis consist of {{c1::smooth muscle cells}} and basement membrane.
extraInfo: This is a proliferative response to extreme pressure.

text: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is often accompanied by {{c1::fibrinoid necrosis}} of the vessel wall.
extraInfo: This combination is termed necrotizing arteriolitis.

text: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis in the kidney can cause a {{c1::flea-bitten}} appearance.
extraInfo: This is due to multiple pinpoint hemorrhages on the renal surface.

text: Unlike essential HTN, Malignant HTN associated with hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis can lead to {{c1::acute renal failure}}.
extraInfo: The rapid narrowing causes severe ischemia and infarction.

text: In diabetes, hyaline arteriolosclerosis characteristically involves both the {{c1::afferent}} and {{c1::efferent}} arterioles of the kidney.
extraInfo: HTN usually only affects the afferent arteriole.

text: The pink material seen in hyaline arteriolosclerosis is {{c1::PAS}}-positive.
extraInfo: PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff) stains glycoproteins.

text: The underlying mechanism of hyaline arteriolosclerosis in hypertension is {{c1::hemodynamic}} stress.
extraInfo: Physical pressure damages the endothelium, allowing protein entry.

text: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis results in {{c1::concentric}} thickening of the arteriolar wall.
extraInfo: This is the hallmark of the 'onion skin' appearance.

text: Arteriolosclerosis leads to narrowing of the vessel {{c1::lumen}}, which results in downstream {{c2::ischemia}}.
extraInfo: This is the primary way these changes cause organ damage.

text: A patient with BP 200/130 and acute vision changes likely has {{c1::hyperplastic}} arteriolosclerosis.
extraInfo: Reflects Malignant HTN with end-organ damage (retinopathy/nephropathy).

text: The 'onion skin' appearance of hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is best seen on {{c1::light}} microscopy.
extraInfo: Standard H&E staining reveals the layered proliferation.

text: {{c1::Hyaline}} arteriolosclerosis involves protein deposition, whereas {{c2::hyperplastic}} arteriolosclerosis involves cellular proliferation.
extraInfo: This is a fundamental mechanistic difference.

text: Malignant hypertension causes {{c1::fibrinoid}} necrosis of the arterioles in addition to hyperplastic changes.
extraInfo: This results in vessel wall death and hemorrhage.

text: {{c1::Essential (benign)}} hypertension is the most common cause of hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
extraInfo: It is a chronic, slow-developing process.

text: In hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, basement membrane {{c1::duplication}} is visible on electron microscopy.
extraInfo: Contributes to the multi-layered 'onion' appearance.

text: {{c1::Hyaline}} arteriolosclerosis is a major component of diabetic nephropathy.
extraInfo: Contributes to the glomerular scarring (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules).

text: The term 'arteriolosclerosis' specifically refers to the {{c1::hardening}} of small arteries.
extraInfo: Sclerosis = hardening.

text: Arteriolosclerosis is most commonly and severely found in the {{c1::kidney}}.
extraInfo: The renal vasculature is highly sensitive to blood pressure changes.

text: Malignant hypertension is usually associated with a diastolic BP > {{c1::120}} mmHg.
extraInfo: This triggers the hyperplastic response.

text: Increased {{c1::vascular permeability}} is the immediate precursor to hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
extraInfo: Whether via HTN or DM, the barrier is breached.

text: {{c1::Necrotizing arteriolitis}} is the term for hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with associated fibrinoid necrosis.
extraInfo: Seen in the most severe cases of malignant hypertension.

text: An aortic aneurysm is defined as a localized abnormal dilation of {{c1::all 3 layers}} of the arterial wall.
extraInfo: True aneurysms involve the intima, media, and adventitia.

text: The most common location for an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm is {{c1::infrarenal}}.
extraInfo: They usually occur between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation.

text: The single most important modifiable risk factor for the development of AAA is {{c1::tobacco use (smoking)}}.
extraInfo: Smoking is a stronger risk factor for AAA than for coronary artery disease.

text: The primary underlying cause of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms is {{c1::atherosclerosis}}.
extraInfo: Atherosclerosis causes transmural inflammation and degradation of the extracellular matrix.

text: The classic triad of an AAA rupture consists of {{c1::hypotension}}, {{c2::pulsatile abdominal mass}}, and {{c3::flank/back pain}}.
extraInfo: Only about 50% of patients present with the full triad.

text: The USPSTF recommends a one-time screening for AAA using {{c1::ultrasound}} in men aged {{c2::65–75}} who have ever {{c3::smoked}}.
extraInfo: Screening reduces AAA-related mortality in this high-risk population.

text: The risk of AAA rupture increases significantly once the diameter exceeds {{c1::5.5}} cm.
extraInfo: Surgical repair (EVAR or open) is usually indicated at this threshold or if growing >0.5 cm in 6 months.

text: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms are most commonly associated with {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}} and {{c2::hypertension}}.
extraInfo: Cystic medial necrosis involves the loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers.

text: In younger patients, TAAs are frequently associated with connective tissue disorders such as {{c1::Marfan syndrome}} or {{c2::Ehlers-Danlos syndrome}}.
extraInfo: Marfan syndrome is due to mutations in the FBN1 gene (fibrillin-1).

text: A {{c1::bicuspid aortic valve}} is a significant risk factor for the development of an ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm.
extraInfo: This is often seen in Turner syndrome as well.

text: Compression of the {{c1::left recurrent laryngeal nerve}} by a TAA can cause hoarseness.
extraInfo: This is sometimes referred to as Ortner syndrome when caused by cardiovascular pathology.

text: A TAA can cause dysphagia by compressing the {{c1::esophagus}}.
extraInfo: Compression of the airway can also lead to dyspnea or a brassy cough.

text: Tertiary syphilis can cause aneurysms by affecting the {{c1::vasa vasorum}} of the aorta.
extraInfo: Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum leads to ischemia of the media.

text: The characteristic gross appearance of the aortic intima in syphilitic aortitis is described as {{c1::tree-barking}}.
extraInfo: This is caused by contraction of fibrous scars following inflammation.

text: Syphilitic aneurysms typically involve the {{c1::ascending aorta}} and aortic arch.
extraInfo: This often results in aortic root dilation and aortic valve insufficiency.

text: A {{c1::mycotic}} aneurysm is an aneurysm resulting from an infection of the arterial wall.
extraInfo: Common causes include Salmonella, Staph aureus, or emboli from infective endocarditis.

text: Most Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms are {{c1::asymptomatic}} and are discovered incidentally on imaging.
extraInfo: This is why screening programs are vital for high-risk individuals.

text: Dilation of the aortic root in TAA can lead to the murmur of {{c1::aortic regurgitation (insufficiency)}}.
extraInfo: This is a high-pitched, blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur.

text: Unlike dissection, which involves a tear in the {{c1::intima}}, an aneurysm is a dilation of all wall layers.
extraInfo: However, a TAA is a major risk factor for subsequent aortic dissection.

text: The gender most commonly affected by AAA is {{c1::male}}.
extraInfo: The male-to-female ratio is approximately 4:1.

text: A TAA located in the {{c1::descending}} aorta is more commonly associated with atherosclerosis and hypertension.
extraInfo: Ascending TAAs are more likely due to cystic medial necrosis or genetic syndromes.

text: Atherosclerosis causes AAA by increasing the {{c1::diffusion distance}} from the lumen, leading to ischemia of the inner media.
extraInfo: This weakens the wall, allowing for compensatory dilation.

text: On a chest X-ray, a thoracic aortic aneurysm may appear as a {{c1::widened mediastinum}}.
extraInfo: Differential diagnosis for widened mediastinum includes aortic dissection and mediastinal masses.

text: The surgical mortality for an elective AAA repair is significantly {{c1::lower}} than for an emergency repair of a ruptured AAA.
extraInfo: Elective mortality is <5%, while rupture mortality exceeds 50%.

text: In patients with {{c1::Turner syndrome}} (45,XO), there is an increased risk of bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, and TAA.
extraInfo: Prophylactic monitoring is essential in these patients.

text: Calcification of the {{c1::ascending}} aorta seen on X-ray is a highly suggestive sign of syphilitic aortitis.
extraInfo: Atherosclerotic calcification usually involves the descending aorta or arch.

text: Proteases such as {{c1::matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)}} play a key role in the degradation of elastin in AAA pathogenesis.
extraInfo: An imbalance between MMPs and their inhibitors leads to wall weakening.

text: The 'blue toe syndrome' in AAA is caused by {{c1::distal embolization}} of mural thrombus or cholesterol crystals.
extraInfo: The aneurysm sac often contains laminated thrombus.

text: The most common symptom of a symptomatic, non-ruptured TAA is {{c1::chest or back pain}}.
extraInfo: The pain is often described as deep and steady.

text: Traumatic aortic rupture most commonly occurs due to {{c1::sudden deceleration}} injuries.
extraInfo: Classic examples include high-speed motor vehicle accidents or falls from great heights.

text: The most common site for traumatic aortic rupture is the {{c1::aortic isthmus}}.
extraInfo: This is the area just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.

text: The aortic isthmus is located just distal to the origin of the {{c1::left subclavian artery}}.
extraInfo: This point represents the transition between the mobile arch and fixed descending aorta.

text: The aortic isthmus is a high-risk site because it is tethered by the {{c1::ligamentum arteriosum}}.
extraInfo: The relative immobility of the descending aorta compared to the arch creates shear stress.

text: A hallmark finding of traumatic aortic rupture on chest X-ray is a {{c1::widened mediastinum}}.
extraInfo: Mediastinal width greater than 8 cm at the level of the aortic arch is often used as a threshold.

text: Traumatic aortic rupture typically results from {{c1::blunt}} chest trauma.
extraInfo: Penetrating trauma can also cause it, but blunt deceleration is the high-yield USMLE mechanism.

text: On chest X-ray, traumatic aortic rupture may show an {{c1::obscured}} aortic knob.
extraInfo: Loss of the clear contour of the aortic knob suggests a surrounding hematoma.

text: The {{c1::CT angiography}} is the gold standard for diagnosing traumatic aortic rupture in hemodynamically stable patients.
extraInfo: It is highly sensitive and specific for detecting intimal flaps or pseudoaneurysms.

text: In hemodynamically unstable patients, {{c1::transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)}} can be used to diagnose aortic rupture.
extraInfo: TEE can be performed at the bedside in the ER or operating room.

text: Traumatic aortic rupture is frequently associated with {{c1::motor vehicle accidents}} and falls from height.
extraInfo: The rapid change in velocity causes the heart and arch to move while the descending aorta remains fixed.

text: Traumatic aortic rupture is a life-threatening condition where most patients die {{c1::at the scene}}.
extraInfo: Approximately 80 percent of patients do not survive to reach the hospital.

text: On X-ray, the trachea may be deviated to the {{c1::right}} in cases of traumatic aortic rupture.
extraInfo: This is due to the mass effect of the mediastinal hematoma.

text: A {{c1::left-sided}} pleural effusion (hemothorax) is often seen on chest X-ray in aortic rupture.
extraInfo: Blood from the rupture tracks into the left pleural space.

text: Traumatic aortic rupture can cause {{c1::apical capping}}, which is blood over the left lung apex.
extraInfo: This is a classic radiologic sign of extrapleural blood.

text: The descending aorta is relatively {{c1::fixed}} compared to the mobile aortic arch, leading to shear stress during deceleration.
extraInfo: The fixation is due to its attachments to the posterior thoracic wall and intercostal arteries.

text: In traumatic aortic rupture, the {{c1::left main bronchus}} may be depressed inferiorly on imaging.
extraInfo: The overlying hematoma or the pseudoaneurysm itself pushes the bronchus downward.

text: Aortic rupture may present with {{c1::upper extremity hypertension}} and diminished lower extremity pulses.
extraInfo: This 'pseudocoarctation' syndrome occurs due to obstruction of flow at the site of the tear.

text: {{c1::TEVAR}} is a common modern management for traumatic aortic rupture.
extraInfo: Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair is often preferred over open surgery in suitable anatomy.

text: The nasogastric tube may be deviated to the {{c1::right}} on chest X-ray due to {{c1::mediastinal hematoma}}.
extraInfo: Similar to tracheal deviation, the hematoma shifts midline structures.

text: Traumatic aortic rupture involves tearing of the {{c1::tunica intima}}, media, and sometimes adventitia.
extraInfo: Partial tears can lead to the formation of a traumatic pseudoaneurysm.

text: If all three layers of the aorta are torn, it results in {{c1::immediate exsanguination}} and death.
extraInfo: Free rupture into the pleural space leads to rapid hypovolemic shock.

text: In survivors, the rupture is often contained by the {{c1::tunica adventitia}} or surrounding mediastinal structures.
extraInfo: This containment prevents immediate death but remains a surgical emergency.

text: Blunt trauma to the chest can cause a sudden increase in {{c1::intra-aortic pressure}}, contributing to rupture.
extraInfo: This is known as the 'water hammer' effect.

text: Traumatic aortic rupture is the {{c1::second}} most common cause of death in blunt trauma victims.
extraInfo: Head injury remains the leading cause of death in these patients.

text: On imaging, the {{c1::aortopulmonary window}} is often obliterated due to hemorrhage.
extraInfo: The space between the arch and pulmonary artery fills with blood.

text: The aortic isthmus represents the transition between the {{c1::mobile aortic arch}} and the fixed descending aorta.
extraInfo: Differential acceleration between these two segments causes the tear.

text: A patient in a high-speed collision with a {{c1::widened mediastinum}} likely has a traumatic aortic rupture.
extraInfo: This is the classic USMLE presentation board scenario.

text: {{c1::Aortography}} was historically the gold standard but has been largely replaced by CT angiography.
extraInfo: Invasive angiography is now mostly used during endovascular repair (TEVAR).

text: Pulse pressure may be {{c1::narrowed}} in cases of traumatic aortic rupture leading to cardiac tamponade or shock.
extraInfo: Proximal extension into the pericardium can cause tamponade, though most ruptures are distal.

text: Aortic dissection involves a longitudinal {{c1::intimal}} tear that creates a false lumen.
extraInfo: The blood flows between the intima and media, potentially leading to rupture or organ ischemia.

text: The most common risk factor for aortic dissection is {{c1::hypertension}}.
extraInfo: Chronic high pressure causes mechanical stress on the aortic wall.

text: The underlying pathology of the aortic media often associated with dissection is {{c1::cystic medial necrosis}}.
extraInfo: This is common in connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome.

text: Stanford Type {{c1::A}} dissection involves the ascending aorta.
extraInfo: It may also involve the arch or descending aorta, but involvement of the ascending portion defines Type A.

text: Stanford Type {{c1::B}} dissection is limited to the descending aorta, distal to the {{c2::left subclavian artery}}.
extraInfo: Type B is generally managed medically unless complications arise.
