extraInfo: Dexrazoxane is an iron-chelating agent that prevents free radical formation.

text: In South America, {{c1::Chagas disease}} (caused by Trypanosoma cruzi) is a frequent cause of dilated cardiomyopathy.
extraInfo: Often associated with megacolon and megaesophagus.

text: Physical exam findings in dilated cardiomyopathy often include an {{c1::S3}} gallop and {{c2::systolic}} regurgitant murmurs.
extraInfo: S3 is due to blood rushing into a dilated, compliant ventricle.

text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) primarily causes {{c1::diastolic}} dysfunction due to {{c2::concentric}} hypertrophy.
extraInfo: The ventricle becomes stiff, impairing filling.

text: HCM is the most common cause of {{c1::sudden cardiac death}} in young athletes, often due to {{c2::ventricular arrhythmia}}.
extraInfo: Screening in family members is crucial.

text: HCM is usually autosomal dominant and most commonly involves mutations in the {{c1::β-myosin heavy chain}} or {{c2::myosin-binding protein C}}.
extraInfo: Mutations affect the sarcomere proteins.

text: The classic morphological finding in HCM is {{c1::asymmetric septal hypertrophy}}.
extraInfo: The septum is significantly thicker than the posterior wall.

text: The histologic hallmark of HCM is {{c1::myofiber disarray}} and interstitial fibrosis.
extraInfo: Disorganized arrangement of myocytes on microscopy.

text: Obstruction in HOCM (Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy) is caused by the {{c1::systolic anterior motion (SAM)}} of the mitral valve against the hypertrophied septum.
extraInfo: This creates a Venturi effect that narrows the LV outflow tract.

text: The murmur of HCM {{c1::increases}} with Valsalva or standing and {{c2::decreases}} with squatting or handgrip.
extraInfo: Maneuvers that decrease preload (Valsalva) worsen the outflow tract obstruction.

text: An {{c1::S4}} gallop is frequently heard in patients with HCM.
extraInfo: S4 is due to atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle.

text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy causes {{c1::diastolic}} heart failure and is characterized by decreased ventricular {{c2::compliance}}.
extraInfo: Filling is restricted, but systolic function is often preserved initially.

text: {{c1::Amyloidosis}} is a common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy and may show {{c2::apple-green birefringence}} under polarized light with Congo red stain.
extraInfo: Can be due to AL (plasma cell dyscrasia) or ATTR (transthyretin) amyloid.

text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy associated with non-caseating granulomas is caused by {{c1::Sarcoidosis}}.
extraInfo: Can also lead to conduction blocks and arrhythmias.

text: {{c1::Löffler endocarditis}} is a restrictive cardiomyopathy associated with {{c2::hypereosinophilia}} and endomyocardial fibrosis.
extraInfo: Eosinophilic granules release basic protein which damages the endocardium.

text: Hemochromatosis can cause restrictive cardiomyopathy early on, though it more commonly presents as {{c1::dilated}} cardiomyopathy later in the disease.
extraInfo: Iron deposition in the myocardium.

text: EKG in restrictive cardiomyopathy (especially amyloidosis) typically shows {{c1::low voltage}} despite the appearance of thick walls on echo.
extraInfo: The 'thick' walls are due to infiltrative material, not actual myocyte hypertrophy.

text: {{c1::Kussmaul sign}} (a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration) can be seen in {{c2::restrictive}} cardiomyopathy.
extraInfo: Also commonly associated with constrictive pericarditis.

text: First-line pharmacological treatment for symptomatic HCM includes {{c1::β-blockers}} or non-dihydropyridine {{c2::calcium channel blockers}}.
extraInfo: These drugs increase diastolic filling time by slowing the heart rate.

text: In patients with HCM, {{c1::diuretics}} and {{c2::nitrates}} should be avoided as they decrease preload and worsen the obstruction.
extraInfo: Decreased LV volume brings the septum and mitral valve closer together.

text: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a form of {{c1::dilated}} cardiomyopathy that occurs during late pregnancy or {{c2::early postpartum}}.
extraInfo: Often associated with high prolactin levels.

text: Cocaine use can cause dilated cardiomyopathy via {{c1::chronic vasoconstriction}} and direct {{c2::myocardial toxicity}}.
extraInfo: Can also cause acute MI due to coronary vasospasm.

text: {{c1::Endocardial fibroelastosis}} is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy typically seen in {{c2::infants}}.
extraInfo: Characterized by thick fibroelastic tissue in the endocardium.

text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is often difficult to distinguish from {{c1::constrictive pericarditis}}; however, {{c2::BNP}} is usually more elevated in restrictive cardiomyopathy.
extraInfo: Imaging (CT/MRI) showing a thickened pericardium favors constrictive pericarditis.

text: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy ('broken heart syndrome') presents as ventricular apical ballooning, mimicking {{c1::dilated}} cardiomyopathy, often triggered by {{c2::stress}}.
extraInfo: Believed to be caused by catecholamine surge.

text: {{c1::HFrEF}} is defined by an ejection fraction (EF) of {{c2::≤ 40}}%.
extraInfo: HFrEF stands for Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction.

text: {{c1::HFpEF}} is defined by an ejection fraction (EF) of {{c2::≥ 50}}%.
extraInfo: HFpEF stands for Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction.

text: HFrEF is primarily a disorder of {{c1::systolic}} dysfunction, characterized by impaired {{c2::contractility}}.
extraInfo: Commonly due to MI or dilated cardiomyopathy.

text: HFpEF is primarily a disorder of {{c1::diastolic}} dysfunction, characterized by impaired {{c2::filling/relaxation}}.
extraInfo: Commonly due to chronic hypertension.

text: HFrEF typically results in {{c1::eccentric}} hypertrophy due to {{c2::volume}} overload.
extraInfo: The ventricle dilates to accommodate more volume.

text: HFpEF typically results in {{c1::concentric}} hypertrophy due to {{c2::pressure}} overload.
extraInfo: The ventricular wall thickens to handle high afterload.

text: In {{c1::eccentric}} hypertrophy, sarcomeres are added in {{c2::series}}.
extraInfo: This leads to chamber dilation.

text: In {{c1::concentric}} hypertrophy, sarcomeres are added in {{c2::parallel}}.
extraInfo: This leads to wall thickening.

text: The classic heart sound associated with HFrEF is an {{c1::S3}} gallop.
extraInfo: Associated with rapid ventricular filling into a dilated/compliant chamber.

text: The classic heart sound associated with HFpEF is an {{c1::S4}} gallop.
extraInfo: Associated with atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle.

text: A patient with HFrEF will have an {{c1::increased}} Left Ventricular End-Diastolic Volume (LVEDV).
extraInfo: The heart dilates (remodeling) to compensate for poor stroke volume.

text: A patient with HFpEF usually has a {{c1::normal}} Left Ventricular End-Diastolic Volume (LVEDV).
extraInfo: The primary issue is stiffness, not volume, though pressures are elevated.

text: Chronic hypertension is the most common cause of {{c1::HFpEF}}.
extraInfo: The high afterload leads to concentric hypertrophy and stiffening.

text: Myocardial infarction and dilated cardiomyopathy are classic causes of {{c1::HFrEF}}.
extraInfo: Loss of viable myocardium leads to pump failure.

text: B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) is released from the {{c1::ventricles}} in response to increased {{c2::tension/stretch}}.
extraInfo: BNP is used clinically to rule out heart failure in the setting of dyspnea.

text: {{c1::ANP}} is released from the atria in response to increased atrial stretch.
extraInfo: Atrial Natriuretic Peptide.

text: The effect of BNP includes {{c1::vasodilation}} and {{c2::natriuresis}}.
extraInfo: It acts as a natural antagonist to the RAAS system.

text: Heart failure leads to {{c1::activation}} of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) to maintain blood pressure.
extraInfo: This compensatory mechanism eventually becomes maladaptive, leading to further remodeling.

text: The S3 heart sound occurs during the {{c1::early}} phase of diastole.
extraInfo: Occurs during the rapid filling phase.

text: The S4 heart sound occurs during the {{c1::late}} phase of diastole.
extraInfo: Occurs during the 'atrial kick'.

text: Sympathetic nervous system activation in heart failure increases afterload via {{c1::alpha-1}} mediated vasoconstriction.
extraInfo: This increases the workload on an already failing heart.

text: {{c1::Orthopnea}} is shortness of breath when lying flat, relieved by sitting up.
extraInfo: Caused by redistribution of blood from the lower extremities to the lungs.

text: {{c1::Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)}} is characterized by sudden dyspnea and coughing that awakens the patient from sleep.
extraInfo: Caused by increased venous return when recumbent.

text: In HFpEF, the ventricular {{c1::compliance}} is decreased.
extraInfo: Compliance = Delta V / Delta P.

text: On a Pressure-Volume loop, HFrEF shows a {{c1::rightward}} shift and {{c2::reduced}} height of the loop.
extraInfo: Reduced height represents decreased stroke volume.

text: On a Pressure-Volume loop, HFpEF shows a {{c1::steeper}} diastolic filling curve.
extraInfo: Reflects decreased compliance/increased stiffness.

text: {{c1::Neprilysin}} is the enzyme responsible for the degradation of natriuretic peptides like BNP.
extraInfo: Inhibition (e.g., Sacubitril) increases BNP levels.

text: Heart Failure with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) is defined as an EF of {{c1::41-49}}%.
extraInfo: A transitional category between HFrEF and HFpEF.

text: Chronic compensatory {{c1::tachycardia}} in heart failure leads to increased myocardial oxygen demand and decreased {{c2::diastolic filling time}}.
extraInfo: This worsens the underlying cardiac dysfunction.

text: High-output heart failure (HOHF) is characterized by a(n) {{c1::decreased}} systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
extraInfo: Decreased SVR leads to a compensatory increase in cardiac output.

text: In high-output heart failure, the primary hemodynamic trigger is a(n) {{c1::increased}} venous return to the heart.
extraInfo: The heart cannot keep up with the increased metabolic demand or blood volume despite high CO.

text: {{c1::Wet beriberi}} is the classic cause of high-output heart failure due to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.
extraInfo: Dry beriberi presents primarily as peripheral neuropathy.

text: Wet beriberi (thiamine deficiency) causes heart failure by inducing peripheral {{c1::vasodilation}}.
extraInfo: This reduces SVR, leading to high-output states.

text: A common patient demographic for wet beriberi is individuals with {{c1::alcoholism}} or severe malnutrition.
extraInfo: Chronic alcohol use impairs thiamine absorption and storage.

text: On physical exam, high-output heart failure often presents with a(n) {{c1::wide}} pulse pressure.
extraInfo: Pulse pressure = Systolic BP - Diastolic BP.

text: The peripheral pulses in high-output heart failure are often described as {{c1::bounding (or water-hammer)}}.
extraInfo: This is due to the rapid stroke volume and low diastolic pressure.

text: Unlike low-output HF, the skin in high-output heart failure is typically {{c1::warm}} to the touch.
extraInfo: This is a result of peripheral vasodilation.

text: {{c1::Paget disease of bone}} can cause high-output heart failure due to the formation of multiple small arteriovenous (AV) shunts in hypervascular bone.
extraInfo: The increased vascularity acts as a shunt, bypassing resistance.

text: Severe {{c1::anemia}} causes high-output heart failure by decreasing blood viscosity and reducing oxygen delivery.
extraInfo: Lower viscosity reduces SVR; reduced O2 delivery triggers a compensatory CO increase.

text: {{c1::Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis)}} can lead to HOHF by increasing metabolic demand and upregulating beta-adrenergic receptors.
extraInfo: This increases both heart rate and stroke volume.

text: Large {{c1::arteriovenous (AV) fistulas}} (congenital or acquired) can lead to HOHF by bypassing the high-resistance capillary beds.
extraInfo: Often seen post-trauma or in dialysis patients with large access sites.

text: Wet beriberi can lead to {{c1::dilated}} cardiomyopathy.
extraInfo: This is mentioned in the rapid review context of vitamin deficiencies.

text: {{c1::Obesity}} is a common cause of high-output state because the heart must pump more blood to supply the increased adipose tissue.
extraInfo: Increased blood volume is required to perfuse the extra tissue.

text: In the early (warm) phase of {{c1::septic shock}}, cardiac output is often high, representing a temporary high-output state.
extraInfo: Massive peripheral vasodilation occurs due to inflammatory cytokines.

text: {{c1::Pregnancy}} is a physiologic condition that significantly increases cardiac output, though it rarely causes HF on its own.
extraInfo: CO increases by 30-50% in pregnancy.

text: The heart sound {{c1::S3}} is frequently heard in high-output states due to rapid ventricular filling.
extraInfo: S3 is associated with high volume inflow into a dilated ventricle.

text: Thiamine (B1) is a necessary cofactor for the enzyme {{c1::pyruvate dehydrogenase}}, and its deficiency impairs ATP production in the myocardium.
extraInfo: This leads to the myocardial dysfunction seen in wet beriberi.

text: Treatment for wet beriberi involves immediate administration of {{c1::thiamine (B1)}}.
extraInfo: Always give thiamine before glucose in malnourished patients to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

text: In HOHF caused by Paget disease, the elevated blood flow occurs specifically in the {{c1::bone}}.
extraInfo: Hypervascularity in the Pagetic bone functions as an AV shunt.

text: The compensatory mechanism for low oxygen in anemia involves {{c1::sympathetic}} nervous system activation to increase heart rate.
extraInfo: This contributes to the high-output state.

text: A patient with HOHF and high Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) likely has {{c1::Paget disease of bone}}.
extraInfo: ALP is a marker of bone turnover.

text: In patients with HOHF, the venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is typically {{c1::increased}}.
extraInfo: Because blood passes through the tissues too quickly or through shunts, less oxygen is extracted.

text: {{c1::Myeloproliferative}} disorders (like Polycythemia Vera) usually cause low-output states, but extreme splenomegaly can occasionally cause high-output states via shunting.
extraInfo: Contrast this with anemia, which more classically causes high-output states.

text: {{c1::Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu)}} can cause HOHF due to large AV malformations in the liver or lungs.
extraInfo: Telangiectasias and AVMs are hallmarks of this AD disease.

text: Chronic HOHF eventually leads to heart failure because the increased {{c1::workload}} eventually results in myocardial exhaustion and remodeling.
extraInfo: High output cannot be sustained indefinitely.

text: In HOHF, despite the high CO, the effective arterial blood volume (EABV) is often {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: This triggers the RAAS system, leading to fluid retention and edema.

text: Wet beriberi is distinguished from dry beriberi by the presence of {{c1::edema}} and cardiac involvement.
extraInfo: Dry beriberi involves symmetric peripheral neuropathy (sensory and motor).

text: Hemodynamically, HOHF is defined by a Cardiac Index (CI) of >{{c1::3.9 - 4.0}} L/min/m².
extraInfo: Normal CI is roughly 2.5 to 4.0.

text: Shock is defined as {{c1::inadequate tissue perfusion}} and oxygenation.
extraInfo: All forms of shock eventually lead to multi-organ failure if untreated.

text: In hypovolemic shock, the Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: PCWP is an indicator of left-sided preload; low volume means low pressure.

text: In hypovolemic shock, Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR) is {{c1::increased}}.
extraInfo: This is a compensatory mechanism to maintain MAP despite low cardiac output.

text: In hypovolemic shock, Cardiac Output (CO) is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: Caused by low stroke volume due to loss of intravascular volume.

text: In cardiogenic shock, the Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) is {{c1::increased}}.
extraInfo: Blood backs up into the left atrium and pulmonary circulation because the heart cannot pump efficiently.

text: In cardiogenic shock, Cardiac Output (CO) is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: This is the primary insult, often caused by MI, arrhythmia, or heart failure.

text: In cardiogenic shock, Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR) is {{c1::increased}}.
extraInfo: Compensatory vasoconstriction occurs to maintain BP.

text: In distributive (septic) shock, Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR) is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: This is the hallmark of distributive shock due to massive peripheral vasodilation.

text: In early septic shock, Cardiac Output (CO) is typically {{c1::increased}}.
extraInfo: Also known as 'Hyperdynamic' shock.

text: In septic shock, the Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) is {{c1::decreased or normal}}.
extraInfo: Peripheral pooling of blood reduces venous return.

text: Mixed venous oxygen saturation (MvO2) is {{c1::increased}} in septic shock.
extraInfo: Tissues are unable to extract oxygen efficiently, and high CO speeds up transit time.

text: Cardiac tamponade is a cause of obstructive shock that leads to {{c1::increased}} PCWP.
extraInfo: Pressure on the heart prevents filling but increases measured wedge pressure.

text: A massive pulmonary embolism causes obstructive shock with a {{c1::decreased}} PCWP.
extraInfo: The blockage is before the left heart, reducing blood flow to the left atrium.

text: Neurogenic shock is characterized by a {{c1::decreased}} heart rate (bradycardia).
extraInfo: Loss of sympathetic tone leaves parasympathetic (vagal) tone unopposed.

text: In neurogenic shock, Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR) is {{c1::decreased}}.
extraInfo: Loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone leads to vasodilation.

text: Patients in hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock typically have {{c1::cold and clammy}} skin.
extraInfo: Due to sympathetic-mediated peripheral vasoconstriction.

text: Early septic shock presents with {{c1::warm and dry}} skin.
extraInfo: Due to peripheral vasodilation (warm shock).

text: The first-line treatment for anaphylactic shock is {{c1::epinephrine}}.
extraInfo: Mechanism: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction, Beta-1 HR/Contractility, Beta-2 Bronchodilation.

text: The first-line vasopressor for septic shock is {{c1::norepinephrine}}.
extraInfo: It provides potent alpha-1 agonism and some beta-1 agonism.

text: A common inotrope used in cardiogenic shock to increase contractility is {{c1::dobutamine}}.
extraInfo: B1 agonist; use with caution as it can also cause vasodilation (B2).

text: MvO2 is {{c1::decreased}} in hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock.
extraInfo: Tissues extract more oxygen because blood flow is slow (low CO).

text: Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) is an indirect measurement of {{c1::Left Atrial Pressure}}.
extraInfo: Assuming no mitral valve disease.

text: SIRS criteria include a temperature of >{{c1::38}}°C or <{{c2::36}}°C.
extraInfo: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome.

text: SIRS criteria include a white blood cell count of >{{c1::12,000}} or <{{c2::4,000}}.
extraInfo: Or >10% bands.

text: SIRS criteria include a heart rate >{{c1::90}} bpm.
extraInfo: Tachycardia is a common compensatory response to inflammation or shock.

text: Adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian crisis) causes {{c1::distributive}} shock.
extraInfo: Requires corticosteroid replacement; often refractory to fluids and pressors.

text: In a tension pneumothorax, the mediastinal shift leads to {{c1::decreased}} venous return.
extraInfo: This results in obstructive shock.

text: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) calculation: {{c1::1/3 SBP + 2/3 DBP}}.
extraInfo: Diastole counts for more of the cardiac cycle at normal heart rates.

text: Pulse pressure is typically {{c1::widened}} in distributive shock and {{c2::narrowed}} in hypovolemic shock.
extraInfo: Widened pulse pressure is due to low diastolic pressure from vasodilation.

text: Syncope is defined as a transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) due to {{c1::global cerebral hypoperfusion}} followed by spontaneous recovery.
extraInfo: It is characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and complete spontaneous recovery.

text: The three main categories of syncope are {{c1::reflex (neurally mediated)}}, {{c2::orthostatic hypotension}}, and {{c3::cardiac}}.
extraInfo: Reflex syncope is the most common cause in the general population.

text: Vasovagal syncope is often preceded by a prodrome of {{c1::nausea}}, {{c2::pallor}}, and {{c3::diaphoresis}}.
extraInfo: Triggers include emotional stress, pain, or prolonged standing.

text: Situational syncope is a type of reflex syncope triggered by specific actions such as {{c1::micturition}}, {{c2::defecation}}, or {{c3::coughing}}.
extraInfo: These triggers increase vagal tone or decrease venous return via the Valsalva maneuver.

text: Carotid sinus syndrome causes syncope triggered by pressure on the carotid sinus, such as from {{c1::shaving}} or a {{c2::tight collar}}.
extraInfo: It is more common in elderly males.

text: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a drop in systolic BP of ≥{{c1::20}} mmHg or diastolic BP of ≥{{c2::10}} mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.
extraInfo: The primary mechanism is an inadequate compensatory increase in systemic vascular resistance upon standing.

text: Drug-induced orthostatic syncope is frequently caused by {{c1::diuretics}}, {{c2::alpha-blockers}}, or {{c3::vasodilators}}.
extraInfo: Common in elderly patients on multiple antihypertensive medications.

text: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension can be caused by autonomic failure in conditions like {{c1::Parkinson disease}} or {{c2::diabetes mellitus}}.
extraInfo: In these cases, the compensatory heart rate increase is often blunted.

text: Cardiac syncope due to {{c1::arrhythmia}} is often sudden in onset and occurs without a prodrome.
extraInfo: Common causes include sick sinus syndrome, AV blocks, or ventricular tachycardia.

text: Exertional syncope is a classic presentation of {{c1::aortic stenosis}}.
extraInfo: The fixed cardiac output cannot meet the demand of systemic vasodilation during exercise.

text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) causes exertional syncope due to {{c1::systolic anterior motion (SAM)}} of the mitral valve leading to outflow tract obstruction.
extraInfo: Often seen in young athletes.

text: Syncope occurring while the patient is {{c1::supine}} is highly suggestive of a cardiac arrhythmia.
extraInfo: Reflex syncope almost never occurs in the supine position.

text: The most important initial diagnostic test in the workup of syncope is a(n) {{c1::12-lead ECG}}.
extraInfo: It screens for conduction abnormalities, ischemia, and interval prolongations.

text: Long QT syndrome can lead to syncope via the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia known as {{c1::Torsades de pointes}}.
extraInfo: Can be congenital or acquired (e.g., electrolyte imbalances or drugs).

text: {{c1::Brugada syndrome}} is a genetic disorder causing syncope and sudden death, characterized by pseudo-right bundle branch block and ST elevation in V1–V3.
extraInfo: More common in males of Asian descent.

text: In vasovagal syncope, there is a sudden increase in {{c1::parasympathetic}} activity and a withdrawal of {{c2::sympathetic}} activity.
extraInfo: This leads to bradycardia (cardioinhibitory) and vasodilation (vasodepressor).

text: Syncope caused by {{c1::pulmonary embolism}} is usually associated with shortness of breath and right heart strain.
extraInfo: Occurs when a large embolus (e.g., saddle embolus) obstructs >50% of the pulmonary circulation.

text: Subclavian steal syndrome causes syncope or presyncope during {{c1::arm exercise}}.
extraInfo: Blood is 'stolen' from the vertebral artery to supply the arm distal to a subclavian stenosis.

text: {{c1::Convulsive syncope}} involves brief myoclonic jerks during a syncopal episode but lacks a prolonged postictal state.
extraInfo: This is frequently misdiagnosed as a seizure.

text: Unlike a seizure, syncope usually has a very rapid recovery of {{c1::orientation and consciousness}}.
extraInfo: A postictal state (confusion) lasting >10 minutes suggests seizure.

text: {{c1::Postprandial}} syncope occurs after eating and is most common in elderly patients with autonomic dysfunction.
extraInfo: Caused by blood pooling in the splanchnic circulation.

text: The {{c1::Tilt table test}} is used to confirm a diagnosis of reflex syncope when the diagnosis is uncertain.
extraInfo: It attempts to reproduce the vasovagal response in a controlled setting.

text: Syncope caused by {{c1::atrial myxoma}} is typically positional, occurring when the tumor obstructs the mitral valve.
extraInfo: Often associated with a 'tumor plop' on auscultation.

text: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome can cause syncope due to the development of {{c1::AFib with rapid ventricular response}} via an accessory pathway.
extraInfo: ECG shows a delta wave and short PR interval.

text: Third-degree (complete) heart block results in syncope due to {{c1::atrioventricular (AV) dissociation}} and a slow escape rhythm.
extraInfo: Often requires a permanent pacemaker.

text: {{c1::Hypovolemia}} (e.g., hemorrhage, dehydration) is a common cause of orthostatic syncope.
extraInfo: Associated with a significant increase in heart rate upon standing.

text: The term 'vasodepressor response' refers specifically to the {{c1::loss of vascular tone}} leading to hypotension in reflex syncope.
extraInfo: The 'cardioinhibitory response' refers to the bradycardia.

text: Adams-Stokes attacks are sudden syncopal episodes caused by {{c1::paroxysmal complete heart block}}.
extraInfo: Characterized by sudden collapse without warning.

text: Psychogenic pseudosyncope is characterized by TLOC without {{c1::drop in blood pressure or heart rate}}.
extraInfo: Patients often have closed eyes and a longer duration of 'unconsciousness' compared to true syncope.

text: Acute infective endocarditis is most commonly caused by {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus::organism}} and typically affects {{c2::previously normal::valve status}} valves.
extraInfo: S. aureus is highly virulent and causes rapid valve destruction and large vegetations.

text: Subacute infective endocarditis is most commonly caused by {{c1::Viridans streptococci::organism}} and typically affects {{c2::previously damaged::valve status}} valves.
extraInfo: Viridans streptococci have low virulence and produce smaller vegetations; common after dental procedures.

text: In intravenous drug users (IVDUs), infective endocarditis most frequently affects the {{c1::tricuspid::valve}} valve.
extraInfo: 'Don't TRI Drugs' mnemonic: Tricuspid valve is involved in IVDUs.

text: The most common organism causing infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users is {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
extraInfo: Often presents with septic pulmonary emboli due to right-sided involvement.

text: {{c1::Roth spots::Finding}} are round white spots on the retina surrounded by hemorrhage, seen in infective endocarditis.
extraInfo: These are considered immunologic phenomena in the Duke criteria.

text: {{c1::Osler nodes::Finding}} are painful, raised, red-purple lesions found on the pads of fingers and toes.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: 'Osler' = 'Ouch!' (Painful). These are immunologic phenomena.

text: {{c1::Janeway lesions::Finding}} are small, painless, erythematous lesions on the palms or soles.
extraInfo: These are vascular phenomena caused by septic microemboli.

text: Osler nodes in infective endocarditis are caused by {{c1::immune complex::mechanism}} deposition.
extraInfo: Contrast this with Janeway lesions, which are embolic.

text: Janeway lesions in infective endocarditis are caused by {{c1::septic emboli::mechanism}}.
extraInfo: Because they are embolic, they are typically painless.

text: Dark red linear streaks under the nail beds seen in IE are known as {{c1::splinter hemorrhages}}.
extraInfo: These are classified as vascular phenomena in the Duke criteria.

text: Infective endocarditis caused by {{c1::Streptococcus gallolyticus::organism}} is highly associated with underlying colon cancer.
extraInfo: Formerly known as Streptococcus bovis. If found, a colonoscopy is mandatory.

text: The {{c1::HACEK::Group name}} organisms are a well-known cause of culture-negative endocarditis.
extraInfo: HACEK stands for Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella.

text: The most common cause of culture-negative endocarditis in a patient with exposure to farm animals (e.g., sheep) is {{c1::Coxiella burnetii}}.
extraInfo: Causes Q fever; diagnosis often requires serology rather than standard culture.

text: Subacute endocarditis occurring after dental procedures is most frequently caused by {{c1::Viridans streptococci}}.
extraInfo: Specifically Streptococcus sanguinis, which produces dextrans that bind to fibrin-platelet aggregates.

text: The most common presenting symptom of infective endocarditis is {{c1::fever}}.
extraInfo: Seen in >90% of cases.

text: Patients with infective endocarditis may develop hematuria and proteinuria due to {{c1::glomerulonephritis}} caused by {{c2::immune complex}} deposition.
extraInfo: This is an immunologic phenomenon.

text: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within 60 days of surgery) is most commonly caused by {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}.
extraInfo: S. epidermidis produces biofilms on prosthetic material.

text: The two major Duke criteria for diagnosing IE are {{c1::positive blood cultures}} and {{c2::echo evidence of vegetation/regurgitation}}.
extraInfo: Major criteria are the most specific for the diagnosis.

text: Patients with subacute infective endocarditis often present with {{c1::anemia of chronic disease::hematologic finding}}.
extraInfo: This contributes to the fatigue and pallor seen in these patients.

text: In intravenous drug users with tricuspid IE, the most common extra-cardiac complication is {{c1::septic pulmonary emboli}}.
extraInfo: Presents as multiple nodular opacities on chest X-ray, sometimes with cavitation.

text: The most common predisposing heart condition for subacute IE in developed countries is {{c1::mitral valve prolapse::condition}}.
extraInfo: Bicuspid aortic valve is another high-yield predisposing factor.

text: Vegetations in infective endocarditis are primarily composed of {{c1::platelets}}, {{c2::fibrin}}, and microorganisms.
extraInfo: They are 'friable' and can easily break off to cause emboli.

text: The standard first-line antibiotic for infective endocarditis prophylaxis in high-risk patients undergoing dental procedures is {{c1::amoxicillin}}.
extraInfo: Used to prevent Viridans streptococci bacteremia.

text: Prophylaxis for IE is indicated for dental procedures in patients with {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}}, {{c2::previous IE history}}, or unrepaired cyanotic CHD.
extraInfo: It is no longer recommended for simple MVP or most other valvular diseases.

text: {{c1::Bartonella::organism}} species are a cause of culture-negative endocarditis often associated with homelessness, body lice, or cat scratches.
extraInfo: B. quintana (lice) and B. henselae (cats).

text: In acute endocarditis, the onset is {{c1::rapid::speed}} and the vegetations are usually {{c2::large}}.
extraInfo: Subacute IE is more insidious with smaller vegetations.

text: A rare cause of culture-negative endocarditis associated with weight loss, joint pain, and diarrhea is {{c1::Tropheryma whipplei}}.
extraInfo: Whipple's disease can present with cardiac involvement.

text: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is the most common cause of infective endocarditis overall in most modern studies.
extraInfo: Historically it was Viridans, but S. aureus has taken the lead due to healthcare-associated infections.

text: The classic physical exam finding of a {{c1::new heart murmur}} in the setting of fever should always raise suspicion for IE.
extraInfo: Usually represents new valvular regurgitation.

text: Syphilitic heart disease is a manifestation of {{c1::tertiary}} syphilis.
extraInfo: It typically appears decades after the initial infection.

text: The primary underlying pathology in syphilitic heart disease is {{c1::endarteritis}} of the {{c2::vasa vasorum}}.
extraInfo: This leads to ischemic injury of the aortic wall.

text: In syphilitic aortitis, there is destruction of the {{c1::tunica media}} of the aorta.
extraInfo: Loss of elastic fibers leads to dilation of the vessel.

text: Syphilitic heart disease characteristically involves the {{c1::ascending}} aorta.
extraInfo: This is in contrast to atherosclerosis, which more commonly affects the abdominal aorta.

text: The macroscopic appearance of the aorta in syphilitic heart disease is described as {{c1::tree bark}}.
extraInfo: This is due to scarring and contraction of the intima following medial damage.

text: Syphilitic involvement of the aorta can lead to the formation of an {{c1::aneurysm}}.
extraInfo: Typically an aneurysm of the ascending aorta or aortic arch.

text: Dilation of the aortic root in syphilis often leads to {{c1::aortic regurgitation}}.
extraInfo: The valve leaflets themselves are usually normal but are pulled apart by the dilating root.

text: Syphilitic heart disease is associated with {{c1::plasma cell}}-rich infiltrates in the adventitia.
extraInfo: This is a key histologic finding in the vasa vasorum.

text: Aortic regurgitation from syphilis results in a {{c1::diastolic}} murmur.
extraInfo: It is often a high-pitched, blowing murmur heard best at the right sternal border.

text: Syphilitic aortitis can cause narrowing of the coronary artery origins, a condition known as {{c1::coronary ostial stenosis}}.
extraInfo: This can lead to myocardial ischemia or angina.

text: The causative agent of the infection leading to syphilitic heart disease is {{c1::Treponema pallidum}}.
extraInfo: A spirochete bacterium.

text: A clinical sign often associated with tertiary syphilis (and thus syphilitic heart disease) is {{c1::Argyll Robertson}} pupils.
extraInfo: Pupils that constrict with accommodation but do not react to light.

text: Calcification of the {{c1::ascending}} aorta seen on X-ray is highly suggestive of syphilitic aortitis.
extraInfo: Atherosclerosis usually calcifies the descending or abdominal aorta.

text: Chronic aortic regurgitation in syphilis leads to {{c1::left ventricular hypertrophy}}.
extraInfo: Specifically, eccentric hypertrophy due to volume overload.

text: The type of endarteritis seen in the vasa vasorum in syphilis is described as {{c1::obliterative}} endarteritis.
extraInfo: This leads to luminal narrowing and vessel wall ischemia.

text: Aortic regurgitation in syphilis presents with a {{c1::widened}} pulse pressure.
extraInfo: Manifests as signs like 'water-hammer' pulse or head bobbing.

text: The diagnostic screening test for syphilis is {{c1::VDRL}} or RPR.
extraInfo: These are non-treponemal tests.

text: The confirmatory test for a diagnosis of syphilis is {{c1::FTA-ABS}} or TP-PA.
extraInfo: These are treponemal-specific tests.

text: The primary treatment for all stages of syphilis, including tertiary heart involvement, is {{c1::Penicillin G}}.
extraInfo: IV administration is often required for late-stage complications.

text: The aortic aneurysm in syphilis is typically {{c1::saccular}} or fusiform in shape.
extraInfo: It involves the aortic arch or ascending aorta.

text: Destruction of {{c1::elastic}} tissue in the media is the hallmark of syphilitic aortitis.
extraInfo: This weakens the structural integrity of the vessel.

text: Syphilitic heart disease is rarely seen in the modern era due to effective treatment during the {{c1::primary}} or {{c2::secondary}} stages.
extraInfo: Early antibiotic use prevents progression to tertiary disease.

text: Tabes dorsalis and syphilitic heart disease both occur in the {{c1::tertiary}} stage of syphilis.
extraInfo: Tabes dorsalis involves the posterior columns of the spinal cord.

text: The 'tree bark' appearance is due to the contraction of {{c1::fibrous}} scars within the aortic wall.
extraInfo: It creates an irregular, wrinkled intimal surface.

text: Syphilitic heart disease leads to 'functional' aortic stenosis/regurgitation? {{c1::Regurgitation}}.
extraInfo: The dilation of the ring causes the valve to become incompetent.

text: Vasa vasorum endarteritis leads to {{c1::atrophy}} of the muscular and elastic elements of the media.
extraInfo: Resulting from lack of blood supply to the outer layers of the aorta.

text: In syphilitic aortitis, the inflammatory process begins in the {{c1::adventitia}}.
extraInfo: Specifically targeting the vessels that supply the aorta itself.

text: True or False: Syphilitic heart disease frequently involves the mitral valve. {{c1::False}}.
extraInfo: It primarily involves the aorta and the aortic valve.

text: The interval between primary infection and the development of syphilitic aortitis is typically {{c1::10 to 30}} years.
extraInfo: It is a late-stage complication.

text: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) is also known as {{c1::marantic}} endocarditis.
extraInfo: It is frequently associated with advanced malignancy or chronic wasting diseases.

text: The vegetations in NBTE consist of {{c1::sterile}} thrombi made of fibrin and platelets.
extraInfo: Unlike infective endocarditis, no microorganisms are present.

text: NBTE is most commonly associated with advanced {{c1::malignancy}}, particularly adenocarcinomas.
extraInfo: It is considered a paraneoplastic manifestation.

text: The specific malignancy most classically associated with NBTE is {{c1::pancreatic}} adenocarcinoma.
extraInfo: Lung and gastric cancers are also common causes.

text: NBTE is associated with {{c1::hypercoagulable}} states such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
extraInfo: Pro-coagulant state leads to fibrin deposition on valves.

text: NBTE vegetations are typically found along the {{c1::lines of closure}} of the valve leaflets.
extraInfo: This location is similar to where rheumatic endocarditis vegetations form.

text: The most common heart valve affected by NBTE is the {{c1::mitral}} valve.
extraInfo: The aortic valve is the second most common.

text: In contrast to infective endocarditis, the vegetations in NBTE are {{c1::non-destructive}} to the valve.
extraInfo: They do not cause perforation or structural damage to the leaflets.

text: The most significant clinical complication of NBTE is {{c1::systemic embolization}}.
extraInfo: The vegetations are friable and easily dislodge.

text: NBTE can lead to {{c1::ischemic stroke}} when vegetations embolize to the cerebral circulation.
extraInfo: This often presents as a sudden-onset focal neurologic deficit in a cancer patient.

text: The term "marantic" refers to the association of NBTE with severe {{c1::wasting}} or malnutrition.
extraInfo: Derived from the Greek word 'marantikos' meaning wasting away.

text: Blood cultures in a patient with NBTE will be {{c1::negative}}.
extraInfo: This is because the vegetations are sterile and not caused by infection.

text: NBTE vegetations are described as {{c1::friable}}, meaning they are easily crumbled or broken.
extraInfo: This friability explains the high rate of embolic events.

text: {{c1::Libman-Sacks}} endocarditis is a specific form of NBTE associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
extraInfo: Vegetations in SLE can occur on both sides of the valve leaflets.

text: NBTE and {{c1::Trousseau}} syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis) both reflect an underlying hypercoagulable state of malignancy.
extraInfo: Both are seen in advanced adenocarcinomas.

text: Pathologically, NBTE vegetations are characterized by a lack of {{c1::inflammatory}} cells.
extraInfo: This distinguishes them from the inflammatory vegetations of rheumatic fever or infection.

text: The pathogenesis of NBTE involves {{c1::endothelial}} injury followed by platelet and fibrin deposition.
extraInfo: Cytokines from malignancy or chronic illness promote this process.

text: Cardiac {{c1::murmurs}} are often absent in NBTE because the vegetations are small and do not cause significant valve dysfunction.
extraInfo: This can make the clinical diagnosis challenging.

text: {{c1::Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)}} is more sensitive than transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for detecting NBTE.
extraInfo: Small vegetations are often missed on standard TTE.

text: NBTE does not result in {{c1::commissural fusion}}, helping to distinguish it from chronic rheumatic heart disease.
extraInfo: The underlying valve structure remains largely intact.

text: NBTE should be suspected in a patient with malignancy who presents with {{c1::new-onset focal neurologic deficits}}.
extraInfo: Always consider embolic stroke from NBTE in cancer patients.

text: NBTE vegetations typically occur on {{c1::previously normal}} heart valves.
extraInfo: Unlike subacute bacterial endocarditis, which usually requires pre-existing damage.

text: Vegetations in NBTE are generally {{c1::small}} in size, typically ranging from 1 to 5 mm.
extraInfo: Despite their small size, they carry a high risk of embolization.

text: Management of NBTE primarily focuses on {{c1::anticoagulation}} and treating the underlying disease.
extraInfo: Treating the primary cancer is essential.

text: {{c1::Heparin}} is the preferred anticoagulant for NBTE, especially in the context of malignancy.
extraInfo: Warfarin is often considered less effective in these hypercoagulable states.

text: NBTE is described as a {{c1::non-inflammatory}} condition because pathology shows thrombus without white blood cell infiltration.
extraInfo: This is a key histologic feature.

text: NBTE primarily involves the {{c1::left-sided}} valves of the heart.
extraInfo: Right-sided involvement is rare.

text: Emboli from NBTE can lead to {{c1::splenic}} or renal infarctions, presenting as acute abdominal or flank pain.
extraInfo: Systemic emboli can affect any organ system.

text: In NBTE, the vegetations are attached {{c1::loosely}} to the valve surface.
extraInfo: This loose attachment contributes to their high propensity for embolization.

text: Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is a consequence of pharyngeal infection with {{c1::group A ̢-hemolytic streptococci}}.
extraInfo: S. pyogenes.

text: ARF is caused by a {{c1::type II}} hypersensitivity reaction involving {{c2::molecular mimicry}}.
extraInfo: Antibodies against GAS antigens cross-react with host tissues.

text: Antibodies to the {{c1::M protein}} of GAS cross-react with self-antigens in the heart.
extraInfo: The M protein is a key virulence factor of GAS.

text: The most common valve affected in acute rheumatic heart disease is the {{c1::mitral}} valve.
extraInfo: Mitral > Aortic > Tricuspid.

text: In chronic rheumatic heart disease, the most common valve affected is the {{c1::mitral}} valve, followed by the {{c2::aortic}} valve.
extraInfo: Commonly leads to mitral stenosis.

text: The characteristic histological finding in the myocardium of ARF is the {{c1::Aschoff body}}.
extraInfo: Represents a granuloma-like structure.

text: {{c1::Anitschkow}} cells are enlarged macrophages with ovoid, wavy nuclei found within Aschoff bodies.
extraInfo: Seen in the heart during acute rheumatic fever.

text: Anitschkow cells are also known as "{{c1::caterpillar cells}}" due to the appearance of their nuclei.
extraInfo: The chromatin is condensed into a central wavy ribbon.

text: The Jones criteria for ARF require evidence of preceding {{c1::GAS}} infection plus 2 major or 1 major and 2 minor criteria.
extraInfo: Evidence of infection includes positive throat culture, rapid strep test, or elevated ASO titers.

text: In the JONES mnemonic, 'J' stands for {{c1::Joint (migratory polyarthritis)}}.
extraInfo: Large joints are usually affected, like the knees and elbows.

text: In the JONES mnemonic, 'O' (heart shape) stands for {{c1::Carditis}}.
extraInfo: Can involve endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium (pancarditis).

text: In the JONES mnemonic, 'N' stands for {{c1::Nodules (subcutaneous)}}.
extraInfo: Painless, firm, and small.

text: In the JONES mnemonic, 'E' stands for {{c1::Erythema marginatum}}.
extraInfo: A faint, reddish, ring-shaped rash.

text: In the JONES mnemonic, 'S' stands for {{c1::Sydenham chorea}}.
extraInfo: Caused by molecular mimicry affecting the basal ganglia.

text: Sydenham chorea is characterized by involuntary, purposeless movements of the {{c1::face}} and {{c2::arms}}.
extraInfo: Often presents months after the initial infection.

text: Erythema marginatum is a {{c1::nonpruritic}} rash with {{c2::red, wavy margins}}.
extraInfo: Typically found on the trunk and limbs, but not the face.

text: The most common cause of death during the acute phase of rheumatic fever is {{c1::myocarditis}}.
extraInfo: Heart failure and arrhythmias can occur.

text: Chronic rheumatic heart disease is characterized by {{c1::thickening}} of valve leaflets and {{c2::fusion}} of the commissures.
extraInfo: Leads to valvular dysfunction.

text: Classic "fish-mouth" appearance of the valve is seen in chronic {{c1::mitral stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Due to commissural fusion and chordae shortening.

text: Chronic rheumatic heart disease is the most common cause of {{c1::mitral stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Globally, this remains a significant cause of heart disease.

text: Rheumatic fever follows {{c1::pharyngeal}} infection, but NOT {{c2::skin}} infection (impetigo).
extraInfo: PSGN can follow either, but RF only follows pharyngitis.

text: A minor Jones criterion for ARF includes a prolonged {{c1::PR interval}} on ECG.
extraInfo: Reflects first-degree AV block.

text: Elevated titers of {{c1::ASO (antistreptolysin O)}} or {{c2::anti-DNase B}} indicate a recent GAS infection.
extraInfo: ASO is common for pharyngitis; anti-DNase B is also used.

text: Subcutaneous nodules in ARF are typically found over {{c1::bony prominences}} (e.g., extensor surfaces).
extraInfo: Usually associated with severe carditis.

text: In the acute phase, rheumatic fever typically causes valve {{c1::regurgitation}}.
extraInfo: Due to inflammation and dilation of the valve ring.

text: Early mitral valve involvement in ARF presents as mitral {{c1::regurgitation}}, while late involvement presents as mitral {{c2::stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Mitral stenosis develops years after the initial episode.

text: Secondary prevention of rheumatic fever involves long-term prophylaxis with {{c1::penicillin}}.
extraInfo: To prevent recurrent GAS infections and further heart damage.

text: Aschoff bodies consist of {{c1::foci of fibrinoid necrosis}} surrounded by lymphocytes and macrophages.
extraInfo: Found in any of the three layers of the heart (pancarditis).

text: Acute Rheumatic Fever occurs approximately {{c1::2-4 weeks}} after an untreated GAS pharyngitis.
extraInfo: The latent period is characteristic of the autoimmune process.

text: {{c1::Pleuritic}} chest pain in acute pericarditis is often relieved by {{c2::sitting up and leaning forward}}.
extraInfo: Pain is typically sharp and worse with inspiration or lying flat.

text: The most common cause of acute pericarditis is {{c1::idiopathic}} (often presumed {{c2::viral}}).
extraInfo: Coxsackievirus B is a frequently cited viral trigger.

text: A pathognomonic physical exam finding for acute pericarditis is a {{c1::pericardial friction rub}}.
extraInfo: Best heard with the diaphragm at the left lower sternal border.

text: ECG in acute pericarditis characteristically shows diffuse {{c1::ST-segment elevation}} and {{c2::PR-segment depression}}.
extraInfo: ST elevation is typically concave (saddle-shaped).

text: {{c1::Uremic}} pericarditis occurs in patients with renal failure and typically lacks classic ST-segment changes.
extraInfo: It is an indication for urgent dialysis.

text: {{c1::Dressler}} syndrome is an autoimmune-mediated pericarditis that occurs weeks to months after a myocardial infarction.
extraInfo: It involves the formation of antibodies against myocardial antigens.

text: Fibrinous pericarditis usually occurs {{c1::1–3}} days after a transmural MI.
extraInfo: This is a localized reaction to myocardial necrosis, unlike the delayed autoimmune Dressler syndrome.

text: The first-line treatment for idiopathic or viral acute pericarditis is {{c1::NSAIDs}} and {{c2::colchicine}}.
extraInfo: Colchicine is added to decrease the risk of recurrence.

text: In constrictive pericarditis, the {{c1::Kussmaul}} sign refers to a paradoxical increase in JVP during inspiration.
extraInfo: Normally, JVP should decrease during inspiration.

text: The {{c1::pericardial knock}} is a high-pitched sound heard in early diastole in patients with constrictive pericarditis.
extraInfo: It results from the sudden cessation of ventricular filling by the rigid pericardium.

text: A classic finding on imaging for constrictive pericarditis is {{c1::pericardial calcification}} on CT or X-ray.
extraInfo: This is highly suggestive of the diagnosis in the setting of heart failure symptoms.

text: Tuberculous pericarditis is a major cause of {{c1::constrictive}} pericarditis in developing countries.
extraInfo: TB is a common infectious cause of chronic pericardial thickening.

text: Unlike cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis is associated with a prominent {{c1::y}} descent on the JVP waveform.
extraInfo: In tamponade, the y-descent is often blunted or absent.

text: In constrictive pericarditis, the ventricular pressure tracing shows a characteristic {{c1::"dip and plateau"}} or "square root" sign.
extraInfo: This represents rapid early diastolic filling followed by an abrupt stop.

text: Post-{{c1::radiation}} therapy to the chest is a known risk factor for developing chronic constrictive pericarditis.
extraInfo: Common in patients treated for Hodgkin lymphoma or breast cancer.

text: Pericarditis associated with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is an example of {{c1::serous/fibrinous}} pericarditis.
extraInfo: Lupus is a classic autoimmune cause of pericardial inflammation.

text: The PR-segment depression in acute pericarditis is most visible in lead {{c1::II}} and PR-segment elevation is seen in lead {{c2::aVR}}.
extraInfo: This is a very specific early EKG finding for pericarditis.

text: In acute pericarditis, the ST-segment elevation is usually {{c1::concave}} upward (in contrast to the convex elevation in MI).
extraInfo: The 'saddle-shaped' ST elevation is a high-yield descriptor.

text: Dressler syndrome is specifically treated with {{c1::Aspirin}} or {{c2::NSAIDs}}.
extraInfo: Aspirin is often preferred post-MI over other NSAIDs to avoid interfering with myocardial healing.

text: Chronic constrictive pericarditis results in impaired {{c1::diastolic}} filling of the heart.
extraInfo: Systolic function is usually preserved until late stages.

text: In the JVP waveform of constrictive pericarditis, both {{c1::x}} and {{c2::y}} descents are sharp and prominent.
extraInfo: This leads to the 'W' shaped JVP pattern.

text: Pulsus paradoxus is common in tamponade but occurs in only about {{c1::one-third}} of patients with constrictive pericarditis.
extraInfo: It is less frequent in constrictive pericarditis than in cardiac tamponade.

text: A "bread and butter" appearance of the pericardium is seen in {{c1::fibrinous}} pericarditis.
extraInfo: Grossly, the pericardium appears shaggy and covered in fibrin.

text: The pericardial friction rub is best heard at the {{c1::left lower sternal border}} with the patient leaning forward.
extraInfo: It is often loudest during expiration.

text: {{c1::Colchicine}} is added to NSAIDs in acute pericarditis to reduce the rate of recurrence.
extraInfo: It inhibits tubulin polymerization and reduces inflammatory response.

text: In the US, common causes of constrictive pericarditis include idiopathic/viral, {{c1::prior cardiac surgery}}, and radiation.
extraInfo: Cardiac surgery is an increasingly common cause of pericardial scarring.

text: Constrictive pericarditis restricts filling of {{c1::all four}} heart chambers.
extraInfo: This results in equilibration of diastolic pressures in all four chambers.

text: Acute pericarditis can cause a {{c1::pericardial effusion}}, which may lead to cardiac tamponade if the fluid accumulates rapidly.
extraInfo: Clinical signs like muffled heart sounds and hypotension suggest tamponade.

text: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain that radiates to the {{c1::trapezius ridges}} is highly suggestive of acute pericarditis.
extraInfo: This radiation is due to irritation of the phrenic nerves which innervate the pericardium.

text: {{c1::Kussmaul sign}} is defined as a paradoxical {{c2::increase}} in JVP on inspiration.
extraInfo: Normally, inspiration leads to negative intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return and decreases JVP.

text: The mechanism of Kussmaul sign is that the {{c1::Right Ventricle}} cannot accommodate the increased {{c2::venous return}} during inspiration.
extraInfo: This causes blood to back up into the vena cava, increasing the jugular venous pressure.

text: In healthy individuals, inspiration causes {{c1::negative}} intrathoracic pressure which leads to a {{c2::decrease}} in JVP.
extraInfo: The Kussmaul sign is the pathological 'paradoxical' reversal of this normal finding.

text: Kussmaul sign is a characteristic finding in {{c1::constrictive pericarditis}}, which involves pericardial {{c2::fibrosis}} and calcification.
extraInfo: This limited space for expansion restricts ventricular filling during inspiration.

text: Causes of Kussmaul sign include constrictive pericarditis, {{c1::restrictive cardiomyopathy}}, and {{c2::right HF}}.
extraInfo: It can also be seen in massive pulmonary embolism and right atrial/ventricular tumors.

text: In resource-limited countries, the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis is {{c1::Tuberculosis (TB)}}.
extraInfo: In developed nations, it is more commonly idiopathic, viral, or post-surgical/radiotherapy.

text: A physical exam finding specific to constrictive pericarditis is a high-pitched sound in early diastole known as the {{c1::pericardial knock}}.
extraInfo: This occurs due to the sudden cessation of ventricular filling by the rigid pericardium.

text: Myocarditis is a major cause of {{c1::Sudden Cardiac Death (SCD)}} in adults aged {{c2::< 40}} years.
extraInfo: Presentation is highly variable and can include dyspnea, chest pain, or arrhythmias.

text: A characteristic clinical sign of myocarditis is persistent {{c1::tachycardia}} that is {{c2::out of proportion}} to fever.
extraInfo: This helps distinguish it from normal physiological responses to infection.

text: The histological hallmark of viral myocarditis is a {{c1::lymphocytic}} infiltrate with {{c2::focal necrosis}}.
extraInfo: Common viral causes include Coxsackie B, Adenovirus, and Parvovirus B19.

text: Parasitic myocarditis is commonly caused by {{c1::Trypanosoma cruzi}} (Chagas disease) or {{c2::Toxoplasma gondii}}.
extraInfo: Trypanosoma cruzi is a frequent cause of dilated cardiomyopathy in South America.

text: The bacterial cause of myocarditis associated with Lyme disease is {{c1::Borrelia burgdorferi}}.
extraInfo: This can present with various degrees of heart block.

text: Myocarditis caused by toxins can be due to {{c1::carbon monoxide}} or {{c2::black widow venom}}.
extraInfo: Other causes include drugs like doxorubicin and cocaine.

text: The most common cardiac tumor overall is a {{c1::metastasis}}, with {{c2::melanoma}} being a frequent primary source.
extraInfo: Primary cardiac tumors are much rarer than metastatic ones.

text: {{c1::Myxoma}} is the most common primary cardiac tumor in {{c2::adults}}.
extraInfo: 90% of these tumors occur in the atria, specifically the left atrium.

text: Atrial myxomas are often described as a {{c1::'ball valve'}} obstruction, which can lead to {{c2::syncopal episodes}}.
extraInfo: The syncope often depends on the patient's physical position.

text: Constitutional symptoms of myxoma (fever, weight loss) are mediated by the production of {{c1::IL-6}}.
extraInfo: IL-6 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine produced by the tumor cells.

text: Auscultation of an atrial myxoma may reveal an early diastolic {{c1::'tumor plop'}} sound.
extraInfo: This sound can mimic the murmur of mitral stenosis.

text: Histology of a myxoma shows gelatinous material and cells immersed in {{c1::glycosaminoglycans}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: Adults make 6 myx-ed drinks (IL-6, Myxoma).

text: {{c1::Rhabdomyoma}} is the most frequent primary cardiac tumor in {{c2::children}}.
extraInfo: These are hamartomatous growths often found in the ventricles.

text: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are strongly associated with the genetic condition {{c1::tuberous sclerosis}}.
extraInfo: These tumors often regress spontaneously as the child grows.

text: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} syndrome.
extraInfo: It is an autosomal dominant disorder of the blood vessels.

text: Findings in Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome include {{c1::recurrent epistaxis}} and {{c2::AVMs}} (e.g., in the brain, lung, or liver).
extraInfo: Telangiectasias are blanching lesions on the skin and mucous membranes.

text: Drug-induced myocarditis can be caused by the chemotherapy agent {{c1::doxorubicin}} or the drug of abuse {{c2::cocaine}}.
extraInfo: Doxorubicin is also notably associated with dilated cardiomyopathy.

text: Kussmaul sign can be seen with {{c1::right atrial}} or {{c2::ventricular tumors}} that impair right-sided heart filling.
extraInfo: This is another example of a space-occupying lesion preventing the accommodation of venous return.

text: ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the preferred treatment for hypertension in patients with {{c1::diabetes mellitus}}.
extraInfo: These drugs are protective against diabetic nephropathy.

text: In patients with heart failure, {{c1::beta-blockers}} must be used cautiously and are contraindicated in {{c2::cardiogenic shock}}.
extraInfo: They should only be used in compensated heart failure.

text: Autoimmune causes of myocarditis include {{c1::Kawasaki disease}}, {{c2::sarcoidosis}}, and SLE.
extraInfo: Giant cell myocarditis and polymyositis/dermatomyositis are also causes.

text: Complications of myocarditis include heart failure, {{c1::mural thrombus}} with systemic emboli, and {{c2::dilated cardiomyopathy}}.
extraInfo: Arrhythmias and heart block are also significant risks.

text: Myocarditis is defined as {{c1::inflammation}} of the myocardium.
extraInfo: It can lead to myocardial injury and ventricular dysfunction.

text: The most common viral cause of myocarditis in the US is {{c1::Coxsackievirus B}}.
extraInfo: Other viral causes include Adenovirus, HIV, and Parvovirus B19.

text: Myocarditis is a significant cause of {{c1::sudden cardiac death}} in young adults under 40 years of age.
extraInfo: It often presents with arrhythmias or acute heart failure.

text: Rare myocarditis and pericarditis are associated with {{c1::mRNA}} vaccines (e.g., SARS-CoV-2), particularly in {{c2::young males}}.
extraInfo: This is typically a transient, self-limiting reaction.

text: A common long-term complication of viral myocarditis is {{c1::dilated cardiomyopathy}}.
extraInfo: Inflammation leads to remodeling and enlargement of the heart chambers.

text: In South America, the parasite {{c1::Trypanosoma cruzi}} is a major cause of myocarditis (Chagas disease).
extraInfo: Chronic Chagas disease can lead to apical aneurysms and conduction blocks.

text: Bacterial myocarditis caused by {{c1::Corynebacterium diphtheriae}} is due to an exotoxin that inhibits {{c2::protein synthesis (EF-2)}}.
extraInfo: Diphtheria toxin causes systemic effects including myocarditis and polyneuropathy.

text: The diagnostic "gold standard" for myocarditis is {{c1::endomyocardial biopsy}}.
extraInfo: However, it is often diagnosed clinically or via cardiac MRI due to the risks of biopsy.

text: Histologically, viral myocarditis typically demonstrates a {{c1::lymphocytic}} infiltrate with focal myocyte necrosis.
extraInfo: The inflammation is often patchy, which can lead to false negatives on biopsy.

text: Hypersensitivity myocarditis, often caused by drugs like {{c1::Clozapine}}, is characterized by an infiltrate rich in {{c2::eosinophils}}.
extraInfo: Other causes include diuretics and sulfonamides.

text: {{c1::Giant cell}} myocarditis is a rare, aggressive form of myocarditis characterized by multinucleated cells and a poor prognosis.
extraInfo: It usually requires aggressive immunosuppression or heart transplant.

text: Patients with myocarditis often present with a {{c1::viral prodrome}} (e.g., fever, malaise, myalgias) followed by cardiac symptoms.
extraInfo: Cardiac symptoms include chest pain and dyspnea.

text: Myocarditis typically results in {{c1::systolic}} heart failure with a {{c2::reduced}} ejection fraction.
extraInfo: This is due to impaired contractility of the inflamed muscle.

text: In acute myocarditis, laboratory findings often show elevated {{c1::Troponin I or T}}.
extraInfo: This indicates active myocardial cell death/necrosis.

text: Myocarditis associated with Rheumatic Fever is characterized by the presence of {{c1::Aschoff bodies}}.
extraInfo: Aschoff bodies are granulomas found in the heart muscle.

text: Aschoff bodies in Rheumatic Fever contain {{c1::Anitschkow cells}}, which are specialized macrophages with "caterpillar" nuclei.
extraInfo: These are pathognomonic for Acute Rheumatic Fever.

text: {{c1::Lyme disease}} (Borrelia burgdorferi) can cause myocarditis, which most commonly presents as {{c2::AV block}}.
extraInfo: This is often referred to as 'Lyme carditis'.

text: An {{c1::S3}} gallop may be heard on physical exam in patients with myocarditis who develop heart failure.
extraInfo: The S3 reflects rapid ventricular filling into a dilated, compliant ventricle.

text: ECG findings in myocarditis are often non-specific but may include {{c1::ST-segment}} changes and T-wave inversions.
extraInfo: These changes can mimic an acute myocardial infarction.

text: {{c1::Cocaine}} use can cause myocarditis via excessive sympathetic stimulation and direct toxic effects.
extraInfo: It can also cause coronary vasospasm and infarction.

text: Myocarditis can present with chest pain that is {{c1::pleuritic}} in nature if there is concurrent pericarditis.
extraInfo: This is known as myopericarditis.

text: {{c1::Cardiac MRI}} is a useful non-invasive diagnostic tool that shows {{c2::late gadolinium enhancement}} in myocarditis.
extraInfo: This enhancement typically occurs in the mid-wall or subepicardium.

text: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a form of myocarditis/heart failure occurring in the {{c1::last month}} of pregnancy or within {{c2::5 months}} after delivery.
extraInfo: Risk factors include multiparity and hypertension.

text: Chagasic myocarditis is transmitted to humans by the {{c1::Reduviid}} bug (also known as the "kissing bug").
extraInfo: The parasite is deposited in feces and enters through the bite wound or mucous membranes.

text: Chronic myocarditis leads to global {{c1::cardiomegaly}} visible on a chest X-ray.
extraInfo: The heart assumes a "balloon-like" appearance.

text: Management of heart failure in myocarditis includes standard therapy such as {{c1::ACE inhibitors}} and beta-blockers.
extraInfo: Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.

text: Sudden death in acute myocarditis is usually caused by {{c1::ventricular arrhythmias}}.
extraInfo: Inflamed tissue creates an unstable substrate for electrical conduction.

text: HIV patients can develop myocarditis due to the virus itself or due to {{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} in immunocompromised states.
extraInfo: Toxoplasma is a protozoan parasite.

text: The primary mechanism of myocyte injury in viral myocarditis is a {{c1::T-cell}} mediated immune response.
extraInfo: The immune system attacks virus-infected myocytes, leading to damage.

text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is also known as {{c1::Osler-Weber-Rendu}} syndrome.
extraInfo: It is an autosomal dominant disorder of blood vessels.

text: The inheritance pattern of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
extraInfo: This means a child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the condition.

text: HHT is characterized by multiple {{c1::telangiectasias}} found on the skin and mucous membranes.
extraInfo: These are small, dilated blood vessels that often blanch with pressure.

text: A common and often initial presenting symptom of HHT is recurrent {{c1::epistaxis}}.
extraInfo: Nosebleeds occur due to telangiectasias in the nasal mucosa.

text: The major underlying vascular abnormality in HHT involves the formation of {{c1::arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)}}.
extraInfo: AVMs lack a intervening capillary bed, connecting arteries directly to veins.

text: Arteriovenous malformations in the {{c1::lungs}} can result in a right-to-left shunt.
extraInfo: This bypasses the pulmonary filter, leading to various systemic complications.

text: The right-to-left shunt caused by pulmonary AVMs in HHT may lead to chronic {{c1::hypoxemia}}.
extraInfo: This can manifest as shortness of breath or exercise intolerance.

text: Pulmonary AVMs in HHT increase the risk of {{c1::paradoxical}} emboli reaching the systemic circulation.
extraInfo: Bacteria or clots can bypass the pulmonary capillary filter.

text: A classic high-yield complication of pulmonary AVMs in HHT is the development of {{c1::brain}} abscesses.
extraInfo: Bacteria in the blood bypass the lungs and travel directly to the CNS.

text: Chronic GI bleeding from telangiectasias in HHT frequently leads to {{c1::iron deficiency}} anemia.
extraInfo: Bleeding is often occult and increases with age.

text: AVMs located in the {{c1::liver}} can lead to high-output heart failure.
extraInfo: Large shunts increase the venous return and workload of the heart.

text: Common sites for visible telangiectasias in HHT include the lips, tongue, and {{c1::fingertips}}.
extraInfo: Careful physical exam of these areas is diagnostic.

text: In HHT, AVMs bypass the {{c1::capillary}} beds, resulting in low resistance flow.
extraInfo: This is the physiological basis for the complications like shunting and bruits.

text: Most mutations causing HHT involve genes in the {{c1::TGF-β}} signaling pathway.
extraInfo: This pathway is critical for angiogenesis and vessel wall integrity.

text: The gene {{c1::ENG}} (encoding endoglin) is frequently mutated in HHT type 1.
extraInfo: Type 1 is more strongly associated with pulmonary AVMs.

text: The gene {{c1::ACVRL1}} (encoding ALK1) is frequently mutated in HHT type 2.
extraInfo: Type 2 is more strongly associated with hepatic involvement.

text: Patients with pulmonary AVMs require {{c1::antibiotic prophylaxis}} before dental procedures.
extraInfo: This is done to prevent the hematogenous spread of bacteria to the brain (abscess).

text: Arteriovenous malformations in the {{c1::CNS}} can cause hemorrhagic stroke or seizures.
extraInfo: Screening for brain AVMs is often recommended in diagnosed patients.

text: Telangiectasias in HHT are typically {{c1::blanching}} upon pressure.
extraInfo: This distinguishes them from petechiae or purpura.

text: Recurrent nosebleeds in HHT arise from the {{c1::nasal mucosa}}.
extraInfo: The telangiectasias here are fragile and prone to rupture.

text: Bleeding in the {{c1::GI tract}} in HHT is often occult and increases in severity with age.
extraInfo: Gastroscopy or colonoscopy may show multiple angiodysplasia-like lesions.

text: Mutations in the {{c1::SMAD4}} gene cause a syndrome of HHT combined with juvenile polyposis.
extraInfo: These patients are at risk for both vascular issues and GI malignancy.

text: Chronic hypoxemia from large pulmonary AVMs can cause digital {{c1::clubbing}}.
extraInfo: This is a sign of long-standing low oxygen saturation.

text: Examination of the lungs in a patient with a large pulmonary AVM may reveal a {{c1::bruit}}.
extraInfo: The sound is caused by turbulent flow through the malformation.

text: Severe hepatic AVM involvement in HHT can lead to {{c1::portal hypertension}}.
extraInfo: This occurs due to increased blood flow into the portal venous system.

text: HHT is pathologically classified as a {{c1::vascular dysplasia}}.
extraInfo: It involves the abnormal development of blood vessel walls.

text: Initial screening for pulmonary AVMs in HHT is usually done via {{c1::bubble echocardiography}}.
extraInfo: Delayed appearance of bubbles in the left atrium indicates an intrapulmonary shunt.

text: In HHT, the lack of capillaries between arteries and veins leads to {{c1::low}} resistance in the circulatory circuit.
extraInfo: This low resistance is what drives high-output heart failure.

text: Clinical diagnosis of HHT uses the {{c1::Curaçao}} criteria.
extraInfo: Criteria include: epistaxis, telangiectasias, visceral lesions, and a first-degree relative with HHT.

text: The most common primary cardiac tumor in adults is the {{c1::myxoma}}.
extraInfo: In contrast, metastatic tumors are overall more common than primary cardiac tumors.

text: Approximately 90% of cardiac myxomas occur in the {{c1::left atrium}}.
extraInfo: They are usually attached to the interatrial septum.

text: Cardiac myxomas are typically described as a {{c1::ball-valve}} obstruction of the mitral valve.
extraInfo: This can cause syncopal episodes that are often posture-dependent.

text: The characteristic early diastolic sound associated with cardiac myxoma is the {{c1::tumor plop}}.
extraInfo: This occurs as the tumor drops into the mitral orifice.

text: Cardiac myxomas can mimic the clinical presentation of {{c1::mitral stenosis}}.
extraInfo: Symptoms include dyspnea and a diastolic murmur.

text: Histology of a myxoma shows {{c1::stellate (spindle)}} cells within a myxoid stroma.
extraInfo: The stroma is rich in glycosaminoglycans.

text: Cardiac myxomas often produce the cytokine {{c1::IL-6}}, leading to constitutional symptoms.
extraInfo: Symptoms include fever, weight loss, and elevated ESR.

text: A major systemic complication of left atrial myxoma is {{c1::embolization}}.
extraInfo: Fragmented tumor or associated thrombus can travel to the brain (stroke) or extremities.

text: The most common primary cardiac tumor in children/infants is {{c1::rhabdomyoma}}.
extraInfo: These are often discovered in the first year of life.

text: Cardiac rhabdomyoma is highly associated with the genetic condition {{c1::tuberous sclerosis}}.
extraInfo: Up to 50-80% of patients with cardiac rhabdomyomas have tuberous sclerosis.

text: Unlike myxomas, rhabdomyomas are typically located in the {{c1::ventricles}}.
extraInfo: They can be single but are frequently multifocal.

text: Histologically, rhabdomyomas are characterized by {{c1::spider cells}}.
extraInfo: These are clear cells with radial cytoplasmic extensions reaching the cell membrane.

text: The natural history of most cardiac rhabdomyomas is that they {{c1::spontaneously regress}}.
extraInfo: Surgical excision is usually only required if there is significant obstruction or arrhythmia.

text: Metastatic tumors involve the {{c1::pericardium}} more commonly than the myocardium.
extraInfo: This often results in a pericardial effusion or tamponade.

text: The four most common cancers that metastasize to the heart are lung, breast, lymphoma, and {{c1::melanoma}}.
extraInfo: Melanoma has a particularly high predilection for cardiac metastasis.

text: Grossly, a cardiac myxoma has a {{c1::gelatinous}} or friable appearance.
extraInfo: Their friability contributes to the high risk of embolization.

text: Myxomas are usually attached to the interatrial septum at the {{c1::fossa ovalis}}.
extraInfo: This is a high-yield anatomical landmark for USMLE.

text: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are pathologically classified as {{c1::hamartomas}}.
extraInfo: They represent an overgrowth of mature cardiac myocytes.

text: Tuberous sclerosis, associated with rhabdomyomas, is caused by mutations in {{c1::TSC1 or TSC2}}.
extraInfo: TSC1 codes for hamartin; TSC2 codes for tuberin.

text: Syndromic myxomas associated with spotty skin pigmentation and endocrine overactivity are part of {{c1::Carney complex}}.
extraInfo: Carney complex is an autosomal dominant condition (PRKAR1A mutation).

text: Primary cardiac tumors are {{c1::benign}} in approximately 90% of cases.
extraInfo: The most common malignant primary tumor is angiosarcoma.

text: Secondary (metastatic) tumors are {{c1::more}} common than primary cardiac tumors.
extraInfo: Always consider metastasis first when a patient with known cancer presents with new heart failure or effusion.

text: Laboratory evaluation in a patient with myxoma often shows an elevated {{c1::ESR (or CRP)}}.
extraInfo: This is due to the systemic inflammatory response triggered by tumor-secreted IL-6.

text: Symptoms of cardiac myxoma often change with the patient's {{c1::posture}}.
extraInfo: Changing positions can move the tumor in or out of the valve orifice.

text: Rhabdomyomas can cause life-threatening {{c1::arrhythmias}} in neonates.
extraInfo: The tumor mass interferes with normal electrical conduction.

text: On an echocardiogram, a myxoma appears as a {{c1::pedunculated}} mass in the atrium.
extraInfo: The stalk is typically attached to the septum.

text: The most common primary malignant tumor of the heart is {{c1::angiosarcoma}}.
extraInfo: It typically occurs in the right atrium.

text: Myxoma histology often shows a {{c1::myxoid}} background with abundant glycosaminoglycans.
extraInfo: This gives it the characteristic 'jelly-like' appearance on gross inspection.

text: Patients with cardiac myxoma may present with an elevated {{c1::platelet count (thrombocytosis)}}.
extraInfo: This is another manifestation of the IL-6 mediated inflammatory response.

text: {{c1::ACE inhibitors or ARBs}} are the first-line antihypertensives in patients with diabetes mellitus to protect against diabetic nephropathy.
extraInfo: They reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole.

text: In patients with heart failure (HFrEF), the three drug classes that specifically reduce mortality are ACEIs/ARBs, {{c1::beta-blockers}}, and aldosterone antagonists.
extraInfo: Beta-blockers must be started only when the patient is compensated.

text: {{c1::Thiazide diuretics}} are the preferred treatment for hypertension in patients with concurrent osteoporosis.
extraInfo: Thiazides increase renal calcium reabsorption, which can help bone mineral density.

text: In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and proteinuria, {{c1::ACE inhibitors or ARBs}} are first-line to slow the progression of renal failure.
extraInfo: They are contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis.

text: The four main antihypertensives used safely in pregnancy are {{c1::Hydralazine}}, Methyldopa, Labetalol, and Nifedipine.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: He-Man Loves Ne-pa.

text: Beta-blockers are the first-line antihypertensive therapy for patients with a history of {{c1::myocardial infarction (MI)}}.
extraInfo: They reduce myocardial oxygen demand and prevent arrhythmias.

text: In patients with hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), {{c1::alpha-1 blockers}} (e.g., terazosin) can treat both conditions.
extraInfo: They are generally not used as first-line for hypertension alone due to side effects like orthostatic hypotension.

text: {{c1::Non-selective beta-blockers}} (e.g., propranolol) should be avoided in patients with asthma or COPD to prevent bronchospasm.
extraInfo: Cardioselective (beta-1) blockers are preferred if a beta-blocker is necessary.

text: For a patient with hypertension and migraine, {{c1::beta-blockers}} or calcium channel blockers are often used for prophylaxis.
extraInfo: Propranolol is a common choice.

text: {{c1::Thiazide diuretics}} should be avoided if possible in patients with gout because they can trigger flares by increasing uric acid reabsorption.
extraInfo: Losartan is a good alternative as it has uricosuric properties.

text: {{c1::Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers}} (e.g., amlodipine) are the first-line treatment for Raynaud phenomenon.
extraInfo: They promote vasodilation in the peripheral vasculature.

text: In patients with hypertension and hyperthyroidism, {{c1::propranolol}} is used to manage symptoms and block peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
extraInfo: It helps control tachycardia and tremors.

text: In the management of pheochromocytoma, {{c1::alpha-blockers}} (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) must be given before beta-blockers.
extraInfo: Giving beta-blockers first can cause a hypertensive crisis due to unopposed alpha-1 stimulation.

text: Patients with hypertension and essential tremor are best treated with {{c1::propranolol}}.
extraInfo: It is a non-selective beta-blocker that effectively reduces tremor amplitude.

text: In the setting of cocaine use and hypertension, {{c1::beta-blockers}} are contraindicated.
extraInfo: They lead to unopposed alpha-1 adrenergic stimulation, causing severe vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis.

text: In patients with aortic dissection, {{c1::beta-blockers}} are the first-line agents to reduce heart rate and blood pressure (dP/dt).
extraInfo: They reduce the shearing force on the aortic wall.

text: For African American patients without DM or CKD, initial monotherapy for hypertension should be a {{c1::thiazide diuretic or a CCB}}.
extraInfo: These populations tend to be more responsive to these classes than to ACE inhibitors.

text: {{c1::Spironolactone}} is the drug of choice for hypertension caused by primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome).
extraInfo: It is a competitive aldosterone receptor antagonist.

text: If a patient develops a dry cough from an ACE inhibitor, they should be switched to {{c1::an ARB (Angiotensin II Receptor Blocker)}}.
extraInfo: The cough is caused by the accumulation of bradykinin.

text: In patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) or angina, {{c1::beta-blockers}} and CCBs are the preferred antihypertensives.
extraInfo: They reduce myocardial oxygen consumption.

text: In patients with HFrEF, {{c1::spironolactone or eplerenone}} is added to reduce mortality and prevent cardiac remodeling.
extraInfo: Eplerenone is more selective and has fewer endocrine side effects (like gynecomastia).

text: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because they are {{c1::teratogenic}}.
extraInfo: They can cause fetal renal dysgenesis and oligohydramnios.

text: For hypertension management in a patient with SVT (supraventricular tachycardia), {{c1::non-dihydropyridine CCBs}} (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem) or beta-blockers are preferred.
extraInfo: They act on the AV node to slow the heart rate.

text: {{c1::Losartan}} is unique among ARBs because it has uricosuric properties, making it beneficial for patients with hypertension and gout.
extraInfo: It aids in the excretion of uric acid.

text: The use of ACE inhibitors can cause a rise in serum {{c1::creatinine}} by up to 30%, which is considered acceptable.
extraInfo: Anything beyond 30% suggests renal artery stenosis.

text: {{c1::Methyldopa}} is a central alpha-2 agonist frequently used for hypertension in pregnancy.
extraInfo: It is known for its long-standing safety profile in pregnancy.

text: In patients with hypertension and heart failure, ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce mortality by decreasing {{c1::afterload}}.
extraInfo: This improves the ejection fraction and cardiac output.
