text: Non-selective beta-blockers can mask the symptoms of {{c1::hypoglycemia}} in diabetic patients.
extraInfo: Sweating (mediated by sympathetic cholinergic fibers) is the only symptom not masked.

text: {{c1::Hydralazine}} can cause a lupus-like syndrome as a side effect.
extraInfo: It is a direct vasodilator used in pregnancy-induced hypertension.

text: {{c1::Milrinone}} is a {{c2::PDE-3}} inhibitor that increases {{c3::cAMP}} in cardiomyocytes, leading to increased contractility and vasodilation.
extraInfo: Used for short-term management of acute heart failure.

text: {{c1::Nesiritide}} is a recombinant {{c2::B-type natriuretic peptide}} that increases {{c3::cGMP}}, causing vasodilation and natriuresis.
extraInfo: Used in acute decompensated heart failure.

text: {{c1::Digoxin}} inhibits the {{c2::Na+/K+ ATPase}}, which leads to an increase in intracellular {{c3::Ca2+}} via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.
extraInfo: Results in positive inotropy and increased vagal tone (parasympathomimetic).

text: {{c1::Nitroglycerin}} acts by releasing {{c2::nitric oxide}}, which stimulates {{c3::guanylyl cyclase}} to increase cGMP.
extraInfo: Primarily affects veins (decreases preload).

text: {{c1::Hydralazine}} is a vasodilator that increases {{c2::cGMP}}, leading to smooth muscle relaxation, primarily in {{c3::arterioles}}.
extraInfo: Often co-administered with a beta-blocker to prevent reflex tachycardia.

text: {{c1::Minoxidil}} works by {{c2::opening K+ channels}}, which causes {{c3::hyperpolarization}} of vascular smooth muscle cells.
extraInfo: Potent arteriolar vasodilator used for refractory hypertension.

text: {{c1::Sacubitril}} is a {{c2::neprilysin}} inhibitor that increases levels of {{c3::natriuretic peptides}}, bradykinin, and substance P.
extraInfo: Combined with valsartan (ARNI) for HFrEF.

text: {{c1::Statins}} competitively inhibit {{c2::HMG-CoA reductase}}, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis.
extraInfo: Leads to compensatory upregulation of LDL receptors.

text: {{c1::Ezetimibe}} inhibits the {{c2::NPC1L1}} transporter, preventing cholesterol absorption at the {{c3::small intestine brush border}}.
extraInfo: Used to lower LDL; can cause increased LFTs when used with statins.

text: {{c1::Fibrates}} (e.g., Gemfibrozil) activate {{c2::PPAR-α}}, which increases the expression of {{c3::lipoprotein lipase (LPL)}}.
extraInfo: Primarily used to lower triglycerides.

text: {{c1::Alirocumab}} and Evolocumab are {{c2::PCSK9}} inhibitors that prevent the degradation of {{c3::LDL receptors}}.
extraInfo: Extremely effective at lowering LDL levels.

text: {{c1::ACE inhibitors}} decrease levels of {{c2::Angiotensin II}} and increase levels of {{c3::bradykinin}}.
extraInfo: Bradykinin increase causes the characteristic dry cough side effect.

text: {{c1::Losartan}} is an ARB that selectively blocks the {{c2::AT1}} receptor.
extraInfo: Unlike ACE inhibitors, ARBs do not increase bradykinin levels.

text: {{c1::Dobutamine}} is a {{c2::β1}} agonist that acts via the {{c3::Gs}} protein-coupled receptor pathway.
extraInfo: Increases cardiac output in heart failure and cardiogenic shock.

text: {{c1::Clonidine}} and α-methyldopa are {{c2::β2}} agonists that act via the {{c3::Gi}} protein-coupled receptor pathway.
extraInfo: Decreases sympathetic outflow from the CNS.

text: {{c1::Phenylephrine}} is an α1 agonist that activates the {{c2::Gq}} pathway, leading to increased {{c3::IP3 and DAG}}.
extraInfo: Causes vasoconstriction and a reflex decrease in heart rate.

text: {{c1::Verapamil}} is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that acts on {{c2::L-type}} calcium channels in both the heart and vessels.
extraInfo: Has significant negative inotropic and chronotropic effects.

text: {{c1::Amlodipine}} acts primarily on {{c2::vascular smooth muscle}} calcium channels, with minimal effect on the heart.
extraInfo: A dihydropyridine CCB used for hypertension and angina.

text: {{c1::Fenoldopam}} is a {{c2::D1}} receptor agonist used in hypertensive emergencies to cause coronary, peripheral, and renal vasodilation.
extraInfo: Maintains renal perfusion while lowering blood pressure.

text: {{c1::Aliskiren}} is a {{c2::direct renin inhibitor}} that prevents the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
extraInfo: Contraindicated in patients taking ACEIs or ARBs who have diabetes.

text: {{c1::Spironolactone}} is a competitive {{c2::aldosterone}} receptor antagonist in the cortical collecting tubule.
extraInfo: Potassium-sparing diuretic that improves survival in heart failure.

text: {{c1::Cholestyramine}} is a {{c2::bile acid sequestrant}} that prevents the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids.
extraInfo: May lead to slightly increased triglyceride levels.

text: {{c1::Niacin (Vitamin B3)}} inhibits {{c2::hormone-sensitive lipase}} in adipose tissue, reducing VLDL synthesis in the liver.
extraInfo: Most effective agent for increasing HDL.

text: {{c1::Sildenafil}} inhibits {{c2::PDE-5}}, which prevents the breakdown of {{c3::cGMP}}, leading to prolonged smooth muscle relaxation.
extraInfo: Used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension.

text: {{c1::Adenosine}} increases {{c2::K+}} efflux and hyperpolarizes the cell while also decreasing {{c3::Ca2+}} influx.
extraInfo: Drug of choice for terminating supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).

text: {{c1::Bosentan}} is a competitive antagonist of {{c2::endothelin-1}} receptors, used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension.
extraInfo: Must monitor LFTs due to hepatotoxicity.

text: {{c1::Ranolazine}} inhibits the {{c2::late sodium current}}, which reduces diastolic wall tension and oxygen consumption.
extraInfo: Used for refractory angina; may cause QT prolongation.

text: {{c1::Ivabradine}} selectively inhibits {{c2::funny sodium channels (If)}} in the SA node, slowing the heart rate.
extraInfo: Used in HFrEF patients with a heart rate > 70 bpm who cannot tolerate beta-blockers.

text: {{c1::Epoprostenol}} is a {{c2::PGI2 (prostacyclin)}} analog that increases {{c3::cAMP}} to cause vasodilation in the pulmonary bed.
extraInfo: Used for pulmonary arterial pulmonary hypertension.

text: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers can be identified by the suffix {{c1::-dipine}}.
extraInfo: Examples include amlodipine, nifedipine, and nimodipine.

text: The two primary non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are {{c1::verapamil}} and diltiazem.
extraInfo: These act primarily on the heart.

text: Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) work by blocking voltage-gated {{c1::L-type}} calcium channels.
extraInfo: This leads to decreased muscle contractility.

text: Dihydropyridines act predominantly on {{c1::vascular smooth muscle}}.
extraInfo: They cause peripheral vasodilation.

text: Non-dihydropyridines act predominantly on the {{c1::heart (myocardium and nodes)}}.
extraInfo: They have negative inotropic and chronotropic effects.

text: Among the non-dihydropyridines, {{c1::verapamil}} is the most selective for the heart (myocardium).
extraInfo: Mnemonic: Verapamil = Ventricle.

text: {{c1::Diltiazem}} has intermediate effects on both the heart and vascular smooth muscle.
extraInfo: It acts on both the heart and the vessels.

text: {{c1::Nimodipine}} is used to prevent cerebral vasospasm following subarachnoid hemorrhage.
extraInfo: It is highly lipid soluble.

text: {{c1::Clevidipine}} is a dihydropyridine used for hypertensive urgency or emergency via IV administration.
extraInfo: It has a very short half-life.

text: A common side effect of dihydropyridines due to peripheral vasodilation is {{c1::peripheral edema}}.
extraInfo: This is due to increased capillary hydrostatic pressure.

text: Dihydropyridines (especially short-acting ones) can cause {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} in response to decreased blood pressure.
extraInfo: This is why they are often used with beta-blockers.

text: Both nifedipine and verapamil are known to cause {{c1::gingival hyperplasia}} as a side effect.
extraInfo: Common board-tested side effect.

text: {{c1::Verapamil}} is well-known for causing constipation and hyperprolactinemia.
extraInfo: It blocks calcium channels in the GI tract and pituitary.

text: Non-dihydropyridines are contraindicated in patients with severe {{c1::heart failure (HFrEF)}} due to negative inotropic effects.
extraInfo: They can worsen systolic dysfunction.

text: Combining non-dihydropyridines with {{c1::beta-blockers}} can lead to severe bradycardia or AV block.
extraInfo: Both classes suppress the SA and AV nodes.

text: {{c1::Nifedipine}} (dihydropyridine) is often used for the treatment of Raynaud phenomenon.
extraInfo: It causes peripheral vasodilation to improve blood flow.

text: Non-dihydropyridines are categorized as Class {{c1::IV}} antiarrhythmics.
extraInfo: Used for rate control in AFib.

text: In smooth muscle, CCBs decrease the activation of {{c1::myosin light chain kinase (MLCK)}}.
extraInfo: This prevents actin-myosin cross-bridge formation.

text: Dihydropyridines decrease blood pressure by decreasing {{c1::systemic vascular resistance (SVR)}}.
extraInfo: Via arterial vasodilation.

text: Non-dihydropyridines are used for rate control in atrial fibrillation by slowing conduction through the {{c1::AV node}}.
extraInfo: They prolong the refractory period of the node.

text: {{c1::Prinzmetal (variant) angina}} is a classic indication for treatment with calcium channel blockers.
extraInfo: They prevent coronary artery vasospasms.

text: {{c1::Amlodipine}} is a long-acting dihydropyridine commonly used for chronic hypertension management.
extraInfo: It has a long half-life and fewer side effects than nifedipine.

text: In terms of cardiac depression potency, Verapamil is {{c1::greater than (>)}} Diltiazem.
extraInfo: Verapamil is the most potent negative inotrope.

text: Non-dihydropyridines increase the {{c1::PR interval}} on an EKG.
extraInfo: Reflects delayed AV nodal conduction.

text: Common side effects of rapid-onset DHPs include flushing and {{c1::headache}}.
extraInfo: Result from rapid vasodilation.

text: CCBs prevent the contraction of smooth muscle by decreasing intracellular {{c1::calcium}}.
extraInfo: They block the initial influx required for muscle contraction.

text: {{c1::Nifedipine}} is a dihydropyridine that can be used for hypertension in pregnancy.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: He Likes My Neonate (Hydralazine, Labetalol, Methyldopa, Nifedipine).

text: Verapamil may cause {{c1::hyperprolactinemia}} because it blocks calcium channels in pituitary lactotrophs.
extraInfo: This disrupts dopamine-mediated inhibition.

text: Unlike non-dihydropyridines, dihydropyridines have minimal effect on the {{c1::SA or AV nodes}}.
extraInfo: They are vascular-selective.

text: Hydralazine increases {{c1::cGMP}} which leads to smooth muscle relaxation.
extraInfo: Increased cGMP leads to dephosphorylation of myosin light chains.

text: Hydralazine primarily vasodilates {{c1::arterioles}} more than veins.
extraInfo: This results in a significant reduction in afterload.

text: Hydralazine is used for the treatment of severe {{c1::hypertension}} (acute) and heart failure.
extraInfo: In heart failure, it is typically used in combination with an organic nitrate.

text: Hydralazine is a first-line antihypertensive drug safe for use in {{c1::pregnancy}}.
extraInfo: Commonly used in hypertensive emergencies of pregnancy along with labetalol and nifedipine.

text: A classic multiorgan adverse effect of Hydralazine is {{c1::drug-induced lupus}}.
extraInfo: Hydralazine, procainamide, and isoniazid are the most common causes of this syndrome.

text: The antibody characteristic of Hydralazine-induced lupus is anti-{{c1::histone}} antibody.
extraInfo: Anti-dsDNA is usually absent, which helps distinguish it from SLE.

text: Hydralazine is metabolized in the liver via {{c1::acetylation}}.
extraInfo: Individuals who are 'slow acetylators' are at a higher risk for drug-induced lupus.

text: Due to the drop in blood pressure, Hydralazine causes compensatory {{c1::reflex tachycardia}}.
extraInfo: This can precipitate angina or MI in patients with CAD.

text: To prevent reflex tachycardia, Hydralazine is frequently co-administered with a {{c1::beta-blocker}}.
extraInfo: Beta-blockers blunt the sympathetic reflex triggered by peripheral vasodilation.

text: Hydralazine can cause significant {{c1::fluid}} retention and peripheral edema.
extraInfo: This is often managed by co-administering a diuretic.

text: Hydralazine is contraindicated in patients with {{c1::coronary artery disease (CAD)}}.
extraInfo: The compensatory reflex tachycardia increases myocardial oxygen demand.

text: The common neurologic side effect caused by Hydralazine-induced vasodilation is {{c1::headache}}.
extraInfo: Occurs because of the dilation of cerebral vessels.

text: Hydralazine combined with {{c1::isosorbide dinitrate}} has shown a mortality benefit in African American patients with heart failure.
extraInfo: This combination reduces both afterload and preload.

text: Hydralazine-induced lupus typically involves joints and skin but rarely involves the {{c1::kidneys}}.
extraInfo: Renal and CNS involvement are rare in DIL compared to idiopathic SLE.

text: Hydralazine reduces {{c1::Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR)}} via arteriolar dilation.
extraInfo: The effect on venous capacitance is minimal.

text: Hydralazine belongs to the '{{c1::He's LAP}}' mnemonic for pregnancy-safe antihypertensives.
extraInfo: Hydralazine, Methyldopa, Labetalol, Nifedipine.

text: In the liver, Hydralazine is processed by the enzyme {{c1::N-acetyltransferase}}.
extraInfo: Genetic polymorphisms in this enzyme determine the rate of drug metabolism.

text: Hydralazine-induced lupus is considered a Type {{c1::III}} hypersensitivity-like reaction.
extraInfo: Characterized by the formation of immune complexes.

text: Drug-induced lupus from Hydralazine is usually {{c1::reversible}} upon drug cessation.
extraInfo: Symptoms and antibodies typically resolve after the drug is stopped.

text: Hydralazine's MOA involves stimulating {{c1::guanylate cyclase}}, leading to cGMP production.
extraInfo: This inhibits calcium entry into smooth muscle cells.

text: A common musculoskeletal symptom of Hydralazine-induced lupus is {{c1::arthralgia}} (joint pain).
extraInfo: Myalgia and fever are also common presenting signs.

text: Because it decreases afterload, Hydralazine helps increase {{c1::stroke volume}} in heart failure patients.
extraInfo: Lower resistance allows the heart to pump more effectively.

text: Hydralazine can cause a 'lupus-like syndrome' which is associated with HLA-{{c1::DR4}}.
extraInfo: Genetic predisposition can play a role in the development of DIL.

text: Hydralazine use can lead to {{c1::angina}} pectoris due to increased myocardial oxygen demand.
extraInfo: This is why it is often avoided in patients with ischemic heart disease.

text: The reflex tachycardia caused by Hydralazine is mediated by the {{c1::baroreceptor}} reflex.
extraInfo: The sudden drop in BP triggers the sympathetic nervous system.

text: Hydralazine therapy may stimulate {{c1::renin}} release due to decreased renal perfusion pressure.
extraInfo: This contributes to the sodium and water retention seen with the drug.

text: Hydralazine is often preferred over other vasodilators for {{c1::postpartum}} hypertension management.
extraInfo: It has a long-standing safety profile in the obstetric population.

text: While Hydralazine affects cGMP, {{c1::Minoxidil}} affects K+ channels to cause vasodilation.
extraInfo: Both are direct-acting vasodilators but have different molecular targets.

text: Along with Hydralazine and Procainamide, the drug {{c1::Quinidine}} is listed as a cause of Drug-induced lupus.
extraInfo: Referenced in First Aid pharmacology toxicity sections.

text: Hypertensive emergency is defined as severe hypertension (typically >180/120 mmHg) with evidence of acute {{c1::end-organ damage}}.
extraInfo: Examples include encephalopathy, stroke, retinal hemorrhages, acute kidney injury, or MI.

text: The initial goal in hypertensive emergency is to reduce the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) by no more than {{c1::25%}} within the first hour.
extraInfo: Rapid over-correction can lead to cerebral or myocardial ischemia due to altered autoregulation.

text: {{c1::Clevidipine}} is an ultra-short-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker administered IV for hypertensive emergencies.
extraInfo: It has a rapid onset (2-4 minutes) and is metabolized by blood and tissue esterases.

text: {{c1::Fenoldopam}} is a dopamine D1 receptor agonist used in hypertensive emergencies to cause peripheral vasodilation and promote natriuresis.
extraInfo: It is unique because it maintains or increases renal perfusion while lowering blood pressure.

text: A notable side effect of fenoldopam is an increase in {{c1::intraocular pressure}}, so it should be used with caution in patients with glaucoma.
extraInfo: It can also cause reflex tachycardia and headache.

text: {{c1::Nitroprusside}} acts by directly releasing nitric oxide (NO), which increases {{c2::cGMP}} to cause vasodilation.
extraInfo: It dilates both arterioles and venules (decreases preload and afterload).

text: Prolonged infusion of nitroprusside can lead to {{c1::cyanide}} toxicity.
extraInfo: Symptoms include altered mental status, seizures, and lactic acidosis.

text: Nitroprusside must be protected from {{c1::light}} because it is photosensitive and can degrade.
extraInfo: Degradation is often signaled by a change in the color of the solution.

text: {{c1::Labetalol}} is a combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta blocker used in hypertensive emergencies, especially during {{c2::aortic dissection}}.
extraInfo: It reduces both blood pressure and heart rate (decreasing shearing forces).

text: In patients with hypertensive emergency and acute heart failure, {{c1::Nitroglycerin}} is often preferred due to its potent venodilatory effects.
extraInfo: It reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand.

text: {{c1::Nicardipine}} is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker commonly used for BP control in patients with acute {{c2::ischemic stroke}}.
extraInfo: It has a favorable profile for maintaining cerebral blood flow.

text: {{c1::Hydralazine}} is the antihypertensive of choice for hypertensive emergencies in {{c2::pregnancy}} (e.g., preeclampsia/eclampsia).
extraInfo: It works by increasing cGMP to cause smooth muscle relaxation.

text: A rare side effect associated with long-term hydralazine use is {{c1::drug-induced lupus}}.
extraInfo: This is often associated with slow acetylators and anti-histone antibodies.

text: {{c1::Esmolol}} is an ultra-short-acting beta-1 selective blocker with a half-life of approximately {{c2::9 minutes}}.
extraInfo: It is useful for rapid titration during hypertensive emergencies or intraoperatively.

text: For hypertensive emergency caused by catecholamine excess (e.g., pheochromocytoma or cocaine use), {{c1::Phentolamine}} is used.
extraInfo: It is a non-selective alpha-adrenergic antagonist.

text: In the setting of acute aortic dissection, the target systolic blood pressure is {{c1::100-120}} mmHg within 20 minutes.
extraInfo: This is an exception to the 'reduce MAP by 25%' rule.

text: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like nicardipine can cause {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} as a compensatory mechanism for rapid vasodilation.
extraInfo: This may be deleterious in patients with coronary artery disease.

text: Sodium {{c1::thiosulfate}} is administered to treat nitroprusside-induced cyanide toxicity by providing a sulfur donor for rhodanese.
extraInfo: Rhodanese converts cyanide to the less toxic thiocyanate.

text: Fenoldopam-induced vasodilation leads to a decrease in {{c1::potassium}} (hypokalemia) due to its effects on renal handling.
extraInfo: Potassium levels should be monitored during infusion.

text: Unlike other vasodilators, {{c1::Fenoldopam}} is specifically noted for its ability to maintain renal blood flow via {{c2::D1}} receptor activation.
extraInfo: Beneficial in hypertensive patients with renal insufficiency.

text: {{c1::Labetalol}} should be avoided in patients with {{c2::asthma}} or COPD due to its non-selective beta-blocking properties.
extraInfo: Beta-2 blockade can cause bronchoconstriction.

text: Intravenous {{c1::Enalaprilat}} is the active metabolite of enalapril and can be used in hypertensive emergencies, but it is contraindicated in {{c2::pregnancy}}.
extraInfo: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic.

text: Clevidipine is formulated in a {{c1::lipid emulsion}}, which provides approximately 2 kcal/mL of energy.
extraInfo: Caution is required in patients with egg or soy allergies or lipid metabolism disorders.

text: The primary mechanism of Hydralazine is the relaxation of {{c1::arteriolar}} smooth muscle more than venous smooth muscle.
extraInfo: This reduces afterload but causes significant reflex sympathetic activation.

text: In a patient with hypertensive emergency and cocaine toxicity, {{c1::Beta-blockers}} should never be given alone due to the risk of unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation.
extraInfo: This can lead to coronary vasoconstriction and extreme hypertension.

text: Hydralazine-induced reflex tachycardia can be offset by co-administration of a {{c1::beta-blocker}}.
extraInfo: This prevents the 'sympathetic surge' caused by vasodilation.

text: The IV-to-PO conversion for antihypertensives is initiated once the patient is stable and has been at the target BP for {{c1::24}} hours.
extraInfo: The transition should be gradual to avoid rebound hypertension.

text: Cyanide toxicity from nitroprusside can be identified by the presence of a {{c1::cherry-red}} skin color (though rare) and a 'bitter almond' odor on the breath.
extraInfo: Lactic acidosis is a more reliable laboratory finding.

text: {{c1::Nitroglycerin}} is the drug of choice for hypertensive emergency associated with {{c2::acute coronary syndrome}}.
extraInfo: It improves collateral blood flow to ischemic myocardium.

text: Nitrates cause a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in End-Diastolic Volume (EDV).
extraInfo: Venodilation reduces preload, leading to less blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole.

text: Nitrates cause a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in blood pressure.
extraInfo: This represents a reduction in afterload.

text: Nitrates cause a reflex {{c1::increase}} in heart rate.
extraInfo: Baroreceptor response to decreased blood pressure.

text: Nitrates cause a reflex {{c1::increase}} in contractility.
extraInfo: Sympathetic activation occurs in response to the drop in blood pressure.

text: Nitrates {{c1::decrease}} ejection time.
extraInfo: Reduced volume and afterload allow for faster ventricular emptying.

text: The primary goal of nitrate therapy is a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2).
extraInfo: Decreased preload is the main mechanism for lowering oxygen consumption.

text: Beta-blockers cause a(n) {{c1::increase}} in End-Diastolic Volume (EDV).
extraInfo: A slower heart rate increases the time available for diastolic filling.

text: Beta-blockers cause a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in blood pressure.
extraInfo: Reduced cardiac output and renin release contribute to lower BP.

text: Beta-blockers cause a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in contractility.
extraInfo: Negative inotropic effect reduces oxygen demand.

text: Beta-blockers cause a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in heart rate.
extraInfo: Negative chronotropic effect increases diastolic perfusion time but also increases EDV.

text: Beta-blockers {{c1::increase}} ejection time.
extraInfo: Decreased heart rate and contractility lengthen the time it takes to eject blood.

text: Beta-blockers cause a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in MVO2.
extraInfo: Reduced heart rate and contractility are the primary drivers of lower oxygen demand.

text: Combined Nitrates and Beta-blockers result in a(n) {{c1::decrease or no change}} in End-Diastolic Volume (EDV).
extraInfo: Nitrates (which decrease EDV) offset the effect of Beta-blockers (which increase EDV).

text: Combined Nitrates and Beta-blockers result in a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in blood pressure.
extraInfo: Both drug classes contribute to lowering afterload.

text: Combined Nitrates and Beta-blockers result in a(n) {{c1::decrease}} in heart rate.
extraInfo: Beta-blockers override and prevent the reflex tachycardia normally seen with nitrates.

text: Combined Nitrates and Beta-blockers result in {{c1::no change}} in contractility.
extraInfo: The reflex increase from nitrates and the negative inotropy of beta-blockers typically cancel each other out.

text: Combined Nitrates and Beta-blockers result in {{c1::no change}} in ejection time.
extraInfo: The decrease caused by nitrates and the increase caused by beta-blockers offset one another.

text: The greatest reduction in {{c1::MVO2 (myocardial oxygen demand)}} occurs with combined nitrate and beta-blocker therapy.
extraInfo: Synergistic effects on blood pressure and heart rate significantly lower oxygen needs.

text: Nitrates primarily work by causing {{c1::venodilation}}, which reduces preload.
extraInfo: High doses can also cause arterial dilation, but venodilation is the hallmark.

text: Beta-blockers increase EDV because a slower heart rate increases {{c1::diastolic filling time}}.
extraInfo: This is an adverse effect on oxygen demand that is usually outweighed by the benefit of a lower HR.

text: Non-dihydropyridines (e.g., Verapamil) have a hemodynamic profile similar to {{c1::Beta-blockers}}.
extraInfo: Both are negative inotropes and chronotropes.

text: Dihydropyridines (e.g., Nifedipine) have a hemodynamic profile similar to {{c1::Nitrates}}.
extraInfo: Both cause vasodilation and can lead to reflex tachycardia.

text: The main goal of antianginal therapy is to decrease {{c1::MVO2 (myocardial oxygen demand)}}.
extraInfo: This can be achieved by decreasing heart rate, contractility, afterload, or preload.

text: In combination therapy, Beta-blockers help prevent the reflex {{c1::tachycardia}} caused by Nitrates.
extraInfo: This is a key clinical benefit of combining these two classes.

text: In combination therapy, Nitrates help prevent the increase in {{c1::EDV (or preload)}} caused by Beta-blockers.
extraInfo: This neutralizing effect on ventricular wall tension helps further reduce MVO2.

text: Pindolol and Acebutolol should be avoided in angina because they are {{c1::partial agonists (intrinsic sympathomimetic activity)}}.
extraInfo: They can potentially increase heart rate and oxygen demand.

text: Ranolazine inhibits the {{c1::late sodium current}}, reducing diastolic wall tension.
extraInfo: This improves myocardial oxygen efficiency without affecting hemodynamics directly.

text: Unlike other antianginals, Ranolazine has no significant effect on {{c1::heart rate or blood pressure}}.
extraInfo: It is a purely metabolic/ion-channel focused antianginal.

text: Nitrates {{c1::decrease}} ejection time because they reduce afterload and preload.
extraInfo: Less volume to pump and less resistance allows for a shorter systolic phase.

text: Ranolazine inhibits the {{c1::late}} phase of the inward sodium current in myocardial cells.
extraInfo: This reduction in sodium entry prevents calcium overload.

text: By inhibiting the late sodium current, ranolazine reduces {{c1::diastolic}} wall tension.
extraInfo: This helps improve myocardial perfusion.

text: Ranolazine reduces myocardial {{c1::oxygen consumption (MVO2)}} without changing heart rate or BP.
extraInfo: It is unique among antianginals for its lack of hemodynamic effects.

text: Unlike beta-blockers or nitrates, ranolazine does NOT affect {{c1::heart rate}} or blood pressure.
extraInfo: This makes it useful in patients who are already hypotensive or bradycardic.

text: The primary clinical indication for ranolazine is {{c1::chronic stable angina}}.
extraInfo: It is often reserved for patients refractory to other medical therapies.

text: Ranolazine is often used for angina that is {{c1::refractory}} to first-line treatments.
extraInfo: First-line treatments include beta-blockers, CCBs, and nitrates.

text: Ranolazine decreases {{c1::calcium}} overload in myocardial cells by indirectly affecting the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.
extraInfo: Less intracellular Na+ leads to more Ca2+ efflux via the exchanger.

text: The gastrointestinal side effect of ranolazine highlighted in the text is {{c1::constipation}}.
extraInfo: It is listed alongside opioids, antimuscarinics, and non-DHP CCBs.

text: Ranolazine can cause dose-dependent {{c1::QT interval prolongation}} on ECG.
extraInfo: Despite this, it has a very low risk of causing Torsades de Pointes.

text: Ranolazine is metabolized by the {{c1::CYP3A4}} enzyme system.
extraInfo: Dosage adjustments or avoidance may be necessary with inhibitors/inducers.

text: Ranolazine is contraindicated in patients with significant {{c1::hepatic}} impairment.
extraInfo: Due to risk of increased plasma concentrations.

text: Ranolazine improves myocardial {{c1::perfusion}} by reducing diastolic wall stress.
extraInfo: Lower wall stress allows better blood flow through coronary vessels.

text: Common CNS side effects of ranolazine include {{c1::dizziness}} and headache.
extraInfo: These are generally mild and dose-related.

text: Ranolazine's effect on the heart is primarily on {{c1::lusitropy}} (diastolic relaxation).
extraInfo: It helps the heart relax more effectively during diastole.

text: Concurrent use of ranolazine with strong {{c1::CYP3A4 inhibitors}} like ketoconazole is contraindicated.
extraInfo: This would significantly increase ranolazine levels and toxicity risk.

text: Ischemic conditions cause an increase in the {{c1::late}} sodium current ($I_{Na}$).
extraInfo: Ranolazine specifically targets this pathological increase.

text: Accumulation of intracellular sodium during ischemia leads to calcium overload via the {{c1::reverse}} mode of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.
extraInfo: Ranolazine prevents this by blocking the sodium entry in the first place.

text: Ranolazine is classified as an {{c1::antianginal}} agent.
extraInfo: It belongs to its own class due to its unique mechanism.

text: Ranolazine does not significantly alter {{c1::blood pressure}}.
extraInfo: This differentiates it from CCBs and Nitrates.

text: Ranolazine is often utilized as {{c1::add-on}} therapy in patients already on beta-blockers.
extraInfo: It provides synergistic benefit without further lowering heart rate.

text: The 'late sodium current' blocked by ranolazine is denoted as {{c1::Ina}}.
extraInfo: Specifically the persistent or late component.

text: In myocardial cells, ranolazine decreases intracellular {{c1::sodium}} concentrations.
extraInfo: This is its primary direct effect.

text: Ranolazine's reduction of diastolic wall tension leads to a decrease in myocardial {{c1::wall stress}}.
extraInfo: Wall stress is a major determinant of oxygen demand.

text: Ranolazine has been shown to slightly reduce {{c1::HbA1c}} in diabetic patients with angina.
extraInfo: This is a secondary, minor clinical observation.

text: Ranolazine should be avoided in patients with a history of {{c1::long QT syndrome}}.
extraInfo: Due to its own potential to prolong the QT interval.

text: Ranolazine inhibits {{c1::P-glycoprotein}} (P-gp), which can increase levels of drugs like digoxin.
extraInfo: This is an important drug-drug interaction to monitor.

text: Ischemia-induced calcium overload contributes to {{c1::diastolic}} dysfunction.
extraInfo: Ranolazine mitigates this by regulating the Na+/Ca2+ balance.

text: The reduction in myocardial oxygen demand by ranolazine is due to decreased {{c1::tension}} during diastole.
extraInfo: Improved relaxation equals less energy used during the filling phase.

text: Ranolazine is categorized as a {{c1::late sodium current}} blocker.
extraInfo: This is its defining mechanistic classification for exams.

text: Sacubitril is a {{c1::neprilysin}} inhibitor.
extraInfo: Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase.

text: Neprilysin is a {{c1::metalloprotease}} that degrades natriuretic peptides, angiotensin II, and bradykinin.
extraInfo: Inhibition increases levels of these substances.

text: Sacubitril is used in combination with the ARB {{c1::valsartan}}.
extraInfo: This combination is known as an ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor).

text: The combination of sacubitril and valsartan is used to treat {{c1::HFrEF}} (Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction).
extraInfo: It is often used in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB alone.

text: Sacubitril prevents the degradation of {{c1::ANP}}, {{c2::BNP}}, and {{c3::bradykinin}}.
extraInfo: Increased ANP and BNP lead to vasodilation and natriuresis.

text: Neprilysin inhibition leads to increased levels of {{c1::cyclic GMP}} (cGMP) in vascular smooth muscle.
extraInfo: This results from increased natriuretic peptide activity on guanylyl cyclase.

text: Sacubitril must be paired with an ARB because neprilysin also degrades {{c1::angiotensin II}}.
extraInfo: Without an ARB, the increase in Angiotensin II would cause unwanted vasoconstriction.

text: A major side effect of sacubitril/valsartan is {{c1::angioedema}}.
extraInfo: This is largely due to increased bradykinin levels.

text: When switching from an ACE inhibitor to an ARNI, a {{c1::36}}-hour washout period is required.
extraInfo: This reduces the risk of severe angioedema.

text: Sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated in patients with a history of {{c1::angioedema}} related to prior ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy.
extraInfo: The risk of recurrence is high.

text: Sacubitril/valsartan can cause {{c1::hyperkalemia}}, similar to ACE inhibitors.
extraInfo: Potassium levels should be monitored regularly.

text: Sacubitril increases the level of {{c1::BNP}}, rendering it less useful as a heart failure biomarker.
extraInfo: BNP will be elevated due to the drug mechanism, not necessarily worsening failure.

text: The biomarker {{c1::NT-proBNP}} should be used to monitor heart failure in patients taking sacubitril.
extraInfo: NT-proBNP is not a substrate for neprilysin and remains an accurate indicator.

text: Sacubitril/valsartan decreases both {{c1::preload}} and {{c2::afterload}}.
extraInfo: This improves cardiac output and reduces myocardial oxygen demand.

text: Neprilysin also plays a role in the degradation of {{c1::amyloid-beta}} in the brain.
extraInfo: There are theoretical concerns about its long-term effects on cognitive function.

text: Sacubitril is a {{c1::prodrug}} that is activated to sacubitrilat.
extraInfo: Activation occurs via esterases.

text: Inhibition of neprilysin promotes {{c1::natriuresis}} and {{c2::diuresis}}.
extraInfo: This helps alleviate fluid overload in heart failure.

text: Common side effects of sacubitril/valsartan include {{c1::hypotension}} and increased serum creatinine.
extraInfo: Renal function and blood pressure must be monitored.

text: The primary mechanism by which natriuretic peptides reduce blood pressure is via {{c1::vasodilation}}.
extraInfo: This is mediated by the cGMP pathway.

text: ARNI therapy reduces the risk of {{c1::cardiovascular death}} and hospitalization in HFrEF compared to ACE inhibitors.
extraInfo: Based on the PARADIGM-HF trial data.

text: Neprilysin is also known as {{c1::neutral endopeptidase}} (NEP) or CD10.
extraInfo: CD10 is also a marker used in the diagnosis of certain leukemias (ALL).

text: Sacubitril/valsartan is recommended for patients with {{c1::NYHA Class II-IV}} heart failure.
extraInfo: Especially those who remain symptomatic on standard therapy.

text: Sacubitril/valsartan should not be co-administered with {{c1::aliskiren}} in patients with diabetes.
extraInfo: This increases the risk of renal impairment and hyperkalemia.

text: The use of sacubitril/valsartan leads to a reduction in {{c1::cardiac remodeling}}.
extraInfo: The reduction in wall stress helps prevent the progression of heart failure.

text: In the context of ARNI, 'A' stands for {{c1::Angiotensin}}, 'R' for {{c2::Receptor}}, 'N' for {{c3::Neprilysin}}, and 'I' for {{c4::Inhibitor}}.
extraInfo: Standard terminology for the drug class.

text: Sacubitril/valsartan is avoided in pregnancy because {{c1::valsartan}} is teratogenic.
extraInfo: ARBs can cause fetal renal dysgenesis and skull hypoplasia.

text: Sacubitril specifically inhibits the enzyme that breaks down {{c1::substance P}} and bradykinin.
extraInfo: The accumulation of these peptides contributes to the side effect of cough.

text: Neprilysin inhibition causes an increase in {{c1::urinary cyclic GMP}} excretion.
extraInfo: This can be used as a marker of the drug's biological effect.

text: The benefit of sacubitril/valsartan over ACE inhibitors is largely due to the sustained effects of {{c1::natriuretic peptides}}.
extraInfo: These counteract the RAAS and sympathetic nervous systems.

text: Statins inhibit the enzyme {{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}}, which is the rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis.
extraInfo: This leads to increased LDL receptor expression on hepatocytes.

text: Statins are known to decrease {{c1::mortality}} in patients with Coronary Artery Disease (CAD).
extraInfo: They are the first-line treatment for hypercholesterolemia.

text: Two major adverse effects of statins are {{c1::hepatotoxicity (increased LFTs)}} and {{c2::myopathy}}.
extraInfo: Myopathy risk increases when used with fibrates or niacin.

text: Bile acid resins like {{c1::cholestyramine}}, colestipol, and colesevelam work by disrupting {{c2::enterohepatic}} bile acid circulation.
extraInfo: This forces the liver to use more cholesterol to synthesize new bile acids.

text: A unique side effect of bile acid resins is a slight increase in {{c1::triglycerides}}.
extraInfo: They also cause GI upset and decreased absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

text: Bile acid resins can impair the absorption of {{c1::fat-soluble vitamins}} (A, D, E, K).
extraInfo: They also interfere with the absorption of other drugs like warfarin or digoxin.

text: Ezetimibe prevents cholesterol absorption at the {{c1::small intestine brush border}}.
extraInfo: It specifically targets the NPC1L1 transporter.

text: The primary effect of Ezetimibe is to decrease {{c1::LDL}} levels.
extraInfo: It has a minimal effect on HDL and Triglycerides.

text: Fibrates (e.g., gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) activate {{c1::PPAR-̡̑}} to upregulate {{c2::lipoprotein lipase (LPL)}}.
extraInfo: Upregulating LPL increases triglyceride clearance.

text: The primary lipid profile change seen with fibrates is a massive decrease in {{c1::triglycerides}}.
extraInfo: They are the drug of choice for severe hypertriglyceridemia.

text: Fibrates can cause {{c1::cholesterol gallstones}} by inhibiting the enzyme {{c2::cholesterol 7̡̑-hydroxylase}}.
extraInfo: Inhibition of this enzyme decreases bile acid synthesis, increasing cholesterol saturation in bile.

text: Niacin (Vitamin B3) inhibits {{c1::hormone-sensitive lipase}} in adipose tissue, reducing the breakdown of triglycerides to {{c2::free fatty acids}}.
extraInfo: This leads to decreased hepatic VLDL synthesis.

text: Niacin's most potent effect on the lipid profile is increasing {{c1::HDL}}.
extraInfo: It is often used when HDL is low despite other therapies.

text: The side effect of 'flushed face' caused by niacin is mediated by {{c1::prostaglandins}} and can be reduced by {{c2::NSAIDs (aspirin)}}.
extraInfo: Taking aspirin 30 minutes before niacin can blunt this effect.

text: Niacin can lead to {{c1::hyperuricemia}} (which can trigger gout) and {{c2::hyperglycemia}}.
extraInfo: Use with caution in patients with diabetes or gout.

text: PCSK9 inhibitors like {{c1::alirocumab}} and {{c2::evolocumab}} work by inactivating LDL-receptor degradation.
extraInfo: This significantly increases the removal of LDL from the bloodstream.

text: The primary adverse effects of PCSK9 inhibitors include myalgias, delirium, and {{c1::dementia/neurocognitive effects}}.
extraInfo: They are highly effective but administered via injection.

text: Fish oil and omega-3 fatty acids are used at high doses to primarily decrease {{c1::triglycerides}}.
extraInfo: They are believed to decrease FFA delivery to the liver.

text: HMG-CoA is converted to {{c1::mevalonate}} by the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase.
extraInfo: This is the pharmacologic target of statins.

text: In the liver, fibrates induce {{c1::HDL}} synthesis through PPAR-̡̑ activation.
extraInfo: Though their primary goal is triglyceride reduction, they do provide a mild HDL boost.

text: Bile acid resins cause the liver to increase the conversion of {{c1::cholesterol}} into {{c2::bile acids}}.
extraInfo: This depletes intrahepatic cholesterol, leading to compensatory LDL receptor upregulation.

text: The drug class that carries a risk of myopathy, especially when used in combination with statins, is {{c1::fibrates}}.
extraInfo: Gemfibrozil is particularly noted for this interaction.

text: Which lipid-lowering agent causes a fishlike taste? {{c1::Fish oil/Omega-3 fatty acids}}.
extraInfo: Often used as a supplement to lower high TG levels.

text: Niacin reduces the hepatic synthesis of {{c1::VLDL}}.
extraInfo: VLDL is the precursor to LDL, contributing to the overall lowering of LDL as well.

text: Statins increase LDL catabolism by {{c1::increasing LDL receptor}} expression.
extraInfo: This is a response to low intrahepatic cholesterol levels.

text: Which drug prevents the degradation of LDL receptors? {{c1::PCSK9 inhibitors}}.
extraInfo: Examples: Alirocumab and Evolocumab.

text: Ezetimibe primarily affects the {{c1::intestinal lumen/enterocyte}} interface to block cholesterol uptake.
extraInfo: It does not affect the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, unlike bile acid resins.

text: Myopathy from statins is typically characterized by an increase in {{c1::creatine kinase (CK)}} levels.
extraInfo: Patients present with muscle pain and weakness.

text: Statins decrease {{c1::intrahepatic}} cholesterol, which triggers the upregulation of {{c2::LDL receptors}}.
extraInfo: This feedback mechanism is what results in the lowering of serum LDL.

text: Digoxin works by directly inhibiting the {{c1::Na+/K+ -ATPase}} pump.
extraInfo: This pump is located in the plasma membrane with the ATP binding site on the cytosolic side.

text: The inhibition of the Na+/K+ -ATPase by Digoxin leads to an {{c1::indirect}} inhibition of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.
extraInfo: Decreased Na+ gradient reduces the driving force for the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.

text: Digoxin ultimately results in {{c1::increased}} intracellular [Ca2+], which leads to increased cardiac contractility.
extraInfo: Increased intracellular calcium allows for more calcium to be taken up by the sarcoplasmic reticulum for subsequent release.

text: Digoxin acts as a {{c1::positive}} inotrope and a {{c2::negative}} chronotrope.
extraInfo: Inotropy refers to contractility; chronotropy refers to heart rate.

text: Digoxin binds to the {{c1::extracellular}} (potassium-binding) site of the Na+/K+ -ATPase.
extraInfo: It competes with potassium for this specific binding site.

text: The stoichiometry of the Na+/K+ pump is: {{c1::2}} K+ in and {{c2::3}} Na+ out per ATP consumed.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: 2 strikes? K, you're still IN. 3 strikes? Na-h, you're OUT!

text: Digoxin stimulates the {{c1::vagus}} nerve, leading to decreased heart rate.
extraInfo: This parasympathomimetic effect is useful for slowing the heart rate in atrial fibrillation.

text: The primary clinical indications for Digoxin are {{c1::heart failure (HFrEF)}} and {{c2::atrial fibrillation}}.
extraInfo: In HF, it provides symptomatic relief; in AFib, it provides rate control.

text: Digoxin toxicity is classically associated with {{c1::blurry yellow vision}} (xanthopsia).
extraInfo: Other visual changes include flickering lights or halos.

text: The most common ECG change associated with therapeutic Digoxin use is the {{c1::scooped ST segment}}.
extraInfo: This is often called the 'Digoxin effect' and is not necessarily a sign of toxicity.

text: {{c1::Hypokalemia}} predisposes a patient to Digoxin toxicity.
extraInfo: Since K+ and Digoxin compete for the same pump binding site, less K+ means more Digoxin can bind.

text: Acute Digoxin overdose typically results in {{c1::hyperkalemia}}.
extraInfo: Widespread inhibition of Na+/K+ pumps prevents K+ from entering cells, raising serum levels.

text: Digoxin is primarily eliminated via the {{c1::kidneys}}.
extraInfo: Dose adjustments are required in patients with renal insufficiency.

text: The specific antidote for life-threatening Digoxin toxicity is {{c1::Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab)}}.
extraInfo: Indicated for severe arrhythmias or significant hyperkalemia.

text: The most common cardiac arrhythmia seen in Digoxin toxicity is {{c1::premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)}}.
extraInfo: Virtually any arrhythmia can occur, but PVCs are the most frequent.

text: A highly specific (pathognomonic) arrhythmia for Digoxin toxicity is {{c1::bidirectional ventricular tachycardia}}.
extraInfo: This is a rare but classic boards-style finding.

text: Drugs that can increase Digoxin levels by displacing it from tissue binding sites include {{c1::Quinidine, Amiodarone, and Verapamil}}.
extraInfo: These drugs also decrease renal clearance of Digoxin.

text: Besides potassium, low levels of {{c1::magnesium}} can also predispose to Digoxin toxicity.
extraInfo: Hypomagnesemia increases the risk of Digoxin-induced arrhythmias.

text: Digoxin does NOT improve {{c1::mortality}} in patients with heart failure.
extraInfo: It only reduces hospitalizations and improves symptoms.

text: GI symptoms of Digoxin toxicity include {{c1::nausea, vomiting, and anorexia}}.
extraInfo: These are often the earliest signs of toxicity.

text: Digoxin causes {{c1::prolongation}} of the PR interval on ECG.
extraInfo: This is due to increased vagal tone slowing conduction through the AV node.

text: Digoxin causes {{c1::shortening}} of the QT interval on ECG.
extraInfo: This reflects shortened ventricular action potential duration.

text: Digoxin has a {{c1::narrow}} therapeutic index.
extraInfo: Therapeutic levels are typically 0.5-2.0 ng/mL.

text: In the Na+/K+ pump, the pump is {{c1::phosphorylated}} when 3 Na+ are moved out.
extraInfo: The pump is dephosphorylated when 2 K+ are moved in.

text: The use of {{c1::loop diuretics}} can increase the risk of Digoxin toxicity by causing hypokalemia.
extraInfo: Furosemide and Bumetanide are common culprits.

text: Digoxin-induced hypercalcemia can lead to increased risk of {{c1::arrhythmias}}.
extraInfo: Calcium overload in the myocytes triggers afterdepolarizations.

text: Neurological side effects of Digoxin toxicity include {{c1::confusion and hallucinations}}.
extraInfo: Particularly common in elderly patients.

text: The Na+/K+ -ATPase pump uses energy from the hydrolysis of {{c1::ATP}}.
extraInfo: This is an example of primary active transport.

text: Cholinergic effects of Digoxin (nausea/vomiting/diarrhea) are often described as {{c1::parasympathomimetic}}.
extraInfo: It mimics the action of the parasympathetic nervous system.

text: Class I antiarrhythmics work by blocking {{c1::sodium (Na+)}} channels.
extraInfo: They decrease the slope of phase 0 depolarization.

text: Class I antiarrhythmics decrease the slope of {{c1::phase 0}} depolarization.
extraInfo: Phase 0 is the rapid upstroke caused by Na+ influx.

text: Class I agents are state-dependent, meaning they bind more effectively to {{c1::open or inactivated}} channels.
extraInfo: This makes them more effective in rapidly firing tissues.

text: The three Class IA antiarrhythmic drugs are {{c1::Quinidine, Procainamide, and Disopyramide}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: The Queen Proclaims Diso's pyramid.

text: Class IA agents provide moderate Na+ channel blockade and also block {{c1::potassium (K+)}} channels.
extraInfo: K+ channel block is responsible for prolonging the action potential.

text: Class IA antiarrhythmics {{c1::increase}} the effective refractory period (ERP) and action potential duration (APD).
extraInfo: This is due to the combined Na+ and K+ channel block.

text: On an EKG, Class IA antiarrhythmics cause a prolonged {{c1::QT}} interval.
extraInfo: Prolonged QT is a result of delayed repolarization.

text: Class IA drugs are used to treat both {{c1::atrial and ventricular}} arrhythmias.
extraInfo: They are broad-spectrum antiarrhythmics.

text: {{c1::Quinidine}} is associated with cinchonism, which includes headache and tinnitus.
extraInfo: Cinchonism is a classic high-yield side effect.

text: A unique side effect of procainamide is a reversible {{c1::systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)}}-like syndrome.
extraInfo: Look for anti-histone antibodies.

text: Disopyramide can exacerbate {{c1::heart failure}} because of its negative inotropic effects.
extraInfo: It has significant anticholinergic side effects as well.

text: Due to their effect on the QT interval, Class IA drugs can cause {{c1::Torsades de Pointes}}.
extraInfo: Torsades is a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

text: The Class IB antiarrhythmic drugs include {{c1::Lidocaine and Mexiletine}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: I'd Buy Liddy's Mexican Tacos.

text: Class IB agents are characterized by {{c1::weak}} sodium channel blockade.
extraInfo: They rapidly dissociate from the receptor.

text: Unlike Class IA, Class IB agents {{c1::shorten (decrease)}} the action potential duration.
extraInfo: They have the least effect on the EKG at normal heart rates.

text: Class IB agents preferentially bind to Na+ channels in {{c1::ischemic or depolarized}} tissue.
extraInfo: This makes them highly effective post-myocardial infarction.

text: Class IB drugs are primarily used for {{c1::ventricular}} arrhythmias, especially those occurring post-MI.
extraInfo: They have no efficacy against supraventricular arrhythmias.

text: High doses of Class IB agents (like Lidocaine) can cause {{c1::CNS}} toxicity, such as seizures.
extraInfo: CNS effects are the most common dose-limiting toxicity.

text: The Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs are {{c1::Flecainide and Propafenone}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: Can I have Fries Please.

text: Class IC agents cause {{c1::strong}} sodium channel blockade.
extraInfo: They have the slowest dissociation from the sodium channel.

text: Class IC agents have {{c1::minimal (no)}} effect on the action potential duration (APD).
extraInfo: They do not block potassium channels significantly.

text: Class IC agents significantly prolong the ERP in the {{c1::AV node}} and accessory bypass tracts.
extraInfo: This makes them useful for SVTs like Wolff-Parkinson-White.

text: Class IC agents are used for supraventricular tachycardias, including {{c1::atrial fibrillation}}.
extraInfo: They are often used for rhythm control.

text: Class IC agents are contraindicated in patients with {{c1::structural}} heart disease or recent MI.
extraInfo: This is due to high proarrhythmic risk in these patients.

text: The proarrhythmic potential of Class IC drugs was highlighted in the {{c1::CAST}} trial.
extraInfo: The trial showed increased mortality in post-MI patients taking flecainide.

text: The order of Na+ channel binding strength (and use-dependence) is {{c1::IC > IA > IB}}.
extraInfo: 1C binds most tightly and 1B least tightly.

text: Use-dependence means Class I antiarrhythmics are more effective at {{c1::faster}} heart rates.
extraInfo: Sodium channels spend more time in the open/inactivated state at high rates.

text: {{c1::Slow}} acetylators are at a higher risk of developing drug-induced SLE from procainamide.
extraInfo: Acetylation is the primary metabolic pathway for procainamide.

text: Class IB agents are also useful in treating arrhythmias induced by {{c1::digitalis (digoxin)}}.
extraInfo: Digitalis toxicity often causes ventricular irritability.

text: Class II antiarrhythmics consist of the {{c1::̢β-blockers}}.
extraInfo: Examples include metoprolol, propranolol, esmolol, atenolol, and timolol.

text: Class II antiarrhythmics primarily affect the {{c1::SA}} and {{c2::AV}} nodes.
extraInfo: They decrease the slope of phase 4 depolarization in these pacemaker tissues.

text: The cellular mechanism of β-blockers involves decreasing {{c1::cAMP}} and decreasing {{c2::Ca2+}} currents.
extraInfo: This results from blocking β1-receptors on cardiac myocytes and pacemaker cells.

text: In the pacemaker action potential, β-blockers suppress Phase {{c1::4}} depolarization.
extraInfo: This leads to a decreased heart rate (negative chronotropy).

text: On an ECG, Class II antiarrhythmics are known to {{c1::increase}} the PR interval.
extraInfo: This is due to slowed conduction through the AV node.

text: {{c1::Esmolol}} is an ultra-short-acting β-blocker used for acute arrhythmia control.
extraInfo: It is typically administered intravenously.

text: Class II antiarrhythmics are used for rate control in {{c1::atrial fibrillation}} and {{c2::atrial flutter}}.
extraInfo: By slowing AV node conduction, they prevent rapid ventricular response.

text: Class II antiarrhythmics reduce mortality following a {{c1::myocardial infarction (MI)}}.
extraInfo: They prevent sudden cardiac death and reduce myocardial oxygen demand.

text: The sexual side effect commonly associated with β-blocker use is {{c1::impotence (erectile dysfunction)}}.
extraInfo: This is a frequent reason for patient non-compliance.

text: β-blockers can exacerbate respiratory conditions like {{c1::asthma}} and {{c2::COPD}}.
extraInfo: This occurs due to β2-receptor blockade causing bronchoconstriction.

text: In patients with diabetes, β-blockers can {{c1::mask}} the symptoms of hypoglycemia.
extraInfo: They block the adrenergic symptoms of low blood sugar, such as tachycardia and tremors, though sweating usually remains.

text: In the setting of cocaine toxicity, β-blockers can cause {{c1::unopposed α-adrenergic}} stimulation.
extraInfo: This can lead to severe hypertension and coronary vasospasm.

text: The specific antidote for β-blocker overdose is {{c1::glucagon}}.
extraInfo: Glucagon increases cAMP in cardiac myocytes via a different pathway than β-receptors.

text: Metoprolol and Atenolol are classified as {{c1::β1-selective}} antagonists.
extraInfo: These are often preferred in patients with pulmonary disease to minimize β2-mediated bronchospasm.

text: Propranolol and Nadolol are classified as {{c1::non-selective}} β-blockers.
extraInfo: They block both β1 and β2 receptors.

text: Labetalol and Carvedilol are unique because they provide both {{c1::α1}} and {{c2::β}} receptor blockade.
extraInfo: This makes them useful in hypertensive emergencies and chronic heart failure.

text: Class II antiarrhythmics increase the {{c1::refractory period}} of the AV node.
extraInfo: This protects the ventricles from high atrial rates.

text: By slowing the heart rate, β-blockers increase {{c1::diastolic filling time}}.
extraInfo: This can improve coronary artery perfusion, which occurs primarily during diastole.

text: Cardiovascular side effects of Class II drugs include {{c1::bradycardia}}, {{c2::heart block}}, and {{c3::heart failure}} exacerbation.
extraInfo: These result from negative chronotropic and inotropic effects.

text: CNS side effects of β-blockers, particularly lipophilic ones, include {{c1::sedation}}, {{c2::sleep disturbances}}, and {{c3::vivid dreams}}.
extraInfo: Propranolol is highly lipophilic and crosses the blood-brain barrier easily.

text: Class II antiarrhythmics are used to treat {{c1::hyperthyroidism}} associated tachycardias.
extraInfo: Propranolol also inhibits the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

text: The major clinical utility of Class II drugs in the context of SVT is {{c1::rate control}}.
extraInfo: They are usually not first-line for rhythm control but are essential for managing ventricular response.

text: In the SA node, β1 blockade decreases the activity of {{c1::adenylyl cyclase}}.
extraInfo: This leads to lower cAMP levels and reduced protein kinase A activity.

text: β-blockers decrease the slope of the {{c1::pacemaker potential}}.
extraInfo: This is the slow depolarization phase driven by If (funny current) and Ca2+ currents.

text: Metoprolol has been shown to decrease mortality in patients with {{c1::chronic heart failure}}.
extraInfo: Bisoprolol and carvedilol are also used for this indication.

text: Use of β-blockers should be avoided in {{c1::Prinzmetal (variant) angina}}.
extraInfo: Similar to cocaine toxicity, it can cause unopposed alpha-mediated coronary vasospasm.

text: β-blockers cause an increase in the {{c1::Effective Refractory Period (ERP)}} at the AV node.
extraInfo: This explains their efficacy in terminating re-entrant tachycardias involving the AV node.

text: A common clinical use for Timolol is the topical treatment of {{c1::glaucoma}}.
extraInfo: It decreases the production of aqueous humor.

text: The β-blocker that is considered a Class III antiarrhythmic due to its K+ channel blocking properties is {{c1::Sotalol}}.
extraInfo: However, it still possesses significant Class II (β-blocking) activity.

text: Class IV antiarrhythmics primarily consist of {{c1::Verapamil}} and {{c2::Diltiazem}}.
The mechanism of Class IV antiarrhythmics involves the blockade of {{c1::L-type}} calcium channels.
extraInfo: These channels are responsible for the upstroke in pacemaker cells.

text: Class IV antiarrhythmics act primarily on the {{c1::SA}} and {{c2::AV}} nodes.
Class IV antiarrhythmics {{c1::decrease}} the slope of Phase 4 spontaneous depolarization in pacemaker cells.
Class IV antiarrhythmics {{c1::decrease}} conduction velocity at the AV node.
Class IV antiarrhythmics {{c1::increase}} the effective refractory period (ERP).
On an ECG, Class IV antiarrhythmics lead to an increased {{c1::PR interval}}.
extraInfo: This reflects the slowed conduction through the AV node.

text: {{c1::Verapamil}} is more selective for the heart compared to the peripheral vasculature.
{{c1::Verapamil}} is the Class IV antiarrhythmic most commonly associated with constipation.
Class IV antiarrhythmics are used for {{c1::rate}} control in atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter.
Class IV antiarrhythmics are effective for the prevention or termination of {{c1::paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT)}}.
A common dermatological/dental adverse effect of calcium channel blockers is {{c1::gingival hyperplasia}}.
Class IV antiarrhythmics cause {{c1::bradycardia}} due to their action on the SA node.
High doses or toxicity of Class IV antiarrhythmics can result in {{c1::AV block}}.
Class IV antiarrhythmics should generally be avoided in patients with {{c1::HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction)}}.
extraInfo: Due to their negative inotropic effects.

text: In pacemaker cells, Class IV antiarrhythmics decrease the slope of Phase {{c1::0}} (the upstroke).
extraInfo: In pacemaker cells, Phase 0 is calcium-dependent.

text: Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (Class IVs) have significant {{c1::negative}} inotropic effects.
Compared to dihydropyridines, non-dihydropyridines like Verapamil have a {{c1::greater}} effect on the heart.
A common side effect of non-dihydropyridines is peripheral {{c1::edema}}.
Class IV antiarrhythmics {{c1::prolong}} repolarization at the AV node.
Verapamil can cause {{c1::hyperprolactinemia}} by blocking calcium channels in the pituitary.
Verapamil is often contraindicated in patients with {{c1::Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW)}} syndrome who have atrial fibrillation.
extraInfo: It may facilitate conduction down the accessory pathway.

text: Class IV antiarrhythmics slow the firing rate of the {{c1::SA node}}.
{{c1::Diltiazem}} has intermediate selectivity between vascular smooth muscle and the heart.
Class IV antiarrhythmics are specifically used to treat {{c1::supraventricular}} tachycardias, rather than ventricular ones.
The primary ion whose entry is blocked by Class IV drugs is {{c1::calcium (Ca2+)}}.
Class IV antiarrhythmics are known as {{c1::non-dihydropyridine}} calcium channel blockers.
By slowing the AV node, Class IVs {{c1::increase}} the time available for ventricular filling in tachycardia.
{{c1::Verapamil}} is the drug of choice for managing re-entrant supraventricular tachycardias.
Class III antiarrhythmics (K+ channel blockers) include: {{c1::Amiodarone, Ibutilide, Dofetilide, and Sotalol}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: AIDS.

text: Class III antiarrhythmics work primarily by blocking {{c1::potassium (K+)}} channels.
extraInfo: This occurs during the repolarization phase of the cardiac action potential.

text: By blocking K+ channels, Class III drugs delay {{c1::repolarization}} (Phase 3).
Class III antiarrhythmics increase Action Potential Duration (APD) and {{c1::Effective Refractory Period (ERP)}}.
On an ECG, Class III antiarrhythmics cause a prolongation of the {{c1::QT interval}}.
extraInfo: Because they prolong the time for ventricular repolarization.

text: {{c1::Amiodarone}} is unique because it possesses Class I, II, III, and IV actions.
extraInfo: It is the most effective but has the most side effects.

text: Unlike other Class III agents, {{c1::Amiodarone}} is associated with a low risk of Torsades de Pointes.
extraInfo: Despite significantly prolonging the QT interval.

text: {{c1::Sotalol}} is a Class III antiarrhythmic that also has non-selective {{c2::β-blocking}} properties.
Sotalol carries a high risk of causing the arrhythmia {{c1::Torsades de Pointes}}.
extraInfo: Requires close monitoring of the QT interval.

text: {{c1::Ibutilide}} is typically used for the acute chemical cardioversion of atrial fibrillation or flutter.
{{c1::Dofetilide}} is a Class III agent primarily used for the maintenance of {{c2::sinus rhythm}} in patients with atrial fibrillation.
Amiodarone contains {{c1::iodine}}, which contributes to its effects on the thyroid gland.
extraInfo: It is about 40% iodine by weight.

text: Amiodarone can cause either {{c1::hypothyroidism}} or {{c2::hyperthyroidism}}.
extraInfo: Due to the iodine content and the Wolff-Chaikoff or Jod-Basedow effects.

text: The most serious and potentially lethal adverse effect of amiodarone is {{c1::pulmonary fibrosis}}.
extraInfo: Regular check-ups include chest X-rays and PFTs.

text: Patients on chronic amiodarone may develop a characteristic {{c1::blue-gray}} skin discoloration.
extraInfo: Occurs in sun-exposed areas (photosensitivity).

text: Amiodarone commonly causes {{c1::corneal}} microdeposits, though they rarely impair vision.
extraInfo: Usually seen on slit-lamp exam.

text: Amiodarone is highly {{c1::lipophilic}}, leading to an exceptionally long half-life.
extraInfo: Half-life can be 40–60 days, requiring a loading dose.

text: Because it inhibits {{c1::CYP450}} enzymes, amiodarone can increase serum levels of digoxin and warfarin.
Amiodarone can cause {{c1::hepatotoxicity}}, so LFTs should be checked before and during treatment.
Class III antiarrhythmics act during Phase {{c1::3}} of the myocardial action potential.
{{c1::Sotalol}} is contraindicated or requires significant dose adjustment in patients with renal insufficiency.
Neurological side effects of amiodarone include {{c1::tremor, ataxia, and peripheral neuropathy}}.
Class III antiarrhythmics are used for rhythm control in {{c1::atrial fibrillation}}, atrial flutter, and ventricular tachycardia.
Class III drugs increase the refractory period in the atrium, ventricle, and {{c1::Purkinje}} system.
Cardiovascular side effects of amiodarone include {{c1::bradycardia}} and heart block.
The 'S' in the mnemonic AIDS for Class III drugs refers to {{c1::Sotalol}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic: Amiodarone, Ibutilide, Dofetilide, Sotalol.

text: Routine monitoring for chronic amiodarone use includes {{c1::PFTs, LFTs, and TFTs}}.
extraInfo: PFT = Pulmonary, LFT = Liver, TFT = Thyroid.

text: In patients taking sotalol, the {{c1::QT interval}} must be monitored to ensure it does not exceed 500 ms.
Common gastrointestinal side effects of amiodarone include {{c1::constipation}} and nausea.
Adenosine increases {{c1::K+}} efflux out of cells, which leads to {{c2::hyperpolarization}}.
extraInfo: This decreases the calcium current, ultimately slowing AV node conduction.

text: Adenosine is the drug of choice for diagnosing and abolishing {{c1::supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)}}.
extraInfo: It is preferred due to its high efficacy and very short duration of action.

text: Adenosine has an extremely short half-life of less than {{c1::15}} seconds.
extraInfo: Because of this, it must be administered as a rapid IV bolus.

text: The effects of adenosine are antagonized by {{c1::theophylline}} and {{c2::caffeine}}.
extraInfo: These substances act as adenosine receptor antagonists.

text: A common respiratory adverse effect of adenosine is {{c1::bronchospasm}}.
extraInfo: It should be used with caution in patients with asthma or COPD.

text: Common side effects of adenosine include {{c1::flushing}}, hypotension, and chest pain.
extraInfo: The chest pain is often described as a 'sense of impending doom'.

text: Adenosine primarily acts on the {{c1::AV node}} to decrease conduction velocity.
extraInfo: It causes a transient high-grade heart block.

text: Magnesium is the first-line treatment for {{c1::Torsades de pointes}}.
extraInfo: It is also used for arrhythmias caused by digoxin toxicity.

text: Magnesium acts as a {{c1::physiological calcium channel blocker}}.
extraInfo: It helps stabilize the cardiac cell membrane.

text: Ivabradine works by selective inhibition of {{c1::funny sodium channels (If)}}.
extraInfo: These channels are primarily found in the SA node.

text: Ivabradine prolongs SA node {{c1::phase 4}} depolarization.
extraInfo: This results in a decrease in heart rate.

text: Ivabradine decreases heart rate without affecting cardiac {{c1::contractility (inotropy)}} or {{c2::relaxation (lusitropy)}}.
extraInfo: This makes it useful in heart failure where preserving squeeze is vital.

text: A unique visual side effect of Ivabradine is {{c1::luminous phenomena (phosphenes)}}.
extraInfo: Patients may report enhanced brightness in certain parts of their visual field.

text: Ivabradine is indicated for patients with chronic {{c1::HFrEF}} who have a resting heart rate ≥ 70 bpm.
extraInfo: It is used to reduce the risk of hospitalization.

text: Ivabradine can be used for chronic stable angina in patients who cannot tolerate {{c1::beta-blockers}}.
extraInfo: It provides heart rate reduction similar to beta-blockers without the systemic side effects.

text: Besides luminous phenomena, other side effects of Ivabradine include {{c1::bradycardia}} and {{c2::hypertension}}.
extraInfo: The bradycardia is a direct extension of its mechanism of action on the SA node.

text: Adenosine is not effective for converting {{c1::atrial fibrillation}} or {{c2::atrial flutter}}.
extraInfo: It may help in diagnosing these rhythms by slowing the rate to reveal the underlying atrial activity.

text: Adenosine activates {{c1::A1}} receptors in the heart.
extraInfo: This G-protein coupled receptor activation leads to the opening of K+ channels.

text: The specific form of magnesium used for antiarrhythmic treatment is {{c1::magnesium sulfate}}.
extraInfo: It is usually given intravenously.

text: Adenosine decreases {{c1::cAMP}}, which contributes to its effect of decreasing Ca2+ current.
extraInfo: Lower cAMP levels lead to decreased activity of protein kinase A.

text: Because it is so short-acting, adenosine is the preferred agent for {{c1::chemical stress testing}}.
extraInfo: It causes coronary vasodilation to help identify areas of ischemia.

text: Adenosine's 'sense of impending doom' is a transient feeling often occurring within {{c1::seconds}} of administration.
extraInfo: Reassurance to the patient before administration is key.

text: Ivabradine specifically targets the {{c1::SA node}} and has no effect on the AV node or ventricular conduction.
extraInfo: This distinguishes it from other rate-control agents like beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine CCBs.

text: Dipyridamole {{c1::increases}} the effects of adenosine by inhibiting its uptake.
extraInfo: Dose reduction of adenosine may be necessary if the patient is on dipyridamole.

text: Magnesium is used in digoxin toxicity especially when it is associated with {{c1::hypomagnesemia}}.
extraInfo: Magnesium deficiency can exacerbate digoxin-induced arrhythmias.

text: Adenosine is contraindicated in patients with {{c1::2nd or 3rd}} degree heart block.
extraInfo: Except in patients with a functioning artificial pacemaker.

text: Ivabradine is contraindicated in patients with clinically significant {{c1::bradycardia}}.
extraInfo: Starting ivabradine in a patient with a slow heart rate can cause dangerously low rates.

text: Adenosine causes a rapid, temporary cessation of {{c1::AV nodal}} conduction.
extraInfo: This 'breaks' the re-entrant circuit in AVNRT.

text: Ivabradine's effect on If channels results in a {{c1::slower}} slope of the pacemaker potential.
extraInfo: This increases the time between action potentials, lowering the heart rate.
